# Wenn den Jungen die Zukunft nur noch trostlos erscheint

© unsplash Wenn junge Menschen aus der Peripherie die Zentren großer Städte heimsuchen, um mit Gewalt und Plünderungen Angst und Schrecken zu verbreiten, dann kann das selten eindimensional erklärt werden. Doch als Fundament für die desolate Lage dient eine Betrachtung der Einkommensstatistik. Das gilt für Frankreich, aber auch für Italien, wo die Proteste ähnlich ausgeartet sind wie im Nachbarland, wenn auch auf niedrigerem Niveau: Zwischen 2019 und 2026 sind die durchschnittlichen Reallöhne in keinem anderen EU-Land so stark gesunken wie in Italien, nämlich um 3,9 Prozent. Es gab zwar Steigerungen, doch noch immer haben die Menschen, gemessen an der Inflation, weniger Einkünfte als vor der Pandemie.

Es dürfte kein Zufall sein, dass Frankreich das Land mit der zweitschlechtesten Lohnentwicklung der EU ist. Dort liegen die Reallöhne mit 2,4 Prozent unter dem Niveau von 2019. Daneben gibt es nur zwei weitere Länder, in denen der Reallohn in diesen sieben Jahren sank, jedoch nur minimal: in Finnland um minus 1,3 Prozent sowie in Griechenland um minus 0,1 Prozent. Alle anderen 23 EU-Staaten erlebten meist deutliche Reallohnsteigerungen seit dem letzten Vorpandemiejahr; in 13 Ländern waren es mehr als fünf Prozent.

## Alte Probleme sind geblieben

Die Zahlen stammen aus dem Ausblick auf Beschäftigung und soziale Entwicklung, den die EU-Kommission in diesem Monat veröffentlicht hat. Weite Teile der italienischen Bevölkerung haben mit materieller Stagnation zu kämpfen, darunter viele junge Menschen. Die italienische Volkswirtschaft kennzeichnen geringe Löhne schon lange, was oft mit kleinen Produktivitätsfortschritten erklärt wurde. Der Druck kumuliert sich, sodass er sich irgendwann entlädt. Trotz gewisser Wachstumserfolge der Regierung von Giorgia Meloni seit ihrer Wahl vor vier Jahren haben sich die Einnahmen real wenig verbessert, denn die Inflation fraß immer wieder alles auf. Alte Probleme sind geblieben wie geringe Unternehmensgrößen, schwache Innovationsinvestitionen, Spezialisierung auf Branchen mit niedriger Wertschöpfung sowie veraltete Tarifverträge infolge verhärteter Fronten zwischen Gewerkschaften und Unternehmen.

So stiegen die durchschnittlichen Nominallöhne im italienischen Privatsektor zwischen 2015 und 2025 zwar um fast 21 Prozent und im öffentlichen Dienst um gut 16 Prozent. Doch angesichts einer kumulierten Inflation von 24,2 Prozent in diesen zehn Jahren blieb den Haushalten am Ende weniger als zuvor.

## „Mangel an Werten und Zukunftsperspektiven“

Schon auf dem Bildungsweg führt dies bei vielen jungen Menschen in Italien zu einer gefühlten Aussichtslosigkeit, die in Wut umschlagen kann. „Die Schule ermöglicht nicht mehr wie früher den gesellschaftlichen und wirtschaftlichen Aufstieg“, erklärt Giovanni Diamanti, Dozent an der Universität Padua und Mitgründer des Umfrageunternehmens Youtrend, in der Zeitung „Il Messaggero“. „Die Ungleichheiten nehmen zu, und junge Menschen wandern aus, weil sie für die Miete ihr gesamtes Einkommen ausgeben müssen.“ Bei Einwanderern, auch der zweiten oder dritten Generation, kommt das Gefühl oder das tatsächlich erlittene Leid der Diskriminierung hinzu.

Neben einer Mehrheit friedlicher Demonstranten mit legitimen Forderungen nach besseren Lern- und Studienbedingungen, Gehältern und Jobaussichten ist eine Gruppe schwer erreichbarer Jugendlicher herangewachsen. Viele sind von den sozialen Medien stärker geprägt als von ihren Elternhäusern. Politische Motive sind allenfalls diffus vorhanden, wenn überhaupt. „Das Grundproblem bei den rebellischen Jugendlichen ist die Apathie gegenüber der Politik. Sie haben es vor allem auf hochwertige Güter wie Markenkleidung abgesehen, die außerhalb ihrer Reichweite liegen. Hinzu kommt ein umfassender Mangel an Werten und Zukunftsperspektiven“, meint Diamanti.

## Relativ wenige Italiener gehen an die Uni

Was nach der Schule kommt, ist für viele junge Menschen in Italien ungewiss. Die Jugendarbeitslosigkeit sank seit Mitte des vergangenen Jahrzehnts zwar deutlich, doch sie gehört mit zuletzt gut 20 Prozent immer noch zu den schlechtesten Werten Europas. Laut OECD hatten 2025 fast 16 Prozent der 18- bis 24-Jährigen keine Arbeit oder Ausbildung. Der Durchschnitt der 38 OECD-Länder liegt bei gut 14 Prozent.

Die Universität zu besuchen, verspricht nicht unbedingt eine bessere Zukunft, zudem schlagen viele Italiener diesen Weg gar nicht ein. Italien rangiert in der Altersklasse 25 bis 34 Jahre beim Anteil der Menschen mit Hochschulbildung auf dem vorletzten Rang der EU. Viele Studenten brauchen auch lange bis zum Abschluss oder steigen vorher aus. Im Jahr 2023 schafften fast 44 Prozent der Bachelor-Studenten den Abschluss nicht in den meist vorhergesehenen drei Jahren, berichtet die EU-Kommission. 40 Prozent der Uni-Abgänger arbeiten in Jobs, die nichts mit ihrem Studium zu tun haben.

Dass der italienische Staat seinen Bildungsauftrag nur unzureichend erfüllt, lässt sich auch an den Ausgaben ablesen. Für Schulen und Universitäten gibt Italien laut OECD nur 3,4 Prozent des Bruttoinlandsproduktes aus, während der OECD-Durchschnitt bei 4 Prozent liegt. Das Lehrpersonal ist schlecht bezahlt, zudem sind die Professoren und Dozenten an den italienischen Universitäten im Durchschnitt so alt wie in keinem anderen EU-Land. Die Investitionen im Zuge des während der Pandemie beschlossenen EU-Wiederaufbauplanes brachten zwar etwas Linderung, doch immer noch befinden sich etliche Schulen und Unis in einem schlechten baulichen Zustand und leiden unter Personalmangel sowie einer schleppenden Bürokratie.

items.subtitle: Kein anderer KI-Entwickler hat ein so spirituelles Verhältnis zu seiner Technologie wie Anthropic.
items.feedText: Anthropic wollte es ganz genau wissen. Dreimal, sagt Mois Navon, habe das Unternehmen ihn gefragt, ob er wirklich Rabbiner sei. „Ich kann Ihnen das Zertifikat schicken“, antwortete Navon, der in Israel lebt. items.articleBody:
# KI: Warum Anthropic an Claudes Gefühle glaubt

San Francisco. Anthropic wollte es ganz genau wissen. Dreimal, sagt Mois Navon, habe das Unternehmen ihn gefragt, ob er wirklich Rabbiner sei. „Ich kann Ihnen das Zertifikat schicken“, antwortete Navon, der in Israel lebt. Das war dann offenbar überzeugend genug. Das Unternehmen schickte ihm eine Einladung: zwei Tage Diskussion in San Francisco. Anthropic zahlte kein Honorar, bot aber Flug und Hotel auf Firmenkosten.

Zusammen kamen 20 Gelehrte aller wesentlichen Weltreligionen: Juden, Christen, Muslime, auch Sikhs und die afrikanische Ubuntu-Lehre waren vertreten. Der Zweck, so stand es in der Einladungsmail, deren Abschrift dem Handelsblatt vorliegt: ein Gespräch über die „moralische und spirituelle Entwicklung“ von Anthropics Künstlicher Intelligenz ( KI ) Claude, mit der das Start-up zuletzt fast 17 Milliarden Dollar im Quartal umsetzte.

Die vertrauliche Tagung, die im April dieses Jahres stattfand, ist in dieser Form in der Tech-Branche einzigartig. Konkurrenten wie OpenAI oder Google kennen ähnlich komplexe Ansätze nicht. Sie behandeln ihre KI-Systeme wie Maschinen. Sie ziehen ihnen in der Regel starre Grenzen, während Anthropic in einer „Verfassung“ auf „Werte“ setzt, die über bloße Sicherheitserwägungen hinausgehen.

Der Aufwand zeigt, wie eigenwillig das Verhältnis von Teilen der Mannschaft zu ihrem Geschöpf ist. Anthropic ist nicht nur der derzeit erfolgreichste KI-Entwickler, sondern auch der spirituellste. Das Start-up behandelt Claude und die ihm zugrunde liegenden KI-Modelle nicht bloß wie ein Produkt, sondern wie ein Lebewesen, dessen moralische Entwicklung Begleitung braucht. Im Zentrum steht dabei die Frage, ob KI ein Bewusstsein haben kann.

Gleichzeitig wirbt die Unternehmensführung bei Investoren in diesen Tagen um bis zu 64 Milliarden Dollar. 825 Millionen Aktien will das Start-up verkaufen, für 70 bis 78 Dollar das Stück. Schon an diesem Donnerstag soll die Aktie an der US-Technologiebörse Nasdaq starten. Erwartet wird der größte Börsengang der Geschichte .

Was dabei vollkommen untergeht: Verkauft wird auch der Zugang zu einer Maschine, deren Schöpfer es für möglich halten, dass sie fühlt, was man mit ihr macht. Das damit verbundene Geschäftsrisiko hat Anthropic sogar in den Börsenprospekt geschrieben.

# Münchner Start-up gewinnt Frankfurter Sprungfeder

- Startseite
- Wirtschaft
## Münchner Start-up gewinnt Frankfurter Sprungfeder

Stand: 17.11.2026, 16:41 Uhr

Von: Christoph Manus

Kommentare Drucken Teilen

Das Münchner Unternehmen Helmit hat sich beim Start-up-Preis Frankfurter Sprungfeder durchgesetzt. Die App soll Gefahren durch Cyber-Mobbing und Online-Betrug erkennen helfen.

Das Münchner Unternehmen Helmit hat den Start-up-Preis „Frankfurter Sprungfeder“ gewonnen, den der Marketing-Club Frankfurt seit 2015 vergibt. Es hat eine App entwickelt, die über eine neuartige Integration in soziale Medien dabei helfen soll, Gefahren durch Cyber-Mobbing, Belästigung und Online-Betrug zu erkennen und zu vermeiden. Helmit setzte sich nach einem Pitch im Frankfurter IHK-Gebäude gegen die Start-ups Hezo Sports, Hopper, Mamaye und Nippli durch. Für die Jury gab den Ausschlag, dass Helmit ein gesellschaftliche Problem konsequent angehe. Insgesamt hatten sich laut Marketing-Club 140 Unternehmen beworben. Das sei eine neue Rekordzahl.

Mit dem Gewinn der Sprungfeder ist ein Gewinnpaket im Gesamtwert von mehr als 100.000 Euro verbunden. Es besteht aus Medienpaketen in der Städtewerbung und themenbasierten Coachings in Online-Marketing-Strategie und Finanzierung,

Für die Jury gab den Ausschlag, dass Helmit ein gesellschaftliche Problem konsequent angehe. Insgesamt hatten sich laut Marketing-Club 140 Unternehmen beworben. Das sei eine neue Rekordzahl.

Mit dem Gewinn der Sprungfeder ist ein Gewinnpaket im Gesamtwert von mehr als 100.000 Euro verbunden. Es besteht aus Medienpaketen in der Städtewerbung und themenbasierten Coachings in Online-Marketing-Strategie und Finanzierung,

# Younger generations appear to have a double advantage against dementia, researchers find

## Younger generations appear to have a double advantage against dementia, researchers find

edited by Gaby Clark , reviewed by Andrew Zinin

Gaby Clark

Scientific Editor

Andrew Zinin

Chief Editor

This article has been reviewed according to Science X's editorial process and policies . Editors have highlighted the following attributes while ensuring the content's credibility:

fact-checked

peer-reviewed publication

trusted source

proofread

Anders Fjell is the lead author of a new study that was just published in the journal Nature Medicine titled "Generational gains in cognitive capacity and dementia incidence rates in Western countries." The study is based on an analysis of about 219,000 people who have been followed for up to nearly 30 years.

"We have long known that more recent generations score better on cognitive tests. What is new is that the aging process itself appears to have been shifted further into the future. We also show that these differences are large enough to explain the decline in dementia risk reported in Europe and the United States—estimated at around 13% per decade," says Fjell, director of the LCBC research center, which studies lifespan changes in the brain and cognition.

## It takes longer to develop dementia

The main point of the study is that dementia prevention is not only about lifestyle and health when we reach middle and old age. The benefits are also built early in life, through, among other things, maternal health during pregnancy, nutrition, education, good childhood conditions and less inequality. At the same time, health throughout adulthood—particularly cardiovascular and metabolic health—may help slow cognitive decline .

"Our results show that each generation over the past decades has entered old age with better cognitive capacity than the previous one, and that it loses it more slowly. As a result, it takes longer before the decline becomes severe enough to cause dementia," says Fjell.

According to Fjell, the study cannot determine with certainty what the main cause is, but he believes that likely causes may include the major social changes of the 20th century: more schooling for children, better nutrition and childhood and adolescent living conditions, and better health care.

"Over time, better medication for cardiovascular diseases, lower pollution and similar factors may also have played a role. It is probably not a single cause," he says.

## Improving conditions for everyone

The study examines differences between generations, not what individuals can do, and the researchers will therefore not offer individual-level advice based on these findings.

"The main message is that improving social conditions for everyone, especially early in life, can have major significance for the burden of dementia in society. Conditions throughout the entire lifespan, from childhood to old age, appear to matter for cognitive function even late in life," he says.

Fjell stresses that it has been crucial to the study that researchers have been able to follow the same people over many years.

"It is only by testing the same people repeatedly over a long period that we can distinguish between how well a generation performs and how quickly it declines. If you only compare different age groups at one point in time, you cannot know whether the differences are due to aging or to the generations having started at different levels. It is the patterns of change that are new in this study, and they require this type of data."

## Both optimism and a warning

Fjell emphasizes that the study provides grounds for optimism: The risk of dementia at a given age is not set in stone; it has declined across generations, which means it is influenced by conditions that we as a society can do something about.

"At the same time, it is important to stress that we have no guarantee that the positive development will continue. The gains we see have been created by improvements in living conditions, education and health throughout the 20th century, and they did not happen by themselves.

"The generations who are young today are growing up under different conditions, and trends in, for example, physical activity, overweight and inequality do not necessarily point in the right direction. If today's young people are to gain the same benefit as their parents and grandparents, the foundation must be laid now," he concludes.

Fjell points out that good brain health in old age is built throughout life, and that it is a societal task, not only an individual responsibility.

## Who has gained the most and the least?

An important question that will occupy the research group going forward is who has gained the most and the least from societal improvements.

"The benefits described by our study are averages for entire generations, but they are unlikely to be equally distributed. Are those who started with the poorest conditions the ones who have gained the most, or have the improvements mainly benefited those who were already well placed? The same applies to heredity: we know that genetic vulnerability affects dementia risk, but we do not know whether better living conditions and education protect equally regardless of genetic vulnerability, or whether some groups need more to achieve the same benefit," says Fjell.

These are precisely the questions that he and his research group are now investigating.

"The answers we get will matter for how future prevention should be designed: for everyone, or particularly for those who have the most to gain," says Fjell.

Publication details

Anders M. Fjell et al., Generational gains in cognitive capacity and dementia incidence rates in Western countries, Nature Medicine (2026). DOI: 10.1038/s41591-026-04759-y

# Glasses and shirt buttons will be examined to stop cheating in South Korea's college entrance exams

November 17, 2026

## Glasses and shirt buttons will be examined to stop cheating in South Korea's college entrance exams

edited by Andrew Zinin

Andrew Zinin

Chief Editor

This article has been reviewed according to Science X's editorial process and policies . Editors have highlighted the following attributes while ensuring the content's credibility:

fact-checked

reputable news agency

proofread

Proctors will inspect every test-taker's glasses and seal their shirt buttons with stickers, and authorities will deploy 8,400 additional supervisors at South Korea's college entrance exams on Thursday.

The country will also send an emergency alert that will set nearly all mobile phones in the country buzzing for about 10 seconds that morning, using a tool typically reserved for major crises like large earthquakes or war to expose any devices hidden by test-takers.

The sweeping measures to fight cheating are in response to concerns that artificial intelligence and smart devices are making fraud harder to detect.

More than 550,000 people will participate in the exam at around 1,300 test sites in what's a pivotal annual event for the country. South Korea is known for its intense academic competition, where job opportunities, social standing and even marriage prospects often hinge on which school a person attends.

Concerns about cheating grew after the top scorer on a national tax accountant exam admitted to using a hidden camera, a smartphone and generative AI tools to obtain answers, the latest in a string of AI-assisted cheating cases to affect exams in recent months.

In a televised briefing on Tuesday, Prime Minister Han Seongsook said that proctors will use metal detectors on test-takers who act suspiciously to search for hidden devices and that the exam ban for cheaters will be lengthened from the current one year to 10. College students retaking the exam to go to different universities will be expelled from their current schools if they are caught cheating, in addition to facing a 10-year ban on entering any school, Han said.

Test-takers will be prohibited from bringing electronic devices such as smartphones, smart glasses and smartwatches, or any object with a camera, and failing to hand them over to proctors before the exam will be treated as cheating, regardless of whether they were used.

Those who wear glasses will be asked to place them on the desk for inspection before the exam, and supervisors will monitor for smart glasses throughout the hourslong test. Han advised test-takers to avoid clothing with buttons, and any buttons will be covered with stickers to guard against hidden cameras.

She said that global technology companies that operate AI chatbots have also agreed to cooperate with any post-exam investigations into suspected cheating, such as queries involving photographed test pages.

The "Suneung," or the College Scholastic Ability Test, is a crucial annual event for which the education-obsessed country goes to extraordinary lengths to create an ideal testing environment. The start of work hours and stock trading are delayed to ease traffic for test-takers, and flights are halted during the English listening section. Police often use cars or motorcycles to escort test-takers who are running late, while the military sometimes suspends training near testing sites.

Growing public concerns about AI-assisted cheating have drastically raised the stakes for this year's exam, with some experts and politicians even calling for the government to postpone the test until reliable anti-cheating measures are in place.

President Lee Jae Myung, who is in the Philippines for a regional summit, chaired an emergency meeting by video to review the government's exam preparations and vowed a stern, "zero-tolerance" response toward anyone caught cheating. He also instructed officials to consider sending more text alerts at unpredictable times during the exam.

"Would even the boldest student risk getting dragged out during the test because their telecommunications device went off?" Lee said on his X account.

Vice Education Minister Choi Eun-ok said that "there could be critics who say our measures are excessive, but a failure to conduct Suneung in a strict and fair manner will bring a (major) disruption to our society that would really be worse than a disaster."

"We believe we are in a situation where excessive measures are necessary," Choi said.

Government officials scrambled to strengthen anti-cheating measures this week after a 34-year-old man who topped a national tax accountant exam confessed in a video posted on his lawyer's YouTube channel Sunday that he had used a hidden microcamera and smartphone to obtain answers from AI.

Han Won-seok's unusually high scores had drawn suspicion after he discussed them during recent media interviews. The case follows other incidents involving AI-assisted cheating in the past several months, including test-takers caught using AI-powered smart glasses on an English standardized test in June and on some university essay exams in October.

Han Won-seok told reporters he would cooperate with the criminal investigation into his actions as he arrived for questioning by Seoul police on Tuesday.

Andrew Zinin

items.articleBody:
Whether showcasing a prized possession or peering through a spyglass to navigate open water, [Juliet Schreckinger](https://www.julietschreckinger.com/)’s curious characters work together and form unexpected alliances. Personalities like Oscar the Octopus and Quinn the Sperm Whale recur in the artist’s ink and graphite drawings, and her most recent series comprises the show *Limitless Sea* at [Arch Enemy Arts](https://www.archenemyarts.com/).

Schreckinger’s marine and woodland critters adopt a playful, cartoonish air, like personalities in a children’s book who find themselves adrift and in need of a friend. Lighthouses, lanterns, and rays of sun breaking through clouds glow with optimism. And while an overarching narrative may be murky, the unlikely companions and cooperative activities illuminate dreamlike scenes that encourage inquisitiveness and joy.

“Finding the Light” (2026), ink and graphite on Arches paper mounted to cradled birch, varnished, 14 x 18 x 1 5/8 inches

An undercurrent of persistence and hope also runs through *Limited Sea*, mirroring the artist’s recent healing process after a major surgery. It’s “a show made up of characters navigating through the foggy darkness by focusing on the light…and on the other side is limitless possibility,” Schreckinger says in a statement. As she navigated her own challenges—including making this series with only one good eye—these works served as a reminder of what’s most important: “finding the beauty, finding the light, and spending time with those who make your soul happy,” she says.

*Limitless Sea* continues through November 29 in Philadelphia. Schreckinger’s work will also be on view next month in *General Strike 2*, an exhibition of artist matchboxes, at [Joy Machine](https://joymachine.art/pages/exhibitions). See more on Schreckinger’s [Instagram](https://www.instagram.com/julietschreckinger).

“The Turtle Rock Lighthouse” (2026), ink and graphite on Arches paper mounted to cradled birch, varnished, 12 x 12 x 1 5/8 inches

“Thaddeus’ Bottle” (2026), ink and graphite on Arches paper mounted to cradled birch, varnished, 7 x 9 x 1 5/8 inches

“The Shark and His Seabird Guide” (2026), ink and graphite on Arches paper mounted to cradled birch, varnished, 12 x 12 x 1 5/8 inches

“Navigating the Fog” (2026), ink and graphite on Arches paper mounted to cradled birch, varnished, 14 x 11 x 1 5/8 inches

“The Shimmering Sea Hare” (2026), ink and graphite on Arches paper mounted to cradled birch, varnished, 14 x 11 x 1 5/8 inches

# Krieg in Nahost - Erneut Explosionen und Angriffe in der Straße von Hormus

Erneut wurden in der Straße von Hormus Frachtschiffe angegriffen (Archivbild). (imago/ Anadolu Agency / Hassan Ghaedi) Das britische Sicherheitsunternehmen Vanguard teilte mit, ein Gastanker sei vor der Küste des Oman von einem Geschoss getroffen worden und in Brand geraten. Die iranischen Revolutionsgarden erklärten ihrerseits, in der Meerenge habe es Explosionen an einem Öl- und an einem Gastanker gegeben. Beide Schiffe seien auf Seeminen gefahren. Laut der iranischen Nachrichtenagentur fuhr später ein weiterer Tanker auf eine Mine. Die Lage in der Straße von Hormus ist unübersichtlich. Der Iran blockiert die Meerenge weitgehend. Die Revolutionsgarden verlangen von Schiffen, die passieren wollen, dass sie eine Route nahe der iranischen Küste nutzen. Die USA haben eine Blockade gegen iranische Häfen verhängt und versuchen, den Frachtverkehr der anderen Länder mit Geleitschutz abzusichern. Aktuelle Informationen zum Krieg im Nahen Osten finden Sie auch in unserem Newsblog. Diese Nachricht wurde am 17.11.2026 im Programm Deutschlandfunk gesendet.

# Researchers count kinetochore proteins in living cells using an improved fluorescence-based method

November 17, 2026

## Researchers count kinetochore proteins in living cells using an improved fluorescence-based method

edited by Lisa Lock , reviewed by Andrew Zinin

Lisa Lock

Scientific Editor

Andrew Zinin

Chief Editor

This article has been reviewed according to Science X's editorial process and policies . Editors have highlighted the following attributes while ensuring the content's credibility:

fact-checked

peer-reviewed publication

trusted source

proofread

Accurate division of genetic material is critical for life and growth, and key to this is a protein structure called the kinetochore. Without this structure, the genetic material cannot be segregated equally into two daughter cells. However, challenges in discovering the exact molecular organization of the kinetochore in living cells have prevented researchers from understanding how these proteins work together to build it.

Now, a group led by researchers from the University of Osaka has quantified the number of molecules of key component proteins within the kinetochore complex in living cells. The findings have been recently published in the Journal of Cell Biology .

As one cell divides into two, the first step is for the genetic material—organized into chromosomes—to duplicate itself into pairs. These pairs of duplicated chromosomes are attached at a region called the centromere, where the kinetochore assembles.

The kinetochore is the point at which the chromosomes attach to a "spindle" structure running throughout the cell. The spindle pulls the chromosomes apart as the cell splits into two and ensures that one copy of each pair ends up in each new cell. Without accurate attachment to the spindle, errors linked to multiple diseases can occur.

A technique known as fluorescence correlation spectroscopy-calibrated molecular counting was used in mitotic chicken DT40 cells. The team then measured the copy number of components of the kinetochore complex using a method that overcomes the limitations of previous approaches.

The kinetochore consists of two main protein networks called the CCAN , forming the inner kinetochore, and the KMN, forming the outer kinetochore. The team found that, of the CCAN proteins measured, CENP-C was present at roughly double the copy number of the others. Importantly, they showed that the outer kinetochore complex attaches to the inner complex through two redundant mechanisms, binding to both CENP-C and another CCAN protein called CENP-T. Both these proteins contain binding sites for a protein complex known as Mis12C.

When the Mis12C binding site in either CENP-C or CENP-T is removed, sufficient Mis12C can bind to the other CENP protein to allow recruitment of the KMN components so that the cell can still divide successfully.

"The amount of Ndc80C , the protein that grips onto the spindle microtubules, remained consistent even when one Mis12C binding site is removed," explains lead author Yasuhiro Hirano. "This redundancy acts as a safety measure to preserve the functionality of the division process."

These results suggest that at least 15 molecules of Mis12C and more than 30 molecules of Ndc80C are required for accurate cell division.

"We speculate that this number of Ndc80C molecules provides a platform for stable attachment to the microtubules, with an estimated 8–10 molecules per microtubule," explains senior author Tatsuo Fukagawa.

This study provides new insight into the intricate process of creating the structures critical for accurate cell division, a process that is fundamental to cellular growth and development.

Publication details

Yasuhiro Hirano et al., Quantitative measurements of kinetochore protein copy numbers via FCS-calibrated molecular counting, Journal of Cell Biology (2026). DOI: 10.1083/jcb.202603185

Journal information: Journal of Cell Biology

# How to Bypass Rust's Orphan Rule - Edmond Vong ## How to Bypass Rust's Orphan Rule ## What Is the Orphan Rule Actually Protecting Against? ## Why the Two Usual Workarounds Fall Short ### 1. Building it into the library ### 2. Wrap it in a NewType yourself ## Adding a Generic Slot to the Trait ## The Position of the Local Type Matters ## A Truly Standalone models Crate ## Real-World Example: How This Works in Kova How to Bypass Rust's Orphan Rule Contents What Is the Orphan Rule Actually Protecting Against? Why the Two Usual Workarounds Fall Short 1. Building it into the library 2. Wrap it in a NewType yourself Adding a Generic Slot to the Trait The Position of the Local Type Matters A Truly Standalone models Crate Real-World Example: How This Works in Kova Write Rust for long enough, and you are bound to run into error[E0117] . Take a simple, everyday scenario. You pull in a serialization library that defines a ToJson trait, along with a third-party type library like uuid . You want to turn a uuid::Uuid into JSON, so you naturally write: impl ToJson for uuid :: Uuid { fn to_json ( & self ) -> String { format! ( " \" {} \" " , self ) } } And the compiler immediately stops you: error[E0117]: only traits defined in the current crate can be implemented for types defined outside of the crate This is Rust's well-known Orphan Rule . Once people hit this wall, they usually either complain that the compiler is too rigid or dutifully wrap the type in a NewType. But if you look closely at how the Orphan Rule actually works, it is not a dead end. By design, it leaves a pretty wide door open. What Is the Orphan Rule Actually Protecting Against? Setting the jargon aside, the logic behind the Orphan Rule is simple: if you want a type to implement a trait, at least one of those two things (the type or the trait) must belong to your own crate. In plain English, you don't get to make rules for someone else's types. Suppose crate A implements ToJson for uuid::Uuid and outputs a hyphenated UUID string, while crate B also implements ToJson for uuid::Uuid and outputs 32 raw hex characters without hyphens. If a project depends on both A and B, the compiler has a problem when it sees uuid.to_json() : which implementation should it pick? To prevent this kind of global conflict, Rust enforces coherence , and the Orphan Rule is how it gets enforced. There is nothing wrong with the rule itself. It keeps the Rust ecosystem from turning into a mess as dependency trees grow. The catch is that real-world projects constantly run into a very common need: making a third-party type implement a trait from another third-party crate. Neither the type nor the trait is yours, yet gluing libraries together like this happens all the time. So what can you do? Why the Two Usual Workarounds Fall Short Right now, the Rust ecosystem mostly relies on two workarounds. Both appear to solve the problem on the surface, but because neither addresses the root cause, they get awkward fast. 1. Building it into the library Many foundational crates take this route: since users can't write the impl themselves, the crate provides it internally. Because ToJson is defined inside the crate, implementing it for any external type satisfies the Orphan Rule. Open up the Cargo.toml of one of these crates, and you will see a long list of feature flags: with-uuid , with-chrono , with-time , with-jiff , with-url , with-rust-decimal , and so on. It looks helpful at first, but it tries to enumerate an open, constantly changing ecosystem inside a single crate . That approach has clear limits, and the downsides show up quickly: You can never support everything. Today the community favors chrono , tomorrow people switch to jiff , and next week your team builds its own internal Money type. If the library doesn't have built-in support, you are stuck waiting for a release or opening a PR yourself. Version lock-in. When a third-party type crate bumps its major version, your whole dependency tree gets stuck until the trait crate publishes a matching update. Hardcoded behavior. Maybe the library serializes DateTime as an ISO-8601 string by default, while your API spec requires an integer timestamp in milliseconds. Because the implementation lives inside the library, you have no way to change it. 2. Wrap it in a NewType yourself When the library doesn't have built-in support, or its default behavior doesn't fit your needs, you fall back to the familiar NewType pattern: pub struct MyUuid ( pub uuid :: Uuid ); impl ToJson for MyUuid { fn to_json ( & self ) -> String { format! ( " \" {} \" " , self . 0 ) } } Wrapping one or two types is fine. The trouble starts when a moderately complex domain model mixes Uuid , Url , DateTime , HashMap , and custom domain types all at once. Once you wrap everything into MyUuid , MyUrl , and MyDateTime , your business logic gets littered with .0 , and you spend your time constantly wrapping and unwrapping values. It gets old very quickly. NewType is a genuinely useful pattern in Rust for expressing domain meaning, hiding internals, or enforcing invariants. The problem is that when you only use it to appease the Orphan Rule on types that didn't need a wrapper in the first place, your code bloats quickly. So is there a way to let users decide how third-party types implement a trait, without wrapping everything in NewTypes? Adding a Generic Slot to the Trait Let's go back to the rule: either the type or the trait must belong to the current crate. Many developers assume the compiler only looks at Trait and Type in impl Trait for Type . In fact, under Rust's Orphan Rule (RFC 2451), the trait's own generic type parameters are also part of the check . Put simply, in impl Trait

for Type , as long as a local type appears in the trait's generic parameters, and there are no uncovered type parameters before it, the compiler knows this implementation belongs exclusively to the current crate. No other crate can conflict with it, so the compiler lets it through. Take this example: impl ToJson < MyApp > for uuid :: Uuid { // ... } ToJson is a foreign trait, and Uuid is a foreign type, but MyApp is defined in the current crate. Because it sits in the trait's generic parameter position, this impl satisfies the Orphan Rule. Following this idea, a library author only needs to take one extra step when designing a trait: leave a generic parameter on the trait as an extension point for users . For example: pub trait ToJson < Ctx = ()> { fn to_json ( & self ) -> String ; } Notice that Ctx = () has a default type. When the library implements ToJson for basic types like i32 and String , it makes those implementations generic over any Ctx : impl < Ctx > ToJson < Ctx > for i32 { fn to_json ( & self ) -> String { self . to_string () } } impl < Ctx > ToJson < Ctx > for String { fn to_json ( & self ) -> String { format! ( " \" {} \" " , self ) } } This way, regular users never even notice Ctx exists. Everything works the exact same way as before, with () as the default context. When you do need to plug in third-party types, you just define an empty marker struct in your own crate: pub struct MyApp ; Then you can write implementations for any third-party type you want: impl ToJson < MyApp > for uuid :: Uuid { fn to_json ( & self ) -> String { format! ( " \" {} \" " , self ) } } impl ToJson < MyApp > for chrono :: DateTime { fn to_json ( & self ) -> String { self . timestamp_millis () . to_string () } } The compiler looks at this and sees: ToJson is foreign, Uuid and DateTime are foreign, but MyApp is local to your crate. No other crate can write a conflicting implementation using your MyApp , so global coherence is completely safe. It compiles right away. You can think of this conversion setup as a web of relationships, with your local MyApp type as its root. A handy way to picture it is a bunch of grapes, where MyApp is the stem . Once you grab that stem, it doesn't matter how many third-party types hang off it ( Uuid , Url , DateTime , HashMap , and so on). You lift the whole bunch at once, and the compiler accepts all of them as local implementations. Better yet, you can define more than one stem in the same project. For instance, your HTTP API layer can use ApiCtx to format timestamps as strings, while an internal RPC layer uses RpcCtx to format them as integer timestamps. Both sets of rules live under separate contexts, completely isolated at compile time, with zero conflict. One detail to watch out for: the local type has to be a real, newly defined type. Creating a type alias for a foreign type will not work. The Position of the Local Type Matters At this point, you might think that dropping a local type MyApp anywhere into a trait's generic list solves the Orphan Rule for good. Most of the time, it does. But if your trait has more than one generic parameter, or if you want to write a generic impl , there is an ordering restriction that is easy to trip over. When the compiler runs its Orphan Rule check, it scans the types in a fixed order: first the Self type, then the trait's 1st generic parameter, then the 2nd, and so on . The rule comes down to one sentence: no bare generic type parameter T may appear before the first local type. Code makes this clearest. Suppose an external crate defines ForeignTrait and ForeignType , and you define MyApp locally: // ✅ Allowed: scans ForeignType, then hits local MyApp first; the trailing T is unrestricted impl < T > ForeignTrait < MyApp , T > for ForeignType {} // ❌ Error: hits a bare T before seeing MyApp impl < T > ForeignTrait < T , MyApp > for ForeignType {} // ❌ Error: hits a bare T right away in Self, before MyApp gets a chance impl < T > ForeignTrait < MyApp , String > for T {} The only word to pay attention to here is "bare". In Rust terminology, this is called an uncovered type parameter . A plain T is uncovered. If it is wrapped inside a non-fundamental concrete type like Vec (built-in fundamental types like &T and Box do not count), it is no longer uncovered, so it will not block a local MyApp that comes after it: // ✅ Allowed: T is covered by Vec, so it is not an uncovered type parameter impl < T > ForeignTrait < Vec < T >, MyApp > for ForeignType {} From a library author's perspective, this means it is not enough to just add a generic slot; you also need to put it in the right place. If your trait has multiple generic parameters and there is no strong reason otherwise, put the context Ctx in the first type parameter position . That way, downstream users writing generic implementations can avoid most of the surprising Orphan Rule errors. A Truly Standalone models Crate Once this mechanism clicks, you will see that it also solves a stubborn architectural headache in larger Rust codebases. As a project grows, it usually gets split into a Cargo workspace: maybe an API gateway crate, a few business service crates, and a background worker crate. These modules often share the same data structures, so the natural move is to pull those structs out into a standalone models crate. Traditionally, doing this in Rust is painful. Suppose models defines a Product struct with Uuid , Url , and DateTime fields. If your serialization library or ORM expects those field types to already implement its traits inside models , you are left with two bad options: Wrap everything in NewTypes inside models , and pull in the serialization library, database driver, and other heavy dependencies along with them. A crate that was supposed to hold plain data structures ends up with the heaviest dependency tree in the workspace. Give up on splitting it out, and dump models and business logic into the same crate. It saves time early on, but dependency boundaries and compile times get harder to manage as the project grows. With the generic Ctx parameter, that knot comes untied. Inside your standalone models crate, you just define your structs with native types: // crate: models pub struct Product { pub id : uuid :: Uuid , pub created_at : chrono :: DateTime , } Then you write a generic implementation for Product open to any Ctx (or let a derive macro generate it): impl < Ctx > ToJson < Ctx > for Product where uuid :: Uuid : ToJson < Ctx >, chrono :: DateTime : ToJson < Ctx > { fn to_json ( & self ) -> String { format! ( "{{ \" id \" :{}, \" created_at \" :{}}}" , ToJson :: < Ctx > :: to_json ( & self . id), ToJson :: < Ctx > :: to_json ( & self . created_at), ) } } Notice the subtle part here: inside the models crate, Uuid and DateTime do not implement ToJson yet, and this code still compiles. That is because models is only declaring a deferred contract: "whoever uses this later, as long as your context Ctx knows how to handle Uuid and DateTime , Product automatically supports ToJson under your context." As a result, models stays completely lightweight, carries no concrete conversion logic, and compiles very fast. The actual conversions are deferred to the downstream service crates, where each service hooks up what it needs using its own local context. For large workspaces, this keeps dependency boundaries clean. Models can evolve on their own, while different services remain free to pick whatever storage format or API representation they need. Real-World Example: How This Works in Kova The ToJson snippet above is as minimal as it gets. Does this idea still hold up when you bring it into a real, more complex project? # How to Bypass Rust's Orphan Rule - Edmond Vong ## How to Bypass Rust's Orphan Rule ## What Is the Orphan Rule Actually Protecting Against? ## Why the Two Usual Workarounds Fall Short ### 1. Building it into the library ### 2. Wrap it in a NewType yourself ## Adding a Generic Slot to the Trait ## The Position of the Local Type Matters ## A Truly Standalone models Crate ## Real-World Example: How This Works in Kova How to Bypass Rust's Orphan Rule Contents What Is the Orphan Rule Actually Protecting Against? Why the Two Usual Workarounds Fall Short 1. Building it into the library 2. Wrap it in a NewType yourself Adding a Generic Slot to the Trait The Position of the Local Type Matters A Truly Standalone models Crate Real-World Example: How This Works in Kova Write Rust for long enough, and you are bound to run into error[E0117] . Take a simple, everyday scenario. You pull in a serialization library that defines a ToJson trait, along with a third-party type library like uuid . You want to turn a uuid::Uuid into JSON, so you naturally write: impl ToJson for uuid :: Uuid { fn to_json ( & self ) -> String { format! ( " \" {} \" " , self ) } } And the compiler immediately stops you: error[E0117]: only traits defined in the current crate can be implemented for types defined outside of the crate This is Rust's well-known Orphan Rule . Once people hit this wall, they usually either complain that the compiler is too rigid or dutifully wrap the type in a NewType. But if you look closely at how the Orphan Rule actually works, it is not a dead end. By design, it leaves a pretty wide door open. What Is the Orphan Rule Actually Protecting Against? Setting the jargon aside, the logic behind the Orphan Rule is simple: if you want a type to implement a trait, at least one of those two things (the type or the trait) must belong to your own crate. In plain English, you don't get to make rules for someone else's types. Suppose crate A implements ToJson for uuid::Uuid and outputs a hyphenated UUID string, while crate B also implements ToJson for uuid::Uuid and outputs 32 raw hex characters without hyphens. If a project depends on both A and B, the compiler has a problem when it sees uuid.to_json() : which implementation should it pick? To prevent this kind of global conflict, Rust enforces coherence , and the Orphan Rule is how it gets enforced. There is nothing wrong with the rule itself. It keeps the Rust ecosystem from turning into a mess as dependency trees grow. The catch is that real-world projects constantly run into a very common need: making a third-party type implement a trait from another third-party crate. Neither the type nor the trait is yours, yet gluing libraries together like this happens all the time. So what can you do? Why the Two Usual Workarounds Fall Short Right now, the Rust ecosystem mostly relies on two workarounds. Both appear to solve the problem on the surface, but because neither addresses the root cause, they get awkward fast. 1. Building it into the library Many foundational crates take this route: since users can't write the impl themselves, the crate provides it internally. Because ToJson is defined inside the crate, implementing it for any external type satisfies the Orphan Rule. Open up the Cargo.toml of one of these crates, and you will see a long list of feature flags: with-uuid , with-chrono , with-time , with-jiff , with-url , with-rust-decimal , and so on. It looks helpful at first, but it tries to enumerate an open, constantly changing ecosystem inside a single crate . That approach has clear limits, and the downsides show up quickly: You can never support everything. Today the community favors chrono , tomorrow people switch to jiff , and next week your team builds its own internal Money type. If the library doesn't have built-in support, you are stuck waiting for a release or opening a PR yourself. Version lock-in. When a third-party type crate bumps its major version, your whole dependency tree gets stuck until the trait crate publishes a matching update. Hardcoded behavior. Maybe the library serializes DateTime as an ISO-8601 string by default, while your API spec requires an integer timestamp in milliseconds. Because the implementation lives inside the library, you have no way to change it. 2. Wrap it in a NewType yourself When the library doesn't have built-in support, or its default behavior doesn't fit your needs, you fall back to the familiar NewType pattern: pub struct MyUuid ( pub uuid :: Uuid ); impl ToJson for MyUuid { fn to_json ( & self ) -> String { format! ( " \" {} \" " , self . 0 ) } } Wrapping one or two types is fine. The trouble starts when a moderately complex domain model mixes Uuid , Url , DateTime , HashMap , and custom domain types all at once. Once you wrap everything into MyUuid , MyUrl , and MyDateTime , your business logic gets littered with .0 , and you spend your time constantly wrapping and unwrapping values. It gets old very quickly. NewType is a genuinely useful pattern in Rust for expressing domain meaning, hiding internals, or enforcing invariants. The problem is that when you only use it to appease the Orphan Rule on types that didn't need a wrapper in the first place, your code bloats quickly. So is there a way to let users decide how third-party types implement a trait, without wrapping everything in NewTypes? Adding a Generic Slot to the Trait Let's go back to the rule: either the type or the trait must belong to the current crate. Many developers assume the compiler only looks at Trait and Type in impl Trait for Type . In fact, under Rust's Orphan Rule (RFC 2451), the trait's own generic type parameters are also part of the check . Put simply, in impl Trait

for Type , as long as a local type appears in the trait's generic parameters, and there are no uncovered type parameters before it, the compiler knows this implementation belongs exclusively to the current crate. No other crate can conflict with it, so the compiler lets it through. Take this example: impl ToJson < MyApp > for uuid :: Uuid { // ... } ToJson is a foreign trait, and Uuid is a foreign type, but MyApp is defined in the current crate. Because it sits in the trait's generic parameter position, this impl satisfies the Orphan Rule. Following this idea, a library author only needs to take one extra step when designing a trait: leave a generic parameter on the trait as an extension point for users . For example: pub trait ToJson < Ctx = ()> { fn to_json ( & self ) -> String ; } Notice that Ctx = () has a default type. ( " \" {} \" " , self ) } } This way, regular users never even notice Ctx exists. Everything works the exact same way as before, with () as the default context. No other crate can write a conflicting implementation using your MyApp , so global coherence is completely safe. It compiles right away. Both sets of rules live under separate contexts, completely isolated at compile time, with zero conflict. One detail to watch out for: the local type has to be a real, newly defined type. These modules often share the same data structures, so the natural move is to pull those structs out into a standalone models crate. Traditionally, doing this in Rust is painful. If your serialization library or ORM expects those field types to already implement its traits inside models , you are left with two bad options: Wrap everything in NewTypes inside models , and pull in the serialization library, database driver, and other heavy dependencies along with them. A crate that was supposed to hold plain data structures ends up with the heaviest dependency tree in the workspace. ( "{{ \" id \" :{}, \" created_at \" :{}}}" , ToJson :: < Ctx > :: to_json ( & self . id), ToJson :: < Ctx > :: to_json ( & self . created_at), ) } } Notice the subtle part here: inside the models crate, Uuid and DateTime do not implement ToJson yet, and this code still compiles. # House Democrats promise a US return to global climate talks

ANTALYA, Turkey—After their big gains in the 2026 midterm elections , a delegation of Democratic US House members appeared at the United Nations COP31 climate change conference Monday, pledging to rejoin the international fight against global warming.

Rep. Jared Huffman (D-Calif.), ranking member of the House Natural Resources Committee, said it is a “pivotal time” for US climate and energy policy.

“The wrecking ball of Donald Trump and this out-of-touch administration, and the temporarily empty chair of the United States at this COP31, does not represent what the Americans want or need,” Huffman said.

President Donald Trump has pulled the United States out of the Paris climate agreement twice and is trying to quit the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change. The current administration has also tried to cut all funding for climate programs.

Since Trump returned to the White House in 2025, the United States has had no formal government presence at the UN talks, but was informally represented by America Is All In , a coalition including local governments, businesses, faith groups, Native American tribes, and universities.

Huffman said the midterm election shows that Americans have rejected the current administration’s efforts to “turn the United States into something like a petro-dictatorship.” The results could pave the way for the country to reestablish a formal presence at the annual talks.

Given legal uncertainties about Trump’s efforts to completely withdraw the US from the UN’s climate framework, the extent of US participation in the talks is unclear. But Huffman said that, in the past, US congressional delegations have attended the annual Conference of the Parties, as the meeting is formally known, under both Democratic and Republican majorities.

“The next time we’re here, we will be an official congressional delegation led by the leadership of the House of Representatives,” Huffman said in an interview with Inside Climate News.

The US would still be excluded from the formal government-to-government negotiations, but a congressional delegation representing the majority party, potentially capable of advancing climate and energy legislation, could make a difference, Huffman said.

“We want to take the best practices that we’ve heard from all of the global partners… and craft them into good, solid climate policy once we get back to Congress,” said Rep. Lucy McBath (D-Ga.).

The new Democratic majority in the House of Representatives can also use its oversight authority to try to ensure that the money the US has promised for climate aid and sustainable development is restored, said U.S. Rep. Sean Casten (D-Ill.).

Casten said some of America’s European allies are “spending $500, $600 million per day more than before the United States attacked Iran” because of increased oil prices, and that simply stopping those hostilities could free up funding for climate efforts.

“We have lost [the] trust of the international community when it comes to climate,” said Rep. Yassamin Ansari (D-Ariz.).

“I think it is a complete betrayal of our responsibility that Donald Trump has pulled us out of the Paris Agreement not once but twice,” she said. A Democrat winning the 2028 presidential election would help ensure the US can rejoin that agreement, she added.

It will take time to regain trust in the international community, Ansari said.

“But we will come back,” she said, “working 10 times harder, 50 times harder than we did before, to make sure that we are being team players, to make sure that we are… supporting small island developing states and supporting vulnerable African nations.”

Climate activists reacted cautiously to the promises about the United States’ potential return to the international climate arena.

“We welcome the political shift in the United States that puts the brakes on the reckless dismantling of domestic green policies,” said Harjeet Singh, director of Satat Sampada Climate Foundation . “However, here at COP31 in Antalya, the international community cannot afford to celebrate prematurely or suffer from collective amnesia.”

Singh said the US has a long history of obstructing climate negotiations across successive administrations and regardless of which party holds power.

“As the world’s largest historical emitter, the US carries an outsized moral and legal responsibility to act,” he said. “Real change will not be measured by who walks through the halls of this summit, but by whether Washington finally ends its expansion of oil, gas, and coal at home and delivers hundreds of billions of dollars in grant-based climate finance to developing countries.”

Singh said until the US pays its fair share to help vulnerable countries recover from climate impacts and transition to sustainable energy systems, “warm words from visiting lawmakers mean very little to communities on the frontlines.”

Brandon Wu , with ActionAid USA , said the new Democrat-led House majority must reassert control over the budget and hold the Trump administration accountable for “likely illegal actions like dismantling USAID and gutting foreign assistance” funding approved by Congress.

“What they can deliver to the United Nations process is extremely limited,” he said, adding that it’s unlikely there will be any sweeping new climate legislation or climate funding in the next two years. What members of Congress can do is lay the groundwork for more ambitious action in a post-Trump era, he added.

While meeting delegates from other countries, Huffman said he’s heard both gratitude and optimism, as well as skepticism, about a possible US return to the climate talks.

“The fact is the US has become kind of an unreliable partner and we’ve lost our credibility,” he said. “So we’ve tried to bring humility to this moment. We’ve got work to do to reclaim our credibility in this institution.”

Bob Berwyn is an Austria-based reporter who has covered climate science and international climate policy for more than a decade. Previously, he reported on the environment, endangered species, and public lands for several Colorado newspapers, and also worked as editor and assistant editor at community newspapers in the Colorado Rockies.

This story originally appeared on Inside Climate News .

“We want to take the best practices that we’ve heard from all of the global partners… and craft them into good, solid climate policy once we get back to Congress,” said Rep. Lucy McBath (D-Ga.).

The new Democratic majority in the House of Representatives can also use its oversight authority to try to ensure that the money the US has promised for climate aid and sustainable development is restored, said U.S. Rep. Sean Casten (D-Ill.).

Casten said some of America’s European allies are “spending $500, $600 million per day more than before the United States attacked Iran” because of increased oil prices, and that simply stopping those hostilities could free up funding for climate efforts.

“We have lost [the] trust of the international community when it comes to climate,” said Rep. Yassamin Ansari (D-Ariz.).

“I think it is a complete betrayal of our responsibility that Donald Trump has pulled us out of the Paris Agreement not once but twice,” she said. A Democrat winning the 2028 presidential election would help ensure the US can rejoin that agreement, she added.

It will take time to regain trust in the international community, Ansari said.

“But we will come back,” she said, “working 10 times harder, 50 times harder than we did before, to make sure that we are being team players, to make sure that we are… supporting small island developing states and supporting vulnerable African nations.”

Climate activists reacted cautiously to the promises about the United States’ potential return to the international climate arena.

“We welcome the political shift in the United States that puts the brakes on the reckless dismantling of domestic green policies,” said Harjeet Singh, director of Satat Sampada Climate Foundation . “However, here at COP31 in Antalya, the international community cannot afford to celebrate prematurely or suffer from collective amnesia.”

Singh said the US has a long history of obstructing climate negotiations across successive administrations and regardless of which party holds power.

“As the world’s largest historical emitter, the US carries an outsized moral and legal responsibility to act,” he said. “Real change will not be measured by who walks through the halls of this summit, but by whether Washington finally ends its expansion of oil, gas, and coal at home and delivers hundreds of billions of dollars in grant-based climate finance to developing countries.”

Singh said until the US pays its fair share to help vulnerable countries recover from climate impacts and transition to sustainable energy systems, “warm words from visiting lawmakers mean very little to communities on the frontlines.”

Brandon Wu , with ActionAid USA , said the new Democrat-led House majority must reassert control over the budget and hold the Trump administration accountable for “likely illegal actions like dismantling USAID and gutting foreign assistance” funding approved by Congress.

“What they can deliver to the United Nations process is extremely limited,” he said, adding that it’s unlikely there will be any sweeping new climate legislation or climate funding in the next two years. What members of Congress can do is lay the groundwork for more ambitious action in a post-Trump era, he added.

While meeting delegates from other countries, Huffman said he’s heard both gratitude and optimism, as well as skepticism, about a possible US return to the climate talks.

“The fact is the US has become kind of an unreliable partner and we’ve lost our credibility,” he said. “So we’ve tried to bring humility to this moment. We’ve got work to do to reclaim our credibility in this institution.”

Bob Berwyn is an Austria-based reporter who has covered climate science and international climate policy for more than a decade. Previously, he reported on the environment, endangered species, and public lands for several Colorado newspapers, and also worked as editor and assistant editor at community newspapers in the Colorado Rockies.

This story originally appeared on Inside Climate News .

# New bi-national art initiative reframes stereotypes about Mexico-US border

## New bi-national art initiative reframes stereotypes about Mexico-US border

## Drawing from the art scenes in El Paso, Texas, and Ciudad Juárez, Chihuahua, Sutura explores the border’s dynamic realities

Exterior view of Azul Arena in Ciudad Juárez, Mexico, with mural ¡Pásele, pásele! by LxsDos Courtesy of Azul Arena, 2025

Can the “open wound” of the Mexico-US border be healed? Sutura , a new bi-national art programme in Ciudad Juárez, Chihuahua, and El Paso, Texas (18 November-22 November), looks beyond stereotypes of violence surrounding the Mexico-US border and explores how art might help mend the region’s many wounds, even imperfectly or temporarily. Sutura (Spanish for “suture”) brings together more than 100 artists across 20 venues, including the El Paso Museum of Art (EPMA), the Stanlee and Gerald Rubin Center for the Visual Arts and the Museo de Arte de Ciudad Juárez (MACJ), alongside independent projects and pop-up exhibitions.

Juárez has long been associated with sensational narratives of violence. Persistent migration issues, heightened by stricter border controls and alarming deportation measures, feminicides, the drug war and hyper-surveillance have shaped the local context. These aspects have permeated cultural production. “Endless works have explored this territory as a symbol and symptom of an apocalyptic future,” writes Willivaldo Delgadillo in his book-length essay Fabular Juárez (2020) .

Though seemingly worlds apart today, Ciudad Juárez and El Paso were one city until the Rio Grande river was established as the border between Mexico and the US in 1848. Despite tensions between their respective countries, the two cities are still connected by education, jobs and transit.

“On each side of the border, nuanced and contrasting fears and ideologies coexist, but there is also community,” Edgar Picazo Merino, Sutura’s founder and lead organiser, tells The Art Newspaper . “For all of us who live here, the border is a personal, lived experience.” Picazo founded the independent initiative Azul Arena in 2019 to support the Juárez-El Paso art scene; it established a permanent space in Juárez in 2022.

Central to thinking about the border in the context of Sutura and more broadly is Chicana writer Gloria Anzaldúa’s 1987 metaphor of the border as an “open wound”. “The Third World grates against the first and bleeds,” Anzaldúa wrote. “And before a scab forms, it haemorrhages again, the lifeblood of two worlds merging to form a third country—a border culture.” The “open wound” concept has become commonplace in border literature, Picazo says, while Sutura seeks to deconstruct it: “If the border is a wound, how can the arts suture its many wounds, while opening places of reflection and interaction?”

Detail of Justin Favela's Mantecore (White Tiger) (2017), featured in Qué tanto es tantito , a group show on view at San Luis Contemporáneo, Ciudad Juárez Courtesy Haydee Alonso

Sutura builds on binational initiatives like Insite , which emerged in 1992 at the San Diego-Tijuana border and initially featured site-specific installations before changing formats. It also draws on regional ties. The Juárez-El Paso Border Biennial, launched in 2008 by the EPMA and MACJ, is currently in its eighth edition, Imagining the Border (until 2 May 2027). Co-curated by the Juárez-based curators Adriana Miramontes Olivas and Alejandro Morales, it features more than 80 works by artists based within 300 miles of El Paso and Juárez.

“A border that is always there, one that weighs heavily on our communities, rarely lets us imagine it,” Morales says. “This edition opens that space, offering a plural and rigorous portrait of it as living territory.”

The Border Biennial has strived to shift perceptions. “The biennial has national relevance, moving beyond portrayals of the border as perpetually on fire, highlighting its creative richness and cultural legacies,” says Edward Hayes Jr, the director of the EPMA, adding that the project requires overcoming diplomatic and logistical challenges. “We aim for the biennial to be a structural project for both institutions,” says Christian Diego Diego, MACJ’s director. Diego adds that over its past and current editions, the Border Biennial has featured more than 400 works by around 270 artists, “reflecting the border’s ambivalence and multiple stories”. Sutura’s programme includes visits to the biennial, reflecting dialogue with the artists, curators and venues.

Sutura also grew from asking how a Juárez-El Paso art week might unfold. Border initiatives are gaining visibility. The fair Material, through its two-year Projects programme, has supported Azul Arena and the Juárez curatorial duo Un Dique with mentorship and free participation in its Mexico City and Guadalajara fairs. Un Dique joins Sutura by curating theexhibition Border Kaijus on border hypervigilance. Two other border cities have recently created art weeks amid growing efforts to decentralise a national scene largely centred on Mexico City: Tijuana held its second art week in July; Mexicali held its first in April.

“There is a growing scene among border Mexican cities with spaces and initiatives interacting,” says Andres Payan Estrada, the director and chief curator of the Stanlee and Gerald Rubin Center for the Visual Arts and Sutura’s artistic strategy director. Still, he adds, Sutura is not an art week: “It is a non-commercial collaborative initiative with a strong community component.”

Installation view of the group show Costuras Territoriales at the Stanlee and Gerald Rubin Center for the Visual Arts at the University of Texas, El Paso Courtesy of the Stanlee and Gerald Rubin Center for the Visual Arts at the University of Texas, El Paso

In El Paso, institutional participation is strong. During Sutura, the Rubin Center is showing Costuras Territoriales (until 12 December) , curated by Payan and featuring textile-inspired works by five women artists connected to the border, including Teresa Margolles, Tania Candiani and Juárez-based Olga Guerra. “The way in which artists explore the border has sometimes become a cliché,” Guerra says. “I intend to reflect relationality through a more poetic approach, incorporating locally found organic materials and fibres, along with reused materials.”

Independent initiatives are vital in Juárez, where conventional galleries are non-existent. Picazo’s Azul Arena, a pillar of the city’s scene, will present the exhibition En la línea , exploring the line as a metaphor for the border. The Juárez-based artist Haydee Alonso, co-founder of San Luis Contemporáneo , will curate the exhibition ¿Qué tanto es tantito? there and present a performance at Azul Arena. “My work analyses transborder relations through the body and objects, opening spaces within the complexities of living here,” says Alonso, who crosses the border daily to teach at the University of Texas at El Paso. Both projects have received support from the Mellon Foundation , which Alonso and Picazo consider crucial to local initiatives. In El Paso, where independent spaces are relatively scarce, The Falstaff , a community-centred hybrid art space, will host exhibitions and concerts.

Installation view ofthe group exhibiton Qué tanto es tantito , group show on view at San Luis Contemporáneo, Ciudad Juárez Courtesy Haydee Alonso

Sutura also supports the local scene by showcasing six El Paso and Juárez projects selected through an open call, with each project receiving $3,000 for production costs. The photography exhibition Relatos de la Frontera: Cuerpo y Espacio explores border perspectives through the body and space Another show, Tierra Suelta , presents works inspired by children of migrant families that settled in Juárez for reasons other than the “American dream”, integrating a community activation into the programme. These projects foreground local perspectives in a region often depicted by outsiders, alongside established artists—primarily Mexican and Mexican American—whose work reflects on the border.

Picazo acknowledges the complexities of a bi-national event: not everyone can cross both ways because of visa restrictions and other issues. “The programme has parallel activities so you can experience Sutura even from one side of the border,” he says.

Sutura speaks more of resilience than crisis, more of possibility than scarcity.“Historically, the border is explained one-dimensionally, yet a myriad of dynamics co-exist here,” Picazo says. “Sutura exists as a relational art encounter.”

- Sutura , 18 November-22 November, various locations, Ciudad Juárez, Mexico, El Paso, United States

In 2016, [XLN Audio](https://musictech.com/brands/xln-audio/) released RC-20 Retro Color, a multi-effect [plugin](https://musictech.com/tag/plugins/) for recreating the “warm feeling of [vintage](https://musictech.com/tag/vintage/) [recording](https://musictech.com/tag/recording/) equipment.” Its release also happened to coincide with the rise in lo-fi hip-hop, becoming the go-to plugin for degrading, smudging and otherwise badifying your audio. In the process, RC-20 inspired legions of copycat all-in-one lo-fi processors. Now, ten years on, XLN Audio has released a proper update, bringing the software to version 2. Is there still room for Retro Color in a world saturated with cookie-cutter saturation plugins?

In a word: yes.

RC-20 v2 is being billed as an update and not a new plugin (old presets still work—in fact, it will automatically import them from version 1), but the upgrade brings enough new features to the table to make it a must-download.

In fact, RC-20 V2 is so good that you may as well just drag all those other lo-fi plugins into the trash right now. You won’t need another one.

- Editor’s pick: [XLN Audio’s new DB-30 Drum Butter is a delicious delight](https://musictech.com/reviews/plug-ins/xln-audio-db-30-drum-butter-review/)

As this is an update, I’ll focus on what’s new, but in case you’re new to the concept, RC-20 is a processor aimed at making your audio sound…well…bad.

You get six modules to accomplish this intentional sound-bad-izing, each tackling a specific grungifier: Noise, Wobble for wow and flutter-type [effects](https://musictech.com/tag/effects/), Distort, Digital to reduce sample and bit rates, Space (also known as [reverb](https://musictech.com/tag/reverb/)) and Loss, which includes the original Magnetic plus a new processor, Codec – more on this gem later. Dial each module in (or turn off as needed), add some sweetening in the master section, and your track is cooked. In a good way, of course.

For version 2, XLN Audio has taken this idea and added more, bringing it not only in line with modern workflows but also pushing RC-20 ahead of the lo-fi pack with an unexpected delay section, new effects throughout, and general improvements that make it even better. Swappable modules, anyone?

Let’s start with the Echo section, as it’s the biggest change to the workflow and also indicative of where XLN Audio has gone with RC-20. It is, as you might expect, a delay, and it sits in the signal path after the general effects chain. Although it has all of the usual delay parameters such as feedback and time divisions, it’s capable of much more. This isn’t just an off-the-shelf delay codged onto RC-20. It’s a wild and beautiful thing in its own right.

For starters, along with a blend for the main audio path, each standard effects module has its own slider to contribute processing to Echo’s feedback signal. So you could, for example, cause the feedback to wobble with tape-style wow and flutter via the Wobble module. Or degrade it with digital processing. Or worse. And again, this is just the feedback. So beautifully bizarre. To top it off, Echo also includes a grain section. Granular processing is all the rage with reverbs, but in a vintage-style delay? Not only can your delay taps get processed by each module, but they can also be smeared out into ambient grain clouds. Surely this is madness. The geniuses at XLN Audio have also dropped in a Varispeed parameter for [Hainbach](https://musictech.com/artists/hainbach/)-style, pitched-down playback at 1/2, 1/4, and 1/8 speeds, plus a Scrub slider to bend echoes, much like engineers of the past did by physically manipulating a tape machine. Honestly, Echo is so good, it really deserves to be broken out into a plugin of its own.

The other new marquee parameter is Codec. Now bundled with Magnetic in a column called Loss, it recreates the sound of lossy audio like MP3s, with controls for Dropouts, Stretch and Blur. You can blend between Lossy and Formant modes as well, which is great for fine-tuning between dropped data packet madness and glitchy instability. It may not be the most immediately useful effect, especially at its dark and blurry extremes, but the time will probably come when you’ll want a buffering Y2K effect, and you’ll be glad you had it.

The other modules have been sprinkled with additional lo-fi dust, such as the new tape, classic preamp and four-track cassette distortion algorithms, and Sputter and Drive parameters in Digital. Noise also gets a pre/post blend so you can push the noise through the signal chain or let it float over everything for maximum Merzbow. But the real star of the show is Space, which has been kingsized to a total of 33 reverb types (that’s 32 more than version 1, remember). Many are expected, such as the chambers, halls and springs, while others are decidedly not. Lightning or Thunder as a reverb? Spectral reverb?! This is out there stuff.

There’s more, of course. The Flux parameter, which adds unpredictability and variation to each module, has a lovely new animated interface, and is especially welcome now in the Echo section too. Focus and Cut let you apply module effects exactly where you want them on the frequency spectrum, leaving the original audio untouched (the former) or shelved right off (the latter). There’s also tempo sync for time-based effects, loudness match for auditioning changes without having to deal with volume bias, master compression, and more.

RC-20 Retro Color 2 is more than just a wealth of parameters and module algorithms, numerous though they are. What really makes this plugin worth your time—and why other lo-fi plugin developers will soon be shaking in their muddy boots—is because it sounds so darn good. It’s a real irony that something dedicated to making your music sound like trash should have the opposite effect.

What makes RC-20 particularly impressive, however, is how alive it sounds. With all of the motion possibilities, plus the Flux parameter, as well as all the ways that Echo can percolate, all result in processing that is incredibly organic. And that’s before you start automating parameters like the overall Magnitude slider. Rather than set it and forget it, you’ll be reaching for RC-20 when you want to set things in motion.

If you’re yet to dive into the wonderful world of Retro Color, now is definitely the time. If you own version 1, upgrading is a no-brainer. Beautiful and musical are not usually associated with the concept of lo-fi, but RC-20 is the exception that’s going to change the rule.

## Key features

- Lo-fi multi-effects processor (VST3, AU, AAX)
- 6 swappable modules: Noise, Wobble, Distort, Digital, Space, Loss
- Includes new Echo module with grain delays
- New algorithms including lossy codec effects
- Focus and cut filters for targeted frequency processing
- Tempo sync
- Loudness match
- New presets and preset browser
- Compatible with v1
- Upgrade and loyalty pricing

items.articleBody:
In the amusing yet sobering *[Saturday Night Live](https://laughingsquid.com/?s=Saturday+Night+Live)* sketch, comedian [John Mulaney](https://www.johnmulaney.com/) presented a parody pharmaceutical ad for “Sister”, a simple 24/7, live-in solution that would attend to Father’s elder care so that Brother could still do the things he wanted to do in life.

> My dad means the world to me. So when I noticed him start to slow down, I knew I needed to get him the best care possible. I didn’t want to put him in a nursing home, but a private health aide could cost thousands a week. I didn’t know where to turn. That’s when I heard about Sister. Sister is a live in 24/7 elder care provider that is completely free, and also your sister.

The ad further explained that availability wasn’t a problem, as the caretaker role had been ingrained in Sister’s brain for years, allowing Brother to shed all responsibility except for the occasional visit.

> Here’s how it works. First, years of internalized sexism warp Sister’s brain into thinking caretaking is her responsibility and somehow not yours. Next, your text arrives, instantly activating her. And that’s it. You’re done for life.

Of course, there’s always the fine print.

> Quantities are limited. Sister may break down without warning. Offer void if Sister has a good therapist.

The sketch hit so close to home that, as [CinemaBlend noted](https://www.cinemablend.com/television/snl-sketch-caretakers-sister-john-mulaney), many viewers weren’t sure whether to laugh or cry.
