items.articleBody:
Midterm results showed that men under 30 (a supposed MAGA bulwark) shifted back to voting mostly for Democrats. Louise Perry and I spoke about whether that signals the end of the New Right.

Among other things, we discuss whether perceptions of corruption played a role. Voters will overlook a president lining his pockets, so long as they themselves feel prosperous. But the economy feels shaky for many people. Moreover, we discuss whether the online right on X made the same mistake the online left made back when it was still called Twitter: confusing applause from fellow partisans with the preferences of normal people.

Louise and I also speak about whether it’s true that “the left can’t meme.” We converge on an answer that involves censorship, 4chan, sex differences in humor, esoteric messaging, and why so much political imagery now looks like it was made for toddlers. We also get into what I heard Dave Chappelle recently say at Madison Square Garden about Charlie Kirk.

Finally, I asked Louise a question every man has wondered about women’s group chats. Her answer was not what I expected.

[↗ robkhenderson.com](https://www.robkhenderson.com/p/did-the-new-right-meme-itself-out)

items.articleBody:
Optimism is a rare sight in this day and age — which is why scholar Arlene Dávila’s unabashed excitement about Latinx art right now is so invigorating. These artists draw from vernacular traditions, community histories, family memories, and more to reframe the narrative, despite facing a barrage of attacks in recent years. “The work of these new visionaries is a rallying cry,” she writes in an opinion piece today. “Now is the time to write, create, and make art boldly — together.”

Read on for a pulse on the rest of the art world, from novelist Stephanie Wambugu on Mary Lovelace O’Neal’s first posthumous exhibition, to Martin Puryear’s quietly revolutionary sculptures, to a new film reevaluating Frida Kahlo’s legacy and commodification. And it wouldn’t be the art world without some auction drama. Today, heirs of the Jewish publisher Samuel Fischer call on Sotheby’s to withdraw a Van Gogh painting it valued at $180 million, alleging that the work was sold under duress during World War II. Meanwhile, at Christie’s, a Willem de Kooning painting that entered the Whitney’s collection just a few years ago is headed under the hammer as Marquee Week kicks off in NYC.

*—Lisa Yin Zhang, associate editor*

[Latinx Artists Are the New Visionaries](https://hyperallergic.com/latinx-artists-are-the-new-visionaries/)

Latinx communities are facing one of the most aggressive series of attacks in recent history, with many families enduring the pain of separation, persecution, and dehumanization. But if you’ve been paying attention to Latinx arts and culture, you’ll see that as we are being told to hide and disappear, artists are stepping into newfound confidence, showcasing the full value and complexity of our identities. | Arlene Dávila

[↗ hyperallergic.com](https://hyperallergic.com/latinx-artists-are-the-new-visionaries/)

SPONSORED

**“Mighty Miniatures” Features Over 300 Tiny Artworks From Indigenous Communities Across the Western Hemisphere**

Opening November 21 at the National Museum of the American Indian in New York, this exhibition includes masterpieces created over a span of nearly two centuries.

[Learn more](https://hyperallergic.com/mighty-miniatures-features-over-300-tiny-artworks-from-indigenous-communities-across-the-western-hemisphere/)

## News

- Many arts and culture organizations are bracing for what could be a series of [politically targeted attacks from the Trump administration](https://hyperallergic.com/draconian-trump-executive-order-could-strip-art-orgs-of-nonprofit-status/) after reports that the White House is considering an executive order that would strip nonprofits deemed to have alleged “terrorist ties” of their tax-exempt status.
- Heirs of a prominent Jewish publishing family [call on Sotheby’s to withdraw a rare Vincent van Gogh painting](https://hyperallergic.com/restitution-claim-on-180m-van-gogh-shakes-up-sothebys-marquee-week/) highlighted in the marquee auction sales in New York City this week, claiming that the work had been sold under duress amid Nazi persecution in Europe.
- The Whitney Museum of American Art [is selling a Willem de Kooning painting](https://hyperallergic.com/why-is-the-whitney-museum-selling-a-de-kooning-painting/) from its collection to Christie’s for its 20th-century evening sale

SPONSORED

**Advance Your Creative Practice With a Graduate Degree From the University of Louisville**

All MFA and MA students receive generous scholarships, with additional support for research, creative projects, and travel.

[Learn more](https://hyperallergic.com/advance-your-creative-practice-with-a-graduate-degree-from-the-university-of-louisville/)

## From Our Critics

[What Mary Lovelace O’Neal Left Behind](https://hyperallergic.com/what-mary-lovelace-oneal-left-behind/)

*Requiem* is a fitting self-elegy for the painter, precisely because nothing about it feels mournful. | Stephanie Wambugu

[↗ hyperallergic.com](https://hyperallergic.com/what-mary-lovelace-oneal-left-behind/)

[Martin Puryear’s Liberatory Violence](https://hyperallergic.com/martin-puryears-liberatory-violence/)

A concern with liberation and revolution runs throughout his exhibition at the High Museum. | Jasmine Amussen

[↗ hyperallergic.com](https://hyperallergic.com/martin-puryears-liberatory-violence/)

[Tate Turns Julio Le Parc Into Instagram Art](https://hyperallergic.com/tate-turns-julio-le-parc-into-instagram-art/)

The show elides the artist’s political motivations, instead cheerfully encouraging visitors to “let these mesmerizing works engage your senses.” | Natalie Weis

[↗ hyperallergic.com](https://hyperallergic.com/tate-turns-julio-le-parc-into-instagram-art/)

[What Does Frida Kahlo Mean Today?](https://hyperallergic.com/what-does-frida-kahlo-mean-today/)

A new documentary poses this question across socio-cultural contexts, steering clear of whitewashing the artist’s personal history. | Eileen G’Sell

[↗ hyperallergic.com](https://hyperallergic.com/what-does-frida-kahlo-mean-today/)

SPONSORED

**Exhibition as Living Archive: the 1950s Baghdad Modern Art Group in the UAE Today**

All Manner of Experiments: Legacies of the Baghdad Modern Art Group, Curated by Nada Shabout, on view at the NYU Abu Dhabi Art Gallery through January 3, 2027.

[Learn more](https://hyperallergic.com/exhibition-as-living-archive-the-1950s-baghdad-modern-art-group-in-the-uae-today/)

## Hyper Links

- Philosopher Alice Crary reflects on how the New School’s [recent overhauls threaten its academic freedom](https://publicseminar.org/2026/11/if-it-can-happen-at-the-new-school/?ref=hyperallergic.com). [ Public Seminar ]
- Satanic panic is back, if the backlash to Netflix’s The Body, a new horror show [set at a Catholic High School, is any indication](https://www.sheknows.com/entertainment/articles/1235093059/the-body-petition/?ref=hyperallergic.com). [ SheKnows ]
- Anti-Zionism runs strong all around the world, as seen in a [painting unveiling in Napoli, Italy](https://www.instagram.com/reel/DfpT1FxOylM/?utm_source=ig_web_copy_link&mdxt=NTc4MTIwNjQ2YQ==). [Instagram]
- Memester account @diallectuals [speaks out on the Artnet x Kalshi partnership](https://www.instagram.com/p/DfsXFAVn8ie/?xtok=MTV4eGRleWphcHB6MQ%3D%3D&img_index=4&ref=hyperallergic.com). [Instagram]
- A thread on Tumblr-era Williamsburg, the [most romanticized time on today’s internet, from one who lived it](https://www.instagram.com/p/Dfk28ngkogS/?utm_source=ig_web_copy_link&psln=NTc4MTIwNjQ2YQ%3D%3D). [Instagram]

items.articleBody:
Die [Stiftung Warentest](https://www.iphone-ticker.de/tag/stiftung-warentest/) haben wir in den vergangenen 20 Jahren nicht unbedingt als erste Anlaufstelle für praktische Smartphone-Tipps wahrgenommen. Inzwischen hat sich das Bild jedoch verändert.

#### Soll helfen: Das iPhone mit Graustufen

Die Technikberichterstattung der in die Jahre gekommenen Institution wirkt zuletzt wieder deutlich alltagsnäher und weit entfernt vom Image der grauharigen Waschmaschinentester. Das freut uns. Ein aktueller [Auftritt im ZDF-Mittagsmagazin](https://www.zdfheute.de/video/zdf-mittagsmagazin/smartphone-stress-tipps-100.html) liefert dafür ein gutes Beispiel.

Unter der Frage, wie sich Smartphone-Stress reduzieren lässt, gibt die Stiftung Warentest konkrete Empfehlungen, die sich auf iPhone und Android-Geräten ohne zusätzliche Anschaffungen umsetzen lassen. Ausgangspunkt ist eine bekannte Beobachtung: Oft greifen wir zum iPhone, ohne überhaupt etwas Konkretes erledigen zu wollen. Laut dem ZDF-Beitrag verbringen Deutsche durchschnittlich drei Stunden täglich mit ihrem Gerät.

## Benachrichtigungen abschalten, Farben reduzieren

Die erste Empfehlung betrifft die Mitteilungen. Wer nicht ständig auf neue Nachrichten, Hinweise und App-Aktivitäten reagieren möchte, sollte zunächst sämtliche Benachrichtigungstöne deaktivieren. Anschließend lässt sich für jede Anwendung einzeln entscheiden, ob sie überhaupt noch Mitteilungen anzeigen darf. Klingt simpel, muss aber erst mal angegangen werden.

#### Weniger Smartphone-Stress: Was hilft?

Ein zweiter Vorschlag betrifft die Darstellung des Bildschirms. Die Umstellung auf Graustufen nimmt der Benutzeroberfläche ihre auffälligen Farben. App-Symbole verlieren dadurch einen Teil ihrer Signalwirkung. Gerade die gewohnten Farbreize sollen Nutzer schließlich dazu verleiten, bestimmte Anwendungen immer wieder zu öffnen.

Beide Maßnahmen gehören auch zu einem [bereits im Februar vorgestellten Fünf-Schritte-Ansatz](https://www.iphone-ticker.de/zu-viel-zeit-am-iphone-ein-fuenf-schritte-ansatz-fuer-mehr-distanz-273250/), mit dem sich die Smartphone-Nutzung bewusster gestalten lässt. Auch hier spielt eine reizarm eingerichtete Benutzeroberfläche eine wichtige Rolle.

## Fokusmodi schaffen Ruhe ohne Funkstille

Als dritte Maßnahme empfiehlt Warentest, das Smartphone stärker an den eigenen Tagesablauf anzupassen. Also, Fokusmodi aktiv nutzen. [Über unterschiedliche Fokusmodi](https://support.apple.com/de-de/guide/iphone/iphd6288a67f/ios) lässt sich beispielsweise festlegen, dass während der Arbeit nur ausgewählte Kontakte anrufen dürfen. So bleiben Partner oder die Kita erreichbar, während andere Unterbrechungen ausbleiben.

#### Fokusmodi: Kennen viele, nutzen wenige

Das ZDF verweist zudem auf Erkenntnisse aus der Kommunikationsforschung. Weil Smartphones regelmäßig kleine Belohnungen in Form neuer Nachrichten, Videos oder Reaktionen liefern, entwickeln Nutzer die Gewohnheit, immer wieder nachzusehen. Genau diesen Automatismus sollen die vorgeschlagenen Einstellungen unterbrechen.

Wer mehr Abstand benötigt, kann auch zu speziellen [Apps wie MeBeMe](https://www.iphone-ticker.de/kostenlose-iphone-app-will-euch-vom-doomscrolling-loesen-282102/) greifen. Noch hartnäckiger sind Hardware-Lösungen wie die stuttgarter [Zenbox mit ihrer NFC-Sperre](https://www.iphone-ticker.de/digitale-auszeiten-nfc-box-schraenkt-app-nutzung-ein-273804/), die das Öffnen ausgewählter Anwendungen bewusst erschwert.

[★ iPhone-Ticker bei Google bevorzugen ★](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=iphone-ticker.de)

Der Beitrag [Weniger Smartphone-Stress: Warentest gibt einfache Tipps](https://www.iphone-ticker.de/weniger-smartphone-stress-warentest-gibt-einfache-tipps-290829/) Wurde zuerst auf [iphone-ticker.de](https://www.iphone-ticker.de) veröffentlicht.

items.title: Geplante Änderungen der DSGVO: Datenmissbrauch am Arbeitsplatz könnte bald schwerer aufzudecken sein
items.subtitle: Die EU-Kommission hat den Digital Omnibus vorgeschlagen, ohne zuvor eine umfassende Folgenabschätzung durchzuführen.

items.articleBody:
Die EU-Kommission hat den Digital Omnibus vorgeschlagen, ohne zuvor eine umfassende Folgenabschätzung durchzuführen. Eine Studie des Europäischen Gewerkschaftsinstituts untersucht die möglichen Folgen. Nach Einschätzung der Autoren schwächt der Vorschlag die Datenschutzrechte von Beschäftigten in der EU.

Uber-Fahrer nutzten DSGVO-Datenzugriffsanfragen, um ihre Arbeitnehmerrechte zu verteidigen. – Alle Rechte vorbehalten: NurPhoto via Imago

Verlust der Kontrolle über persönliche Daten, übermäßige Überwachung, ungerechte automatisierte Entscheidungen, verborgene Kennzahlen und undurchsichtiges algorithmisches Management: All dies sind Formen von Datenmissbrauch am Arbeitsplatz, die künftig erheblich schwerer nachzuweisen sein könnten. Zu diesem Ergebnis kommt eine Studie des [Europäischen Gewerkschaftsinstituts](https://www.etui.org/publications/conditions-legal-protection), die den vorgeschlagenen Digital Omnibus untersucht.

Der [Digital Omnibus](https://www.europarl.europa.eu/legislative-train/theme-a-new-plan-for-europe-s-sustainable-prosperity-and-competitiveness/file-digital-package) wird derzeit im Europäischen Parlament diskutiert. Das von der Europäischen Kommission vorgeschlagene Gesetzespaket betrifft unter anderem die [Datenschutz-Grundverordnung](https://gdpr-info.eu/) (DSGVO), das zentrale EU-Gesetz zum Schutz personenbezogener Daten. Der Vorschlag könnte beispielsweise Auskunftsanfragen nach der DSGVO einschränken, wenn sie Zwecken dienen, die über den Datenschutz hinausgehen, etwa um Beweise für einen arbeitsrechtlichen Streit zu sammeln.

Die Kommission präsentiert den neuen Rechtsrahmen als Maßnahme zur Vereinfachung und Steigerung der Wettbewerbsfähigkeit. Nach ihren Schätzungen könnte das Paket bis 2029 Verwaltungskosten von bis zu 5 Milliarden Euro einsparen. Mehr als 100 zivilgesellschaftliche Organisationen bezeichneten den Vorschlag hingegen als [„Versuch, Europas stärkste Schutzmaßnahmen gegen digitale Bedrohungen heimlich abzubauen“](https://noyb.eu/sites/default/files/2025-11/The%20EU%20must%20uphold%20hard-won%20protections%20for%20digital%20human%20rights.pdf).

Was könnten diese Änderungen für Beschäftigte bedeuten, die sich dagegen wehren wollen, wie ihre Daten verwendet werden? Da die EU-Kommission für den Digital Omnibus keine Folgenabschätzung durchgeführt hat, erstellten die Autoren Aida Ponce Del Castillo und Thomas le Bonniec im Auftrag des Europäischen Gewerkschaftsinstituts diese Studie.

Um die möglichen Auswirkungen der Änderungen zu untersuchen, wandten die Autoren sie rückwirkend als hypothetisches Szenario auf vier Fälle aus der Arbeitswelt an. Diese hatten zuvor zu behördlichen Maßnahmen oder erfolgreichen Klagen gegen Datenmissbrauch am Arbeitsplatz geführt. [Darunter waren Fälle, an denen die Fahrdienstplattformen Uber und Ola beteiligt waren.](https://netzpolitik.org/2020/uber-fahrer-wollen-transparenz-ueber-daten-und-algorithmen/)

## Beweislast verschiebt sich zu Beschäftigten

In einem der Fälle verlangten sechs Uber-Fahrer Zugang zu personenbezogenen Daten und Informationen darüber, wie sich die Systeme der Plattform auf ihre Arbeit auswirkten. Dazu gehörten Informationen über die Vermittlung von Fahrten, die Preisgestaltung und Bewertungen. Sie wollten nachvollziehen, wie Ubers algorithmische Managementsysteme Entscheidungen über sie trafen oder beeinflussten. Ein ähnliches Verfahren wurde gegen Ola angestrengt, ein Fahrdienstunternehmen mit Sitz in Indien.

2023 gab das Berufungsgericht Amsterdam den Forderungen der Fahrer schließlich statt und verpflichtete Uber und Ola dazu, bestimmte personenbezogene Daten und aussagekräftige Informationen über bestimmte automatisierte Entscheidungssysteme offenzulegen.

Die Fahrer nutzten ihre bestehenden Auskunftsrechte nach der DSGVO, um für ihre Klage wichtige Informationen zu erhalten. Die Autoren der Studie argumentieren, dass vergleichbare Ergebnisse durch die Änderungen des Digital Omnibus künftig schwieriger zu erreichen sein könnten.

Die vorgeschlagenen Änderungen würden diesen Prüfmaßstab verändern. Allein die Tatsache, dass eine menschliche Alternative möglich gewesen wäre, würde künftig nicht mehr ausreichen, um zu argumentieren, dass die automatisierte Verarbeitung nicht notwendig war.

Übertragen auf den Uber-Fall wäre Uber dadurch nach Ansicht der Autoren rechtlich in einer stärkeren Position. Das Unternehmen könnte argumentieren, dass die automatisierte Betrugserkennung für die Erfüllung seines Vertragsverhältnisses mit den Fahrern notwendig war, selbst wenn stattdessen auch ein Mensch die Entscheidung hätte treffen können.

Die Autoren kommen zu dem Schluss, dass der Rechtsweg zu vergleichbaren Ergebnissen wie in den Uber-/Ola-Fällen unter den vorgeschlagenen Änderungen schwieriger geworden wäre: Die Fahrer hätten bei der Beschaffung von Informationen vor größeren Hürden stehen können. Gleichzeitig wäre Uber in einer stärkeren Position gewesen, um automatisierte Entscheidungen rechtlich zu rechtfertigen.

## Regeln für Hochrisiko-KI-Systeme gelten erst später

Ein Teil des [Digital-Omnibus-Pakets zum Thema KI](https://artificialintelligenceact.eu/ai-act-explorer/digital-omnibus/) wurde bereits im Juli dieses Jahres verabschiedet. Dadurch wurde die Anwendung der Anforderungen der EU-KI-Verordnung für Hochrisiko-Systeme um 16 Monate nach hinten auf Dezember 2027 verschoben. Dazu gehören auch Anforderungen an bestimmte KI-Systeme, die im Beschäftigungskontext und beim Management von Beschäftigten eingesetzt werden.

Zusammengenommen könnten sich die beiden Änderungspakete nach Ansicht der Autoren gegenseitig verstärken: Schutzmaßnahmen der KI-Verordnung, die schädliche Praktiken verhindern sollen, würden später greifen. Zugleich könnten Änderungen an der DSGVO es Beschäftigten erschweren, solche Praktiken nachträglich zu untersuchen oder anzufechten.

Anders gesagt: Beschäftigte könnten weniger Schutz vor den Auswirkungen von KI-Systemen haben. Gleichzeitig könnten die Hürden höher werden, anschließend herauszufinden, was passiert ist.

items.articleBody:
Melissa Denes in *The Guardian:*

I n 2024, the novelist [Gary Shteyngart](https://www.theguardian.com/books/gary-shteyngart) flew from New York to Milan in search of the perfect midnight-blue suit. There he chose fabric, before flying to Hong Kong to be fitted for four shirts, and on to Tokyo, where he was measured by master tailor Yuhei Yamamoto and master shoemaker Yohei Fukuda. A short king (“five foot five and a half, with that ‘half’ doing a lot of work”), Shteyngart dreamed of a fit to disappear his 52-year-old moobs (“my tatas”, “my chimichangas”) and melt the heart of the toughest maitre d’ at the most in-demand restaurants.

And guess what? The world’s finest craftsmen will give you all that – though Shteyngart, who emigrated from Leningrad to the US in 1979, argues that a great suit serves a deeper need than vanity. Trying it on two days after Trump’s second election, “it was the final certificate of naturalization … I couldn’t make my adopted country fall out of love with fascism, but at least I could enjoy my new shoes.” Clothes become an advanced form of self-care.

More [↗ theguardian.com](https://www.theguardian.com/books/2026/nov/16/the-sensualist-by-gary-shteyngart-review-a-delectable-romp-through-lifes-pleasures).

items.articleBody:
**Wenn ein Mondorbiter in den Schatten des Mondes eintaucht, sinkt die elektrische Leistung seiner Solarmodule. Eine neue Auswertung zeigt, dass sich aus dem Zeitpunkt dieses Einbruchs zusätzliche Hinweise auf die Flugbahn gewinnen lassen. In Modellrechnungen mit Daten des Satelliten CAPSTONE verringerte das Verfahren unter bestimmten Bedingungen den Positionsfehler um rund 61 Prozent.**

**Westminster (U.S.A.).** Raumsonden benötigen präzise Angaben über Position und Geschwindigkeit, damit sie ihre geplante Bahn einhalten können. Bei Flügen zwischen Erde und Mond stammen solche Informationen häufig aus Funkmessungen großer Bodenstationen, deren Kapazitäten begrenzt sind.

Eine kurze Unterbrechung der Stromerzeugung könnte eine zusätzliche Orientierungshilfe liefern. Sobald Erde oder Mond die Sonne verdecken, verändert sich die Leistung der Solarzellen zu berechenbaren Zeitpunkten. Aus diesen Signalen lassen sich bestehende Bahnprognosen verbessern, ohne eine weitere Kamera oder Antenne einzubauen.

### Stromabfall markiert den Schattenrand

Ein noch nicht fachbegutachteter Forschungs-Preprint von Ian M. Down vom Raumfahrtunternehmen Advanced Space und zwei Mitautoren beschreibt, wie sich solche Übergänge für die Navigation nutzen lassen. Die Methode setzt auf ohnehin vorhandene Messdaten der Energieversorgung sowie auf vorausberechnete Positionen von Sonne, Erde und Mond.

Beim Eintritt in den Halbschatten fällt zunächst nur ein Teil des Sonnenlichts weg. Im Kernschatten kommt an den Solarmodulen vorübergehend kein direktes Sonnenlicht mehr an. Ein mathematisches Modell verknüpft die Zeitpunkte dieser Übergänge mit der Flugbahn, sodass ein Navigationsfilter die bisherige Positionsschätzung korrigieren kann.

Die Schattenränder sind dabei nicht vollkommen gleichmäßig, weil Berge und Krater die Silhouette des Mondes verändern. Beim Erdschatten spielen dagegen die Abplattung des Planeten und seine Atmosphäre eine wichtige Rolle. Für diese Unsicherheiten berücksichtigt die Arbeit unter anderem frühere Auswertungen von 22.539 Beobachtungen von Mondfinsternissen aus den Jahren 1842 bis 2011.

### CAPSTONE-Daten bestätigen die Zeitmessung

Für einen Abgleich hat das Team Daten des 2022 gestarteten Kleinsatelliten CAPSTONE ausgewertet, den Advanced Space für die National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) betrieb. Am 11. Januar 2026 durchquerte die Sonde den Kernschatten des Mondes, während ihre Solarsteuerung etwa alle 14,9 Sekunden Messwerte lieferte. Die daraus bestimmten Zeitpunkte für Schatteneintritt und -austritt wichen nur um 0,37 beziehungsweise 6,04 Sekunden von den aus Bahndaten berechneten Zeitpunkten ab.

Wie stark solche Messungen eine Navigation verbessern könnten, untersuchte das Team anschließend mit statistischen Modellrechnungen. Bei einer angenommenen anfänglichen Positionsunsicherheit von 5,33 Kilometern sank der simulierte Positionsfehler durch die beiden Schattenübergänge um 60,8 Prozent. War die Flugbahn zuvor bereits durch eine aktuelle Funkmessung sehr genau bestimmt, betrug die Verbesserung dagegen lediglich 6,3 Prozent.

In einem zweiten Szenario simulierte das Team eine Passage durch den Erdschatten auf einer Bahn nahe einem Gleichgewichtspunkt zwischen Erde und Mond. Hier verringerte die Auswertung von vier Schattenübergängen den statistischen Positionsfehler bei einer anfänglichen Unsicherheit von rund 346 Kilometern um etwa ein Drittel. Beide Rechnungen zeigen damit vor allem einen möglichen Nutzen, wenn die vorherige Bahnschätzung bereits ungenauer geworden ist.

### Eine Ergänzung, kein Ersatz für Funk

Die Schattenmethode bietet jedoch keine ständig verfügbare Navigationshilfe, weil solche Finsternisse auf vielen Flugbahnen selten auftreten. Ein einzelner Durchgang liefert zudem nur begrenzte räumliche Informationen und ersetzt keine vollständige Ortung durch Bodenstationen. Bei CAPSTONE schrumpfte der rechnerische Vorteil nach einer nahen Mondpassage deutlich und lag zehn Stunden später nur noch bei rund acht Prozent.

Der Ansatz benötigt nach dem Konzept keine neuen Messinstrumente, setzt aber vorhandene Telemetrie, präzise Zeitangaben und ein Modell der Himmelskörperbahnen voraus. Die realen CAPSTONE-Daten belegen bislang die Erkennbarkeit der Schattenübergänge, während die Verbesserung der Navigation rechnerisch ermittelt wurde. Ob sich das Verfahren im regulären Betrieb verschiedener Mondmissionen bewährt, ist damit noch offen.

**Quellen:**

- Forschungs-Preprint auf [arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.28669), doi: 10.48550/arXiv.2610.28669
- Offizielle Hintergrundquelle von [National Aeronautics and Space Administration](https://www.nasa.gov/mission/capstone/) (NASA)
- Offizielle Unternehmensquelle von [Advanced Space](https://advancedspace.com/capstone/)

items.articleBody:
## Stencil and Hand Letter Your Way To Happier Holiday Cards

[↗ Primärquelle: mymodernmet.com](https://mymodernmet.com/stencil-hand-letter-holiday-cards/)

Mid-November is prime time for holiday card crafting. A handmade greeting stands out in a stack of mail, and a DIY version of this yearly tradition doesn’t have to take as much time as you might think. With a simple two-skill approach, you can create a stencil-based design that’s easy to replicate and enhance it with beautiful handlettering.

Making a batch of handmade cards doesn’t have to be complicated. First, create a design. A stencil is ideal for this task to keep the design consistent. You can create your own by cutting a motif from thick paper or thin cardboard. Paint over it to replicate the design across all the cards. Your handmade stencil allows you to easily incorporate a variety of holiday motifs, such as stars, snowflakes, or evergreen trees.

If you’re unsure of how to create an effective stencil, you’re in luck. [My Modern Met Academy](https://academy.mymodernmet.com/) has an online course titled [Introduction to Stencil Art](https://academy.mymodernmet.com/courses/intro-stencil-art), taught by renowned artist Alice Pasquini, who specializes in the technique. The go-at-your-own-pace class will show you how to cut your own stencils and the best practices for doing so.

Once you’ve stenciled the design, it’s time to write. The recipient will see the envelope first, so don’t brush off this task. Pretty addressing turns the entire card—envelope and all—into a keepsake. Beautiful hand lettering works well for addressed names. Inside the card, it’s ideal for greetings like “Happy Holidays!”

Hone your handwriting with [Write Out Your Future: Hand Letter an Inspiring Phrase](https://academy.mymodernmet.com/courses/hand-lettering-for-beginners) with Danison Fronda. In his beginner-friendly online class, also on My Modern Met Academy, the lettering artist covers the basics and helps you take what you learn to develop your own style.

Get your cards in the mail by early December, and you’re sure to receive compliments about your gorgeous holiday greetings all month long. In that case, don’t delay. Enroll in *[Introduction to Stencil Art](https://academy.mymodernmet.com/courses/intro-stencil-art)* and *[Write Out Your Future: Hand Letter an Inspiring Phrase](https://academy.mymodernmet.com/courses/hand-lettering-for-beginners)* today.

items.articleBody:
*Introduction by Sophia Grace Carter*

I n September, the photojournalist Lynsey Addario traveled to Venezuela with *Atlantic* staff writer Anne Applebaum. They arrived in a country devastated by back-to-back earthquakes in June and still reeling from the U.S. military operation that had toppled its president, Nicolás Maduro, in January. Drawing on her reporting there, Applebaum argues in *The Atlantic* ’s December issue that the Trump administration has revived a familiar form of Yankee imperialism, laying claim to Venezuela’s oil troves with little regard for the interests of its people. Addario’s images capture the head-spinning transformations under way—and how some citizens are chafing against the new political order and others are attempting to preserve some semblance of normalcy.

*[[From the December 2026 issue: Anne Applebaum on what the U.S. is really doing in Venezuela](https://www.theatlantic.com/magazine/2026/12/trump-oil-venezuela-exploitation/689033/?utm_source=feed)]*

Addario has covered nearly every major global conflict of the past two decades—the U.S. invasions of Afghanistan and Iraq, the genocide in Darfur, the civil wars in Libya and Syria, Russia’s incursion into Ukraine. But she began her career in Latin America at 21, traveling through the region with her camera. In 2002, she documented the aftermath of a failed coup attempt against the regime of Hugo Chávez, Maduro’s predecessor, and, in 2024, for this magazine, she photographed a group of [migrants crossing the Darién Gap](https://www.theatlantic.com/magazine/archive/2024/09/darien-gap-route-migrants-panama/679156/?utm_source=feed), many of them Venezuelan. Nearly 8 million Venezuelans—about [25 percent of the population](https://unric.org/en/far-from-the-headlines-one-in-four-venezuelans-have-left-the-country/)—have fled the country over the past decade.

On this year’s trip, she witnessed the circumstances that have driven that exodus. Once the richest country in South America, Venezuela now suffers from the world’s highest inflation rate, driven by a quarter century of political fracturing, corruption, economic mismanagement, and U.S. sanctions. Though the country possesses the world’s largest proven oil reserves—more than 300 billion barrels—electricity shortages are a fact of life, and many Venezuelans live in poverty amid crumbling infrastructure.

When the earthquakes struck in June, the government’s ineffectual response left citizens to fend for themselves. The tremors killed at least 6,500 people; injured more than 16,800; and left about 17,000 homeless. In La Guaira, the city hardest hit, government rescue workers didn’t show up for days, so residents and volunteers mobilized to deliver aid on their own, turning schools into makeshift shelters and opening soup kitchens.

Heeding the war photographer Robert Capa’s dictum that “If your pictures aren’t good enough, you’re not close enough,” Addario often spends time talking with her subjects before photographing them, trying to understand their life and circumstances. These conversations can be fraught, and Addario told me that she sometimes becomes the target of her subjects’ anger and frustration. But she can also serve as an outlet for them. In La Guaira, where she encountered people digging through the wreckage with their bare hands in search of the bodies of the missing, she sensed that some were grateful to have their loss memorialized. Months had passed, and they were still there searching. By photographing them, Addario hoped she might help ensure that “they don’t feel like it’s all been forgotten.”

— [Sophia Grace Carter](https://www.theatlantic.com/author/sophia-grace-carter/?utm_source=feed)

Lynsey Addario for *The Atlantic*

Jeanpier Bolívar, 34, and Juan José Meléndez, 27, pull in a nearly empty fishing net on Lake Maracaibo, a brackish estuary where oil extraction began more than a century ago. The lake is South America’s largest body of water—and its largest environmental disaster. Local fishermen say their catches have dwindled as pollution has worsened, and some resort to rinsing their crabs and shrimp with gasoline to remove the crude oil.

Lynsey Addario for *The Atlantic*

A thick sheen of petroleum coats the lake’s surface. More than two decades of neglect have left its waters poisoned by leaks and spills, and dotted with ghostly drilling platforms.

Lynsey Addario for *The Atlantic*

The oil industry has generated enormous wealth, even as many of the people living in the shadow of its pumps and refineries remain mired in poverty.

Lynsey Addario for *The Atlantic*

Residents gather on a street in the city of Maracaibo during a rolling blackout. Though Venezuela has the world’s largest proven oil reserves, the country’s deteriorating electrical grid causes regular power outages lasting six to eight hours.

Lynsey Addario for *The Atlantic*

A street market in Maracaibo in September. Skyrocketing inflation has driven up the cost of basic goods; prices sometimes change from one day to the next.

Lynsey Addario for *The Atlantic*

Venezuelans ride on public transportation in La Vega. The neighborhood was once a stronghold of Hugo Chávez, who ruled Venezuela from 1999 until his death in 2013.

Lynsey Addario for *The Atlantic*

A boy plays in an alley in La Vega.

Lynsey Addario for *The Atlantic*

Venezuelans were still searching for the bodies of loved ones amid mountains of brick and concrete in La Guaira in September, more than two months after back-to-back earthquakes devastated the region.

Lynsey Addario for *The Atlantic*

Women pray during an open-air Mass at the Basílica de Santa Teresa in Caracas. The church was damaged by the June earthquakes and declared unsafe to enter.

Lynsey Addario for *The Atlantic*

Venezuelan security forces barricade streets leading to Miraflores, the presidential palace in Caracas, as protesters demand the release of political prisoners. More than 320 remained incarcerated as of late October.

Lynsey Addario for *The Atlantic*

A woman dressed as the Statue of Liberty bound in chains faces a line of Venezuelan security forces during a demonstration in Caracas.

Lynsey Addario for *The Atlantic*

Anti-American graffiti in Caracas evokes decades of tension between Venezuela and the United States, even as Washington exerts growing influence over the country’s pliant interim government.

items.articleBody:
**Mit der zweiten Beta von macOS 27.3 setzt Apple die im Oktober angekündigten strengeren Zugriffsregeln um. Ordnerfreigaben und App-Steuerung lassen sich künftig deutlich feiner einstellen. Wir haben die Details.**

## Wozu braucht man den Festplattenvollzugriff?

Wer seinen Mac mit Carbon Copy Cloner oder einem ähnlichen Tool komplett sichern will, kennt das: Ohne Festplattenvollzugriff läuft nichts. Genau diese Schnittstelle nutzen inzwischen aber auch immer mehr KI-Apps. Agenten wie Muse durchsuchen Dokumente, Mails, Nachrichten und Fotos, bearbeiten Dateien und dürfen obendrein andere Programme auf dem Rechner steuern. Das spart Zeit, öffnet aber auch ein ziemlich großes Tor zu euren privaten Daten. In Cupertino befürchtet man offenbar, dass viele Anwender gar nicht genau wissen, was sie mit einem Klick auf „Erlauben“ alles freigeben. Schon im Oktober hatte Apple strengere Kontrollen angekündigt. Mit der zweiten Beta von macOS 27.3 werden diese jetzt konkret.

## Ordner statt ganzer Festplatte

Ein neues [Support-Dokument](https://support.apple.com/en-us/149699) beschreibt die Änderungen im Detail. Den Festplattenvollzugriff schafft Apple nicht ab, ergänzt ihn aber um feinere Abstufungen. Fordert eine App den Vollzugriff an, schlägt der Freigabedialog künftig direkt vor, den Zugriff stattdessen auf ausgewählte Ordner zu begrenzen. Auch die Erklärung im Dialog fällt deutlich ausführlicher aus. macOS weist euch ausdrücklich darauf hin, dass der Mac eure privaten Informationen nicht mehr schützen kann, sobald eine App vollen Zugriff erhält.

## Neue Regeln für die App-Steuerung

Dateien zu lesen ist das eine, andere Programme zu bedienen das andere. Auch hier baut der Hersteller um. Der bisherige Bereich „Gerätesteuerung und Datenzugriff“ in den Datenschutzeinstellungen wird zweigeteilt in „Barrierefreiheit“ und „System & App Protection Override“. Der erste Teil ist für Bedienungshilfen gedacht, also für Apps, deren Entwickler dafür eine spezielle Berechtigung von Apple erhalten haben. Der zweite Teil regelt, ob und wie eine App andere Anwendungen steuern darf. Ihr könnt dort festlegen, dass vor jedem Zugriff eine Rückfrage erscheint. Außerdem bestimmt ihr gezielt, welche Programme eine App ansteuern darf und welche nicht.

## Bestehende Freigaben bleiben unangetastet

Wer KI-Apps bereits weitreichende Rechte eingeräumt hat, muss nach dem Update nichts neu einrichten: macOS 27.3 übernimmt vorhandene Berechtigungen unverändert. Die neuen Optionen greifen erst, wenn ihr eine KI-App neu installiert. Ein eigener Blick in die Datenschutzeinstellungen lohnt sich daher trotzdem, vor allem wenn ihr in den vergangenen Monaten mehrere Agenten ausprobiert habt.

items.articleBody:
The COP31 presidency hopes countries will commit to reducing the environmental impact of AI

UN Climate Change/Kiara Worth

Only nine countries have signed an international pledge to make AI greener, despite warnings at the COP31 climate summit that the technology’s growing energy demands threaten climate goals.

The Antalya Artificial Intelligence Pledge was launched on 16 November at the summit in Turkey. Developed by the summit’s presidency and the International Telecommunication Union (ITU), it intends to make AI more sustainable by encouraging cleaner energy use, more efficient [data centres](https://www.newscientist.com/article/2599078-massive-datacentres-use-as-much-electricity-as-an-entire-us-state/) and greater transparency about the technology’s environmental footprint.

[Read more The secret weapon that could finally force climate action](https://www.newscientist.com/article/2508956-the-secret-weapon-that-could-finally-force-climate-action/)

“AI and other frontier technologies are a double-edged sword,” said Simon Stiell, the executive secretary of UN Climate Change, at a press conference on 16 November. “The task ahead is to blunt their dangerous edges, sharpen their catalytic ones and put these technologies responsibly to work.”

But [Ketan Joshi,](https://ketanjoshi.co/) an independent analyst researching AI’s climate impacts, questions that analogy. He says it conflates traditional machine learning, already used in applications such as weather forecasting, with energy-intensive generative AI. “You don’t need to have a giant, energy-hungry generative AI chatbot if you want to have better wind forecasting for a wind power developer,” he says.

The initiative comes as AI’s rapid expansion is placing growing pressure on electricity grids. According to the International Energy Agency, electricity consumption from AI-focused data centres [increased by 50 per cent](https://www.iea.org/reports/key-questions-on-energy-and-ai) in 2025.

Free newsletter

#### Sign up to The Earth Edition

[Sign up to newsletter](https://www.newscientist.com/sign-up/the-earth-edition/)

Joshi says there is little evidence that technology companies are building enough renewable energy capacity to meet this growing demand. Even companies that have invested heavily in renewables, such as Amazon and Google, are increasingly turning to fossil fuels to support their rapid expansion, he says.

The only countries to have [endorsed the pledge](https://app.powerbi.com/view?r=eyJrIjoiOTAwYzBhZDItM2UwMi00MzU4LThhNTEtMTJjOTQwYzk2MGNkIiwidCI6IjIzZTQ2NGQ3LTA0ZTYtNGI4Ny05MTNjLTI0YmQ4OTIxOWZkMyIsImMiOjl9) so far are Andorra, Brazil, Colombia, Luxembourg, Sierra Leone, Somalia, South Korea, Turkey and Uganda.

The pledge is voluntary, with no binding targets for cutting emissions or reducing energy consumption. It sets out four areas for action, including increasing the use of low- and zero-emission energy to power AI infrastructure, improving energy and water efficiency, and measuring the environmental impacts of AI systems. It also calls for greater financial and technical support to help developing countries use AI to tackle climate change.

However, the agreement leaves considerable room for interpretation. The call for using “low- and zero-emission energy”, for example, allows continued reliance on fossil gas rather than committing to renewable electricity.

[Read more Can everyone live a ‘good life’ without destroying the planet?](https://www.newscientist.com/article/2532951-can-everyone-live-a-good-life-without-destroying-the-planet/)

Countries can also choose additional commitments, such as requiring AI companies to disclose their energy consumption and environmental impacts, or introducing sustainability requirements for data centres.

“I’m surprised that more countries haven’t signed up, given the pledge’s limited demands,” says Joshi. “It’s not a pledge that really strikes at the heart of the problem.” He argues that voluntary promises are unlikely to be sufficient without restrictions on the expansion of data centres and stronger AI regulation.

COP31 President Murat Kurum defended the initiative, saying the rapid growth of AI must be “powered and deployed responsibly, and used for the benefit of climate actions”. The ITU says progress on the pledge will be reviewed at annual UN climate summits until 2030, starting at COP32 next year.

Joshi fears the pledge could provide cover for continued expansion via fossil fuel sources. “I think we’re going to be going into an era of a return to greenwashing, a return to sort of empty promises,” he says. “What we really need is stronger and stricter regulation.”

items.articleBody:
The idea of computing with light has been around for over 70 years, but until recently it’s remained largely in the realm of research. Over the past few years, though, optical computing has emerged as a fast-growing industry: Market valuation of companies in this sector now totals US $2.22 billion, up from $0.4 billion in 2022. One projection suggests that the market will continue to grow exponentially in the coming years.

The reason for this sudden surge will surprise no one: AI. In particular, AI inference—the process of using AI models to respond to user queries—has driven much of the construction of huge, power-hungry data centers, and relatively energy-efficient optical systems are seen as a potential way forward.

“Most of the interest in [photonics] is driven by the fact that AI inference has literally become limited by power, and in a rather striking manner,” says Peter McMahon, associate professor of applied and engineering physics at Cornell University, in Ithaca, N.Y., who has researched optical computing for over a decade.

Optics, at least on paper, carries the promise of doing the same math as today’s GPUs at a drastically lower level of power. Switching from electronics to optics would be a pretty radical solution. Nevertheless, like mushrooms after a rainstorm, optical-computing startups are popping up in the United States, China, Germany, and Israel. And while competing against such GPU makers as Nvidia is an ambitious goal, the investment in optical computing has spurred development of complementary approaches, such as designing alternative AI algorithms, taking on scientific computing, and enhancing in-network computing.

Optalysys, based in England, is inserting optical-computing elements into the networking path, where data centers already use light. The company’s basic on-chip optical element, shown in the inset, is a Fourier transform calculator.Optalysys

“I think it would be good for the technology if many of these companies made a good run at it,” says Logan Wright, assistant professor of applied physics at Yale University, in New Haven, Conn., and a former postdoc in McMahon’s lab. “I think that the technology that will be developed through this would be really, really useful, and enable photonic systems that maybe don’t get on this wave of AI but would be capable of doing really quite special things.”

Optics to inference’s rescue?

Inference makes up the bulk of AI energy use. The industry is already spending billions of dollars designing advanced GPUs and other chips to run inference as efficiently as possible. At the heart of the inference computation is one operation, done countless times a second: matrix-vector multiplication.

Back in 1978, optical-computing pioneer Joseph W. Goodman and his coworkers proposed a method for doing matrix-vector multiplication with light. The setup was relatively simple. Let’s say a vector of length N needs to be multiplied by a matrix of size N by N. N light-emitting diodes, all in a row, encode the elements of the vector into the intensity of light—the brighter the light from an individual diode, the greater the value that diode encodes. Then, a cylindrical lens spreads out the light vertically, essentially copying the vector N times. The light then passes through an attenuator of N by N pixels. At each pixel, the light is attenuated according to the corresponding value at that location in the matrix. Passing the light through the attenuator performs the multiplication. Finally, a cylindrical lens oriented perpendicular to the first lens re-collects the light from each row, summing it up. The final vector is measured by a row of detectors.

VECTOR-MATRIX MULTIPLICATION

The most computationally expensive part of common AI today is vector-matrix (or matrix-matrix) multiplication. For a vector of length N (here, N = 3), it takes N2 (here, 9) multiplication steps and three accumulation steps—multiple additions at once.

The argument for why optics might be advantageous over electronics goes something like this: Multiplying a matrix of size N by N by a vector of length N takes N2 multiplication steps. In electronics, each multiplication takes some energy, so the total energy used scales as N2. In optics, however, the multiplication step is passive: As long as the matrix stays the same, passing light through the attenuator costs almost no energy. The only cost is encoding the vector into light and reading out the answer, but the vector is of length N, not N2. So the energy used will scale as N, not N2, as bigger vectors and matrices are multiplied.

Since Goodman’s 1978 proposal, the quality of the available optical elements has improved dramatically. Indeed, in 2022, a team of researchers at Cornell led by McMahon demonstrated an optical neural network that consumed less than one photon of energy—approximately 2.5 x 10-19 joules—per multiplication operation. In a standard computer, a single multiply operation can take between 10-14 and 10-12 joules, which suggests that optics could possibly reduce energy use by a factor of 100,000.

But McMahon cautions against such extrapolation. First, the cost of encoding data into optics was not included in the calculation. Even if the scaling is favorable with light, in practice it’s not just the scaling that matters, it’s also the coefficients. Let’s say the energy cost of doing one multiplication with electronics is 1 picojoule, and the cost to encode one vector element with optics is 1,000 picojoules. The electronic approach still wins if the length N of the vector is fewer than 1,000 elements.

McMahon says this example is not far off from reality: “One of the key questions is, How big do you have to make the system before you start winning? Lots of people have done this calculation for various kinds of neural networks. The very rough answer is somewhere between N equals 1,000 and N equals 10,000.”

It’s also important to keep in mind a computing principle known as Amdahl’s law.

“Amdahl’s law shouldn’t even be called a law. It’s a simple piece of common sense,” McMahon says. “If you have something that’s going to accelerate a computation, and it can accelerate 90 percent of the code, but there’s 10 percent of the code that it can’t accelerate, then the maximum possible speedup you can get is 10x.”

With AI inferencing, the point is to save energy, not time. But Amdahl’s observation still applies. What fraction of today’s AI inferencing code can be better handled with optics is a complicated question that varies by approach. But it’s not 100 percent. Matrix-vector multiplication, or matrix-matrix multiplication, is only part of the inference workload—there are other, nonlinear operations that need to be performed on the data.

Taking all of these caveats into account, optical-computing companies today are aiming for a 10- to 80-fold improvement in energy efficiency over today’s GPUs. The question is whether they can deliver on that promise at scale before traditional electronics catches up to those gains.

Bridging the gap in free space

The startup Lumai, based in Oxford, England, has taken perhaps the most direct inspiration from Goodman and his team. Lumai’s head of product, Phillip Burr, declares that a free-space approach, where the light travels through air rather than on-chip waveguides, is what will enable the company’s tech to beat GPUs.

Instead of the fixed attenuator used in Goodman’s proposal, Lumai is using a modern programmable device called a spatial light modulator—a pixelated membrane akin to a fancy liquid-crystal display that can modulate both the intensity and phase of light. The rest of the design is more sophisticated in practice but similar in principle to Goodman’s design: A vector is encoded into light, copied N times via a lens, passed through the spatial light modulator, collected with another lens, and the result is converted back to digital electronics. The electronics then handle the nonlinear functions. “A full vector-matrix multiply completes in a single optical cycle,” Burr says.

To accurately compare the energy expenditures of the optical and GPU approaches, you must first specify which part of the workload you’re considering. Modern inference is often split into two phases: prefill, where the input query is processed and propagated through the model, and decode, where the output is generated one word (or token) at a time. Prefill is the more computationally intensive of the two. It basically involves doing vector-matrix multiplications for the same matrix over and over. Decode also involves vector-matrix multiplies, but not as intensively—the time-consuming part of decode is reading the necessary matrices in and out of memory.

Vector-matrix multiplication with free-space optics

The Goodman optical computer is the simplest version of a photonic vector-matrix multiplier. Here, the vector elements are encoded into the intensity of light from three light sources, such as LEDs. Then, a cylindrical lens spreads the light vertically. The matrix elements are encoded into the opacity of an attenuator, such that when light passes through each pixel it is multiplied (attenuated) by that matrix value. Finally, another cylindrical lens collects the light horizontally, performing the accumulation step, and a photodetector measures the output vector.

Lumai, and other companies in the space, are focusing on the compute-intensive prefill phase of inference. Lumai claims that its Iris Nova optical server, made available for evaluation in April 2026, is a proof of concept, and its next-generation Iris Aura server will do prefill using roughly one-tenth of the energy a GPU would use.

The startup Neurophos, based in Austin, Texas, is putting a different spin on the Goodman computer design. To pack more punch into a small device, the company is leveraging its expertise in metamaterials—complex structures that can manipulate light at scales smaller than a single wavelength. The structures it has designed are bigger than a wavelength but still quite small—just several micrometers per side.

“The equivalent of the optical transistor that you can get from standard silicon photonics today is like 2 millimeters long,” says Patrick Bowen, CEO of Neurophos. “You just can’t fit enough [of] them on-chip to get a compute density that remotely competes with the latest and greatest [that] TSMC [Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co.] does.”

Bowen’s team designed metamaterial-based modulators that can be programmed to manipulate the phase and intensity of light at the micrometer scale, resulting in an array of 1,000 by 1,000 modulators in a square chip with 5-mm sides. According to Bowen, Neurophos’s modulators switch over 10,000 times as fast as a standard liquid-crystal spatial light modulators do.

Bowen also claims a performance advantage over Nvidia’s Blackwell GPU: “We’re targeting 50 times Blackwell B200’s speed and 35 times its energy efficiency, and have a road map to reach 250 times the speed and roughly 90 times the energy efficiency in subsequent generations.”

The approach is CMOS-compatible, Bowen says, which should allow Neurophos to manufacture its chips on the semiconductor industry’s existing high-volume production lines. The company is currently choosing a site for a production facility ahead of its rack deliveries to customers in 2028.

Both Lumai and Neurophos are betting they’ll get their products to market before traditional CMOS can catch up to their energy savings. “Silicon will keep improving, but digital efficiency gains now come slowly and at rising cost,” Burr says. “Optics offers a different scaling relationship, in which efficiency improves as matrices grow. Larger models, longer context windows, and agentic workloads are all pushing prefill in that direction.”

Bridging the gap on-chip

Free-space optics carries the promise of almost energy-free multiplication, as in Goodman’s design. But another big advance in optics since Goodman’s work in the 1970s is integrated photonics, which allows you to guide and manipulate light on-chip.

“The name of the game is to do as large a vector size as possible to maximize the benefit of using optics, and for that reason the free-space approaches are promising,” says Yale’s Logan Wright. “But it’s still fundamentally harder” to use the free-space approach, “because there’s just so much less infrastructure than in silicon photonics.”

Other companies—like Shanghai-based Lightelligence and Q.ANT, based in Stuttgart, Germany—are trading the 3D advantage of free-space optics for the manufacturability of photonics integrated directly onto a silicon chip.

“There is a good reason that free-space optics are usually limited to 1,000 units a year,” says Q.ANT’s CEO and founder, Michael Förtsch. “The reason for this is lens inspection, assembly strategy, and so on. Semiconductor-manufacturable integrated photonic circuits are at this point way more promising to reach volume production.”

Vector-matrix multiplication with integrated photonics

One way to do vector-matrix multiplication with light on-chip involves encoding vector elements into the amplitudes of pulses of light, traveling sequentially through a waveguide. The multiplication is performed by Mach-Zehnder interferometers: A waveguide splits in two, and the phase of light traveling through one of the paths is shifted by a controlled voltage. When the two paths reunite, the resulting light intensity depends on that phase shift, performing a multiplication. Encoding the matrix elements into the phase shifts turns this into vector-matrix multiplication. A photodetector then collects the light from all three pulses, performing the accumulation step.

In Q.ANT’s approach, the input data is encoded into the phase and amplitude of light pulses via on-chip modulators. A vector in this scheme is represented as a sequence of such pulses, each representing one vector element. The light is guided around the chip with waveguides. The basic computational element is an interferometer: A waveguide splits into two paths, and the light beam traveling down one path is subjected to a phase shift, controlled by a set voltage. When the two paths recombine, the resulting interference performs a computation. Then, photodetectors and analog-to-digital converters turn the result back into digital data. The serialized vector-matrix multiplication approach is slower than Goodman’s computer, where the whole calculation happens at once. However, the slower speed can be mitigated by using multiple wavelengths at once, effectively encoding multiple vectors into light simultaneously.

Q.ANT’s Native Processing Server is already being used in research institutions like the Leibniz Supercomputing Centre in Munich and the Jülich Supercomputing Centre in Jülich, both in Germany. Earlier this year, the company announced a commercial sale to the cloud provider Ionos. Similarly, Lightelligence’s PACE2 processor is capable of multiplying 128-by-128-element matrices. In a paper released in 2025, the company described vector-matrix multiplication at a 1-gigahertz frequency and 3-nanosecond latency, claiming two orders of magnitude lower latency than with traditional GPUs.

The energy advantage is yet to be conclusively demonstrated, however, and Q.ANT’s Förtsch admits there is still a ways to go. The main issue is the energy cost of analog-to-digital conversion and back. As long as a fast, low-energy converter does not exist, Förtsch says, “we don’t see realistic chances that…a general vector-matrix multiplication machine in optics makes sense.”

Beyond matrix-vector multiplication

Not everyone in the field is focused on matrix-vector multiplication, despite it being all the rage in the AI inference world. In fact, while the optical vector-matrix multiply idea goes back to the 1970s, other computations with optics have been investigated as far back as the 1950s. For example, a Fourier transform—a common operation that decomposes a complex wave or signal into its constituent frequencies—can be done in optics with a single lens.

“A digital chip has to approximate [Fourier transforms] in many small steps, using hundreds to thousands of transistors and more compute cycles,” says Q.ANT’s Förtsch. “Models that use such nonlinear functions can reach the same or better accuracy with fewer parameters and fewer operations.”

Even though Q.ANT’s optical processor has been used for traditional vector-matrix multiplication, the company believes its greatest advantages lie in alternative AI architectures that leverage more complex functions. “Tasks such as image classification and segmentation rely heavily on operations like Fourier series, transformations, and other nonlinear functions, which photonics handles natively. We see similar potential in generative AI, especially image and video generation,” Förtsch says.

The Israel-based startup LightSolver is also targeting algorithms that are a more natural fit for its device. “If you look at propagating electromagnetic waves, essentially, they are running differential equations in their nature,” says Ruti Ben-Shlomi, CEO and cofounder of LightSolver. She says differential equations can be solved much faster and with higher energy efficiency on the company’s laser processing unit (LPU) than on a traditional computer.

LightSolver’s LPU is an interesting twist on the Goodman optical-computer design. It has input light, a programmable membrane in the form of a spatial light modulator, and output light, but the whole thing is placed in a cavity, where light bounces back and forth many times before reaching a steady state. In addition, the team places a gain medium inside the cavity. This gain medium functions much like those found inside a laser, causing the bouncing light to build up in intensity.

LightSolver, a startup based in Israel, is using free-space optics to quickly solve differential equations by harnessing the natural properties of light. LightSolver
Once a particular problem is encoded into the modulator, the gain medium is stimulated to emit random photons. They bounce back and forth, increasing in intensity when passing through the gain medium again, experiencing preprogrammed changes through the modulator and interacting with one another until they reach a steady state—the solution. Then, a simple camera takes a picture of the steady-state result. Using emulation, the LightSolver team recently showed that their LPU can solve differential equations 40 to 80,000 times as fast as a GPU, depending on the workflow. They are now working on explicitly benchmarking the energy improvements.
LightSolver’s team is currently working on AI applications for its LPU as well, using the company’s own algorithm to do image generation from text. “We’re not doing vector-matrix multiplication very fast. We are doing something different. We need to assume that the way you train the model, and you then do inference, is completely different. But if you do it differently, you’ll be able to do image generation with dramatic energy-consumption decrease and speedup,” Ben-Shlomi says. LightSolver has a working prototype of its LPU, and the team is working on a larger, rack-mountable box.

Computing in transit

Yet another way to leverage light’s particular strengths is being pursued by Optalysys, a startup based in Leeds, England. Nick New, founder and chief product officer, has a background in free-space optics, and so he understood that taking a Fourier transform is very easy to do with light.

The key idea behind Optalysys’s technology is taking that Fourier capability of optics in free space and making it work on-chip. “Rather than using a lens these days, we have our own component, which is a passive component in the plane of the silicon that does that same job,” New says. And by cleverly designing that component with multiple outputs, the team figured out how to perform different operations as well. “Because of how the Fourier transform response is generated, you can actually pull out different mathematical operations from it,” New says. “We can produce very large, high-precision digital functions at superhigh efficiencies, using our analog photonics approach.”

“We’re effectively adding processing to where there is none right now.” —Nick New, Optalysis

Instead of redesigning an accelerator from scratch, Optalysys is targeting a piece of the AI workload that’s often already in the optical domain: networking. In the data center, racks of computers are connected to each other with fiber optics, and the optical connections are increasingly getting closer and closer to the GPUs and CPUs themselves.

Some computations already happen while the data is en route. These computations, which include combining results from multiple GPUs, are executed inside network switch cards. But the cards naturally use power to do that math. With passive optical components, these computations could be done essentially for free.

New says that in addition to communication between GPUs, Optalysys’s technology could be used to facilitate a GPU’s communication with memory, doing things like compression and format conversion on the fly. Going back to AI inference, this approach could improve the decode part of the workload. Unlike prefill, decode is memory bound: The most costly part is shuffling model data in and out of memory. “We’re more focused on the memory-bound applications, which fits very well with this principle of adding processing into the communication path,” New says. “We’re effectively adding processing to where there is none right now.”

The likely future of optical computing

How likely are optical computers to replace GPUs in the data center? Yale’s Wright is not too optimistic. “The direction of algorithm development is not going to be a direction that is automatically favorable for optics,” he says. “In fact, it’s most likely to go in the opposite direction, because [AI model developers] want it to work better on GPUs.”

However, even if our AI queries aren’t going to be computed in light in the next few years, that investment in the technology won’t be in vain. Says Wright, “The reason that I and many other people in the field are at least somewhat optimistic is that there’s real investment from companies like Nvidia and TSMC in developing co-packaged silicon photonics—not for computing, but for circuit switching and interconnects, and that just kind of opens the door to do a little bit more in the future.”

Whether that technology ends up crunching vector-matrix multiplication, doing bespoke simulations, or performing in-network computations, the computing ecosystem seems ripe for a variety of approaches. “We see the data center of the future as heterogeneous: CPUs, GPUs and photonic NPUs [neural processing units] each take on the tasks they are best suited for,” says Q.ANT’s Förtsch. “Running each task on the most efficient hardware can significantly reduce energy use and operating costs.”

items.articleBody:
**Es gibt gute Nachrichten für alle, die noch die erste Version des Apogee Symphony I/O verwenden. Dank eines Open-Source-Projekts lässt sich das Audiointerface jetzt auch wieder mit modernen Macs nutzen**.

Apogee Symphony I/O MK I und Unofficial Symphony Maestro (Bildquelle: www.generouscorp.com)

Inhalte

- Apogee Symphony I/O MK I und Unofficial Symphony Maestro
- Was ist mit Unofficial Symphony Maestro möglich?
- Community-Projekt
- Links

## Apogee Symphony I/O MK I und Unofficial Symphony Maestro

Das Apogee Symphony I/O MK I gehört nach wie vor zu den beliebten Audiointerfaces, die in professionellen Studios verwendet werden. Allerdings gibt es schon lange keine aktuellen Treiber und Software mehr für das 16 Jahre alte System, was es unmöglich macht, das System mit modernen Macs zu verwenden.

Doch jetzt gibt es Hoffnung am Horizont: Daniel Raffel hat mit Zustimmung von Apogee neue USB- und ThunderBridge-Treiber sowie eine alternative Version der Maestro-Software entwickelt und stellt das gesamte Paket als kostenloses Open-Source-Projekt zur Verfügung.

[Hier ist die Unofficial Symphony Maestro Website](https://www.generouscorp.com/unofficial-symphony-maestro-mk1/)

Unofficial Symphony Maestro (Bildquelle: www.generouscorp.com)

## Was ist mit Unofficial Symphony Maestro möglich?

Unofficial Symphony Maestro kann auf Apple-Silicon-Macs ab dem Betriebssystem macOS 26 über USB oder ThunderBridge betrieben werden.

USB unterstützt 16 Ein- und Ausgänge bei maximal 96 kHz und ThunderBridge erlaubt bis zu 32 Kanäle bei maximal 192 kHz.

Mit der Maestro-App können die Ein- und Ausgänge, Hardware-Metering, Routing und Monitoring gesteuert werden. Es ist auch möglich, die Clock, Samplingrate, die optische I/O, die Verstärkung und Presets zu verwalten.

Unofficial Symphony Maestro (Bildquelle: www.generouscorp.com)

## Community-Projekt

Unofficial Symphony Maestro befindet sich noch in der Beta-Phase. Es können also noch Bugs auftreten. Das Projekt trägt den Namen **Unofficial Symphony Maestro**, denn obwohl Apogee die Entwicklung unterstützt hat, handelt es sich nicht um eine offizielle Software des Herstellers. Entsprechend kann Apogee auch keinen technischen Support für Installation, Kompatibilität oder Fehlerbehebung anbieten. Bei Fragen und Problemen solltet ihr euch daher direkt an das [GitHub-Projekt](https://github.com/danielraffel/unofficial-symphony-maestro-mk1) wenden.

Unofficial Symphony Maestro (Bildquelle: www.generouscorp.com)

## Links

[Die Unofficial Symphony Maestro Website](https://www.generouscorp.com/unofficial-symphony-maestro-mk1/)

[Unofficial Symphony Maestro auf GitHub](https://github.com/danielraffel/unofficial-symphony-maestro-mk1)

items.title: Poll margins versus reality
items.subtitle: It seems to be getting more difficult to accurately estimate election results based on polls.
items.feedText: The New York Times charted the difference between average poll margins against what happened on election day. The actual margins leaned far more towards Democrat in all the key states. Unlike weather predictions, which have grown more accurate with better tools and more data, estimating human preferences gets harder with uncertain turnouts and lower participation in polls. Tags: estimation, New York Times, polling, uncertainty
items.articleBody:
It seems to be getting more difficult to accurately estimate election results based on polls. [The New York Times charted the difference](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/us/politics/poll-error-democrats-midterms.html?unlocked_article_code=1.Q1E.IHS2.e_SVhUhW6Nps&smid=url-share) between average poll margins against what happened on election day.

The actual margins leaned far more towards Democrat in all the key states.

Unlike weather predictions, which have [grown more accurate](https://flowingdata.com/2024/07/08/accuracy-of-temperature-forecasts-where-you-live/) with better tools and more data, estimating human preferences gets harder with uncertain turnouts and lower participation in polls.

**Tags:** [estimation](https://flowingdata.com/tag/estimation/), [New York Times](https://flowingdata.com/tag/new-york-times/), [polling](https://flowingdata.com/tag/polling/), [uncertainty](https://flowingdata.com/tag/uncertainty/)

items.articleBody:
Today, *TIME Magazine* has published their list of [100 “must-read” books of 2026](https://time.com/collection/must-read-books/2026/), including *[Yesteryear](https://bookshop.org/a/132/9780593804216)* by Caro Claire Burke, who is also featured on the magazine’s cover.

The last novelist to be featured on the cover of *TIME* was [Taylor Jenkins Reid](https://time.com/7284944/taylor-jenkins-reid-atmosphere-interview/), in 2025; before that there hadn’t been a novelist on the cover since [Akwaeke Emezi](https://time.com/collections/next-generation-leaders/6047430/akwaeke-emezi-next-generation-leaders/) was featured as part of the magazine’s “Next Generation Leaders” package in 2021 (Amanda Gorman was also [featured in a solo cover](https://lithub.com/amanda-gorman-is-on-the-cover-of-this-weeks-time/) that year). Novelists *used* to show up in this spot all the time, but they have rather fallen off in the magazine’s modern history. In 2010, Jonathan Franzen famously became the first living novelist to be featured on the cover of *TIME* in a decade, followed by [Colson Whitehead, in 2019](https://lithub.com/colson-whitehead-is-the-first-novelist-to-grace-the-cover-of-time-since-2010/). So at least things are picking up this decade.

See Caro Claire Burke’s cover below, and read the cover story [↗ time.com](https://time.com/article/2026/11/17/caro-claire-burke-interview/). (You can also read Lit Hub’s interview with Burke [↗ lithub.com](https://lithub.com/caro-claire-burke-on-tradwives-the-performance-of-selfhood-and-the-good-old-days/).)

Photograph by Tonje Thilesen for TIME @tonjethilesen
