items.articleBody:
Officer Felix Wilder sauntered around the women’s prison like he owned the place.

Prone to showing up to work in gold chains and stylish jeans instead of his concrete gray government uniform, the slender 35-year-old moved, one woman said, “like he had just gotten off of a horse from a long ride.” He spoke slowly and eyed the prisoners as they walked through the drab buildings and shadeless yards of the secluded federal lockup in Aliceville, Alabama.

Ela’s cellmate, who asked to be identified as Ana, watched it all with unease. At 40, she knew exactly what that kind of attention from an officer could mean in a women’s prison.

For 15 years, Ana had served her time at Federal Correctional Institution Dublin, a low-security prison in California, where officers had preyed on the women in their care. Sexual misconduct became so rampant that staff and prisoners alike called it a “rape club.” Eventually, the FBI intervened, and prosecutors charged the warden, the chaplain and nine other officers with sexually abusing female prisoners. Hundreds of women — including Ana — came forward to tell what happened to them, not just to investigators, but also to outside lawyers who [sued the system to demand change](https://www.courtlistener.com/docket/67696587/1/california-coalition-for-women-prisoners-v-united-states-of-america/) at the Bay Area prison.

Ana had hoped to leave that all behind when she was transferred out of Dublin. But tucked between the pine trees and low-slung churches of rural Alabama, the Aliceville prison had its own brand of menace. The facility had newer buildings but fewer freedoms. The roofs leaked, and sometimes the air smelled faintly of mold. The shorthanded staff often locked the women in their cells for days at a time.

And then there were officers like Wilder, who seemed to be choosing their targets.

Thousands of miles from families they couldn’t call during yet another lockdown, Ana and Ela became allies. They paced. They picked at the lukewarm meals delivered on Styrofoam trays. They stared out the narrow slit of a window.

And then Ela broke down, sobbing as her words tumbled out into the stale prison air.

Two years earlier, an officer had pulled her into a closet and raped her, she told Ana, her voice quavering. Now, she said, it was happening all over again — but this time it was the stylish officer in jeans: Felix Wilder.

Ela said she’d reported the first assault and nothing happened. Now, she didn’t know what to do. If the prison didn’t care about one rape, why would it care about two?

As she listened, Ana felt a dull rage churning in her stomach. She thought of all the things she’d seen and survived at Dublin: the rapes, the harassment, the uncertainty of a life subject to the whims of lascivious men with badges. As she tried to comfort her sobbing cellmate, she wondered whether Aliceville was any better. Maybe, she thought, no place was.

Sitting on her metal bunk, she opened the little address book she’d bought from the prison commissary and flipped to the phone numbers for the lead attorneys in the class action lawsuit against Dublin. “Here,” she told Ela, “you can talk to them.”

The arrests and subsequent convictions of Dublin staff — 10 in all — marked the largest sex abuse scandal in the Federal Bureau of Prisons’ history and a rare moment of accountability in a troubled system where many women had learned to stop expecting it. Suddenly, every branch of government stepped in. A federal judge appointed an outside monitor. A slew of agencies issued reports, and the Justice Department dispatched attorneys to visit and evaluate women’s facilities. Congress passed a law to create a new, independent office to oversee the prison system.

But after the judge made that unprecedented move to appoint outside oversight, in early 2024 the bureau abruptly announced it would shut down Dublin and transfer its [more than 600 women](https://www.courthousenews.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/fci-dublin-still-report-real.pdf) — including Ana — to lockups across the country.

Ana had hoped to leave the abuse behind when she was transferred out of Dublin federal prison.

Then, quietly, the window of accountability shut. Little appeared to have come of the promised reforms, the site visits and the reports, and Congress never appropriated funding for the new oversight office. More than a dozen current and former federal prison employees told ProPublica and The Marshall Project they’d seen few or no meaningful improvements. One Justice Department official said the only obvious sign of progress was new sexual assault prevention posters.

“Nothing has really changed,” said Alix McLearen, a top Bureau of Prisons official who retired in 2024 after serving as the agency’s first administrator overseeing the women and special populations branch. “We had a horrible crisis, and crisis leads to opportunity, and this is an opportunity that has been completely squandered.”

An official with the federal prison workers union who — like nearly every current employee interviewed for this story — asked not to be named for fear of retaliation, put it even more bluntly: “Nothing has been done to effectively change sexual abuse of inmates within the BOP. Not on a large scale or small scale.”

For the last five years, the culture that spawned a rape club at Dublin has persisted across the system. Reporters at ProPublica and The Marshall Project set out to determine how pervasive the problem of staff sexual abuse inside federal women’s prisons is — and what, if anything, officials have done to solve it. What we found was sexual assault, misconduct or harassment at most of the 27 facilities that currently hold women. We identified more than 185 cases in which prison employees have been accused of sexually abusing people in women’s prisons since 2021, the year the Dublin scandal broke. The cases implicate more than 96 officers at 16 prisons. Of those, just 19 officers have been arrested or convicted.

In some cases, officers withheld food or medical care, or threatened to put women in solitary confinement if they refused to comply with sexual demands, court records allege. In others, officers locked them in windowless closets or bathrooms, choked them, or forced them to use sex toys or have sex with each other. In more than a dozen instances, the assaults were so brutal that the women were left bruised and bleeding.

Though some abusers have been prosecuted or removed, insiders say the culture of impunity that allows officers to prey on women remains. Officials have repeatedly refused to acknowledge or failed to act on signs of sexual abuse, we found. More than 25 women said that they were abused by officers who had been reported or investigated before, according to lawsuits we reviewed. In some cases, officers have covered for their abusive colleagues, court records allege. Other times, staff say that they, like the prisoners, have hesitated to report misconduct for fear of retaliation.

At a prison camp in West Virginia, an officer who’d been investigated repeatedly for suspected abuse — but allowed to remain on the job — raped a woman so forcefully that he tore her vaginal lining, according to a lawsuit she filed last year. The officer has been charged with sexually assaulting her and two other women at the camp and has pleaded not guilty. His case is set for trial early next year.

At Federal Medical Center Carswell, a facility in North Texas, an officer allegedly forced two women to have a threesome with him in his office, where he’d rigged up a doorbell to alert him if anyone came by, court filings show. A civil lawsuit has been stayed pending a criminal investigation.

> “We had a horrible crisis, and crisis leads to opportunity, and this is an opportunity that has been completely squandered.”
> Alix McLearen, former Bureau of Prisons official

And at Aliceville, Wilder, the officer who allegedly assaulted Ela, also abused at least 17 other women, many of whom were facing deportation after they finished serving their sentences, according to court records and interviews. He allegedly didn’t stop until the FBI showed up at the facility in the fall of 2024, and federal prosecutors eventually charged him with [sexually abusing seven women](https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.alnd.199265/gov.uscourts.alnd.199265.1.0_1.pdf). He has pleaded not guilty and is awaiting trial.

“I’m pretty sure everybody knew what was going on and they just didn’t care,” one of the women told ProPublica and The Marshall Project in a phone interview from the federal prison in Fort Worth, Texas.

We found that abuse continued even as the facilities kept passing federally mandated sexual assault prevention audits. The Texas medical facility had a flawless audit the same year the FBI arrived to investigate a paramedic whom at least 18 women have accused of sexual assault, records show. Likewise, Aliceville got perfect marks during the same time period that Wilder was allegedly preying on Ela and other women.

The officers union called sexual abuse “completely unacceptable” and blamed [persistent staffing shortages](https://www.propublica.org/article/ice-bop-federal-prisons-corrections-officers) for helping to create an environment that allows it to go undetected. “If we are serious about protecting inmates and maintaining safe, secure federal prisons, we have to address the staffing crisis head-on,” the union said in a statement, noting that more watchful eyes would mean “fewer opportunities for inappropriate conduct to occur behind closed doors.”

Bureau of Prisons spokesperson Randilee Giamusso said the federal prison system has “zero tolerance” for sexual abuse and harassment. “We take all allegations of sexual abuse seriously,” she said.

Giamusso highlighted the bureau’s recently revamped policy on sexually abusive behavior, which is intended to ensure that allegations are more thoroughly investigated. It also eliminates any mention of transgender or intersex people, whom federal law identifies as particularly vulnerable to sexual abuse in prison. She did not provide further details or address any specific cases, saying the bureau does not comment on pending litigation. Officers mentioned in this story, as well as representatives for the prisons, either did not respond or declined to comment on specific allegations.

As Ana and the other Dublin women, now scattered to other facilities, realized that no one was going to stop the abuse, they began to take matters into their own hands. Across the country, they encouraged other women to speak out about what had happened to them — and told them what they could do about it.

The volume of abuse allegations ballooned so rapidly that the legal team handling the Dublin case had to refer scores of potential clients to other lawyers, some of whom have taken on so many federal prison sex abuse cases that it’s become the primary focus of their law practice. We continued receiving new lawsuits, tort claims and allegations of abuse up until publication of this story.

“There has been so much reporting on Dublin as an aberration,” said Susan Beaty, one of the lawyers spearheading the class action suit. “But I think it’s actually incredibly representative. I think it’s happening at basically every BOP women’s prison.”

### No Way to Say No

As she comforted her cellmate at Aliceville, Ana thought back to her first months at Dublin — before she’d learned how to recognize abuse in prison and before she’d seen just how much of it there was.

Back then, around 2010, it seemed that almost every day she saw a handful of women eating Mexican takeout for lunch — hot meals too mouth-watering to have come from the spartan prison kitchen.

At the time, Ana was just 25 and at the beginning of a lengthy sentence stemming from her involvement in her husband’s drug-trafficking operation. So while she suspected the smuggled-in meals were the sign of some nefarious quid pro quo arrangement with the officers, she didn’t ask questions, partly because she was afraid and partly because the women shared their coveted contraband meals. “So I would just eat it and shut up,” she said.

Under federal law, all sexual contact between prison staff and people in custody is a felony — and for good reason. Prisoners cannot meaningfully give consent when they’re propositioned by people who control every aspect of their lives, from when they get fed to whether they face disciplinary sanctions that could land them in solitary confinement. So although prison sex abuse sometimes involves violent rape, it often relies on subtle coercion and grooming.

Poor conditions and scarcity behind bars turn basic necessities into valuable commodities that officers can leverage to create the illusion of a “relationship” — one built on exchanging sexual favors for extra privileges and little gifts, like contraband makeup, extra tampons or a few more minutes at visitation.

A makeup bag and yellow mesh bag Ana used during her time at Dublin prison.

As one high-ranking prison official explained: “The women are getting small trinkets. It’s not big things that we can trace. He’s bringing in a hamburger, a Subway sandwich. It’s heartbreaking to look at the value of the things that are being passed.”

Many times, those seeming relationships turn volatile — and violent. In Ana’s case, it began when one Dublin officer started being unusually nice to her, according to her lawsuit. He’d rush across the unit to unlock doors for her or call her into his office to talk alone. Ana thought they’d developed a rapport. But over time, he groomed her with personal questions and meager privileges. Once, he told her he’d had a sexual dream about her. Then, according to her lawsuit, he kissed her and eventually raped her.

Telling prison investigators didn’t seem like an option; Ana had already learned the hard way about the risks of reporting errant staff. A few years earlier, she had helped another prisoner file a complaint about staff misconduct. Afterward, she said, both women were sent to solitary confinement. For two weeks, Ana spent 23 hours a day locked in a cell barely bigger than an elevator. She got cold food, had no access to the phone and was barred from seeing visitors.

Prison officials often isolate those who report abuse, [ostensibly for their own protection](https://www.hsgac.senate.gov/wp-content/uploads/imo/media/doc/Peters%20Testimony.pdf), even though the Justice Department has found this practice has a “[chilling effect](https://www.justice.gov/d9/pages/attachments/2022/11/03/2022.11.02_bop_sexual_misconduct_working_group_report.pdf)” that discourages people from reporting abuse. A federal prison spokesperson said the agency’s policy does not require that people who report abuse be put in solitary — but that sometimes it is the only adequate option.

It’s not just prisoners who are afraid to report wrongdoing. Although staff are required to report misconduct [under bureau policy](https://www.bop.gov/policy/progstat/3420_014.pdf), in lawsuits and interviews, officers say they, too, worry about retaliation.

“You see all the sexual abuse, how they treat inmates. If you bring that to their attention, it’s like you’re doing the wrong thing,” said a former correctional officer at the prison camp for women in Bryan, Texas. In 2024, she reported several co-workers for having sexual contact with incarcerated women. She resigned last year after the warden moved to fire her for unprofessional conduct, documents show.

Even when witnesses or victims do report abuse, investigators rarely conclude that it occurred. As of 2022, less than [10% of allegations](https://www.gao.gov/assets/gao-26-107343.pdf) against Bureau of Prisons employees were substantiated, [meaning investigators found it more likely than not](https://www.bop.gov/policy/progstat/5333_001-1.pdf) that the abuse happened in those cases. In some instances, investigators decided there was evidence the abuse didn’t occur. But more than 75% of the time, they said there wasn’t enough evidence to make a determination either way.

Officers accused of abuse face an internal disciplinary process that [can take years](https://files.gao.gov/reports/GAO-25-107339/index.html). In many cases, they can simply retire or resign, knowing that the agency will no longer have jurisdiction to punish them once they leave. They could still face criminal charges — but bureau insiders say that many cases don’t reach that point because investigators abandon the criminal probes when an officer resigns. “Staff would know that if they were having sex with inmates, the worst that would happen is that you would have to find a new job,” one former prison official said.

The landmark law intended to combat sex abuse, the 2003 Prison Rape Elimination Act — widely known as PREA — mandates employee training and regular audits but lacks a serious enforcement mechanism. Auditors are primarily [looking for policy compliance, not signs of abuse](https://www.gao.gov/products/gao-26-107343). “A facility may have widespread sexual abuse, but they’re still meeting compliance on the things they’re required to do,” said Kendra Prisk, a PREA auditor who has evaluated several federal prisons, including Aliceville.

### Do You Have a Story to Share About This Topic?

Beth Schwartzapfel and I are continuing to report on this issue and want to hear from any prisoners or prison staff who have been sexually harassed or abused in the Federal Bureau of Prisons.

**Keri Blakinger**

I welcome any tips leading to tough accountability stories about the legal system. Right now, I’m particularly interested in hearing from federal prison employees and federal prisoners with information about untold and revelatory stories.

[Contact Me](https://www.propublica.org/people/keri-blakinger)

At Dublin, Ana said she watched the officer who’d been bringing in burritos get walked off the job by investigators. He was, [according to an Associated Press investigation](https://apnews.com/article/business-prisons-california-sexual-abuse-only-on-ap-3a4db9ab478bfdd545ef3c7e08cd273b) and several agency sources, one of about a dozen Dublin workers in the early 2010s who were quietly removed from their posts — but not prosecuted — over sex abuse allegations.

In September 2021, a new round of problems at Dublin burst into public view when the FBI arrested the facility’s warden, Ray Garcia. He was eventually charged with sexually abusing multiple women all over the compound — then lying to cover it up. In one instance, prosecutors say he abused a woman while PREA auditors were visiting. Though Garcia was later convicted and sentenced to nearly six years in prison, his attorney, Kevin Little, told ProPublica and The Marshall Project that Garcia maintained that he is not guilty.

The arrest of such a high-ranking official sent shockwaves through the system. Members of Congress began asking questions. The head of the agency, Michael Carvajal, [announced that he would step down](https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/politics-news/federal-prisons-director-stepping-down-after-rocky-tenure-atop-agency-n1287046), a move he said in a recent interview was driven by concerns that Congress would not support the bureau until he left. Ultimately, 10 Dublin officers pleaded guilty or were convicted at trial, and one walked free after two hung juries.

While several of the Dublin officers could not be reached or did not respond to requests for comment, one did. John Bellhouse, who was a safety supervisor, emailed ProPublica and The Marshall Project from a federal prison in Louisiana, where he is serving a 63-month sentence after he was convicted of sexually abusing two women. Bellhouse insisted he is innocent and said the problem at Dublin was that the lower-ranking staff were “too comfortable” at the facility and too familiar with the prisoners. “It was very junior high school,” he wrote.

To Ana and the other women at Dublin, the rash of charges had made it seem for a moment like there might be change. But it soon became clear the problems were far more entrenched.

### “BOP Was Putting on a Show”

In the wake of the indictments at Dublin, prison officials were dispatched across the country beginning in 2022 to inspect other women’s prisons and generate internal reports.

That spring, at the low-security prison in Tallahassee, Florida, most of the women surveyed for the “Women’s Institution Cultural Assessment” said they were afraid of reprisals if they spoke freely, according to a copy reviewed by ProPublica and The Marshall Project. The last time officials visited, they said, officers had punished the women with “shakedowns” — in which officers ransack cells and destroy belongings — and told them it was in retaliation for talking to the visitors. Despite noting this and “several concerning observations,” the bureau found that sexual safety was “not determined to be a problem” at the facility.

Since then, at least 10 prisoners have filed legal claims saying they were abused by Tallahassee officers in the same year as the assessment. Six said they were sexually assaulted by a [single officer, Lenton Hatten](https://www.justice.gov/archives/opa/pr/former-federal-correctional-officer-sentenced-prison-sexual-abuse-inmate), who had [previously been reprimanded](https://www.courtlistener.com/docket/71848295/1/dover-v-united-states/) by prison officials at another facility for putting money in women’s commissary accounts, “which was a warning sign of inappropriate relations,” according to multiple lawsuits. He was ultimately sentenced to three months in prison for repeatedly abusing one woman after DNA tied him to the crime. In legal filings, attorneys for the prison system admitted that Hatten sexually abused that woman but denied that he assaulted any of the others. They also denied that officials had failed to train or supervise Hatten properly. Neither Hatten nor his attorney responded to requests for comment.

At Carswell, in the summer of 2022, multiple prisoners told officials that prison staff had held town hall meetings before the site visit, threatening repercussions if anyone reported their concerns, the assessment found. Nonetheless, the team concluded that women at Carswell overwhelmingly felt it was a “physically and sexually safe environment.”

But that year, at least seven women were sexually abused by four different Carswell employees, according to allegations in civil lawsuits they’ve since filed. In one case, a woman who was partially paralyzed and required a wheelchair said she was violently sodomized in the shower by an officer who attended her Bible study group. When he heard people coming, she said he dropped her on the floor, leaving her alone to crawl back to her wheelchair, crying and bloodied. Months later, when she finally reported the assault, the nurse on duty told her she’d reported that same officer for sexually harassing other prisoners and nothing had been done about it, according to her lawsuit.

All the suits are still pending. Among the staffers named in them, only Hatten has been prosecuted. In many cases, it’s not clear whether any of the employees were disciplined by the Bureau of Prisons. The prisons agency would not answer questions about the assessments’ findings, though a spokesperson said it has continued to visit prisons and conduct assessments, which it does not release to the public.

Later in 2022, a highly publicized Senate [subcommittee investigation found](https://www.hsgac.senate.gov/wp-content/uploads/imo/media/doc/2022-12-13%20PSI%20Staff%20Report%20-%20Sexual%20Abuse%20of%20Female%20Inmates%20in%20Federal%20Prisons.pdf) the problem of prison sexual assault was more widespread than previously understood and, around the same time, the Justice Department’s inspector general [issued a report](https://oig.justice.gov/sites/default/files/reports/23-001.pdf) criticizing the bureau’s handling of staff misconduct investigations.

Meanwhile, the Bureau of Prisons’ parent agency, the Justice Department, put together [a working group that recommended](https://www.justice.gov/d9/pages/attachments/2022/11/03/2022.11.02_bop_sexual_misconduct_working_group_report.pdf) prison officials “enhance prevention of sexual misconduct” by promoting “stronger leadership” at women’s facilities, improving staff training and installing more cameras.

In mid-2023, the department began dispatching its own teams to survey women’s prisons and make sure they were carrying out the working group’s recommendations. Nikhil Ramnaney, a former Justice Department attorney who [participated in a visit](https://www.justice.gov/archives/opa/pr/readout-justice-departments-sexual-abuse-facility-enhancement-and-review) to the SeaTac lockup in Washington state that summer, said the department notified prison officials in advance, giving them time to prepare. “BOP was putting on a show,” he said. And when Ramnaney and the other visitors interviewed women, the facility’s top officials stood nearby. When asked if they felt safe reporting abuse, the women offered “positive and lukewarm answers,” Ramnaney said. “In hindsight, what else were they going to say?”

Another Department of Justice attorney who visited Carswell offered a similar assessment, and both said the department never released findings from those site visits. Neither could identify any meaningful changes the agency made.

Since then, officials from the [Bureau of Prisons](https://www.justice.gov/d9/2024-12/2024.07.23_colette_peters.pdf) and the [Justice Department](https://files.gao.gov/reports/GAO-26-107343/index.html#_ftn72) have repeatedly said the agency is working to implement the working group’s recommendations. But when asked a series of detailed questions about the status of specific recommendations, the Justice Department deferred to the prison agency. Giamusso, the prisons spokesperson, said in an email that information was “not readily available.” She added, “We have more work to do, and we are committed to doing that work.”

And perhaps most disturbingly, the abuse continued at Dublin, even while the prison was under the scrutiny of the courts and Congress in the wake of Warden Garcia’s arrest. In addition to the hundreds who said they were abused before 2021, at least 47 prisoners alleged abuse by staffers after that. Many of those allegations have not been previously reported, and many of the alleged abusers have not been prosecuted.

The abuse continued even after the agency replaced Garcia. And it continued after a sprawling legal team — including attorneys from the advocacy organization Rights Behind Bars, the law firm Rosen Bien Galvan & Grunfeld and the nonprofit legal group California Collaborative for Immigrant Justice — filed the class action lawsuit against the bureau in the summer of 2023 on behalf of Ana and hundreds of other Dublin women. They [alleged the Bureau of Prisons’ systems](https://rbgg.com/survivors-of-sexual-violence-by-prison-officials-at-fci-dublin-file-class-action-lawsuit/) for preventing and responding to sexual abuse were so inadequate that everyone at Dublin was at risk. The following year, the government [claimed in court filings](https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.cand.416928/gov.uscourts.cand.416928.158.0_1.pdf) that sexual abuse was by then “virtually non-existent” at Dublin and that the facility was “not currently a sexualized environment.”

Ana and the other women at Dublin were shackled and taken to new facilities around the country in what seemed like an unusually torturous process.

A few weeks before that claim, a Dublin officer had allegedly slammed Antonina Troyer against the wall of her cell and raped her, [according to a lawsuit](https://www.courtlistener.com/docket/72087094/1/troyer-v-united-states/) she filed later, which has since been stayed. Troyer said three years after she reported him, she received a letter stating that her allegation was not sustained but offering no further information. The officer, who did not respond to requests for comment, was not prosecuted and still worked for the agency as of November.

“You have a huge system that just steamrolls everybody, and you’re already considered to be not trustworthy,” Troyer said in an interview. “Our word means practically nothing.”

Days later, [the bureau abruptly announced](https://www.nytimes.com/2024/04/15/us/dublin-womens-prison-close.html) that it would shut down Dublin — then asked the judge to dismiss the case. The judge demurred, [saying the idea](https://rbgg.com/wp-content/uploads/Dkt-438-Plaintiffs-Unopposed-Motion-for-Preliminary-Approval-of-Proposed-Consent-Decree-12-06-24-672-7.pdf) that closure solved the agency’s problems “strains credulity.”

Ana and the other women at Dublin were shackled and taken to other facilities around the country in what seemed like an [unusually torturous process](https://www.ktvu.com/news/fci-dublin-prison-closure-women-describe-horrific-journey-across-u-s). In letters and interviews, women recounted how some officers screamed at them, threatened to shoot them or left them without water for hours. “With their behavior and the noise of the cocked guns,” one woman wrote, “I was sure they were going to kill us.” An internal affairs investigation [later determined](https://rbgg.com/wp-content/uploads/FCI-Dublin-Case-423-cv-4155-YGR-3rd-Quarterly-Status-Report-October-1-%E2%80%93-December-31-2025-Dated-April-14-2026.pdf) that all the transport officers had acted “within policy” even though, in some cases, other prison staff corroborated the women’s accounts.

### “It Felt Just Like Another Dublin”

For Beaty and the other San Francisco-based attorneys heading up the legal team for the class action lawsuit, building a case against the federal government now became much more complicated. To interview dozens more survivors, they had to travel across the country to remote prisons.

That October, Beaty and fellow attorney Kara Janssen paid their first visit to Aliceville. They’d just come from a legal conference in Atlanta, where they’d given a presentation on their work at Dublin, then rented cars to drive four hours to a hotel in Tuscaloosa. After another hour on the road — once they’d nearly reached the Mississippi border — the bleak, boxy buildings of a federal prison rose up out of the endless forest.

When the lawyers walked through the front door, the prison staff seemed so unaccustomed to legal visitors that they weren’t sure how to sign them in. “It felt like nobody had come there in a long time,” said Janssen.

Over the next three days, she and Beaty took down statements from more than 70 women, most transfers from Dublin. Some described the rough move or their trouble getting basic medical care. But others told new stories of abuse, this time at Aliceville. The medical staff who forced them to dance. The officers who assaulted them in closets, and the other staff who pretended not to see.

One of the women who talked to them was Ela. She’d landed behind bars five years earlier, after FBI agents arrested her in a meth bust. It was the first time she’d been in real trouble. She was sentenced to seven years in federal prison and eventually ended up in Aliceville, where, in early 2022, an officer pulled her into a closet and pushed her to her knees, forcing her to perform oral sex on him before vaginally raping her, according to a tort claim filed on her behalf. When she reported the incident to prison officials, she said they yelled at her and fired her from her job in the prison’s safety department. Traumatized and distraught, she began cutting herself. Eventually, she asked to see a psychiatrist but left feeling worse after the psychiatrist made fun of her, according to the narrative laid out in her legal claim.

About a year later, Wilder — the officer in stylish jeans — started circling, according to the claim. He was flirtatious at first, talking about his own romantic encounters and asking about her family back home. Then, one day in the spring of 2023, she said he forced her into a utility closet and made her perform oral sex on him. A few months later, he locked her in that same closet for two hours, returning three times to rape her, according to the legal claim.

Ela wasn’t the only woman Wilder allegedly targeted. Other women had reported him for similar behavior, but his abuse continued until the fall of 2024, according to court filings and interviews. That September, investigators questioned Ela about her earlier abuser, who had [by then pleaded guilty](https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.alnd.185331/gov.uscourts.alnd.185331.28.0.pdf) to assaulting two other women. But even though Ela had already confided in Ana about Wilder, she was reluctant to tell prison officials. “I was very scared to speak out,” she said in emails in Spanish to ProPublica and The Marshall Project.

Investigators paid another visit days later — and that time she told them everything. “I would not want the chain of victims to continue,” she said. “We had to put a stop to it.” Wilder was walked off the prison property that day. But officers threw Ela into solitary confinement for nearly two weeks. They told her it was for her safety — “which really wasn’t safe at all because it was a nightmare,” she said.

> “You have a huge system that just steamrolls everybody, and you’re already considered to be not trustworthy. Our word means practically nothing.”
> Antonina Troyer, formerly incarcerated at Federal Correctional Institution Dublin

And while Wilder was eventually indicted for sexually abusing seven women, 11 others — including Ela — have also accused him of sexual assault in civil claims, including two lawsuits. In both of those cases, a court has paused the proceedings until the criminal charges against him are resolved. Apart from his not guilty plea, Wilder has not responded in court or to repeated requests for comment.

“A lot of people were really scared,” Janssen said. “It felt just like another Dublin.” As she got in the car to leave, Janssen broke down crying.

In the months following the Aliceville trip, the lawyers traveled to prisons in California, Connecticut, Texas, Florida and Wisconsin to speak to Dublin victims. At almost every stop, women told them of abuse happening in that institution, too.

In early 2025, over [the new Trump administration’s objections](https://apnews.com/article/federal-prisons-dublin-sexual-abuse-lawsuit-settlement-efd50a189859f73e4945a4e2e104137d), Gonzalez Rogers, the judge in the Dublin class action suit, approved a sweeping consent decree — a first for the federal prison system. It included pathways to early release, increased protections against retaliation and two more years of court-mandated oversight for the Dublin survivors.

It would not be enough to protect those who were still incarcerated. Even as their lawyers prepared civil suits, Ana and the other Dublin women became targets for harassment at their new prisons. At some facilities, staff derisively referred to them as “Dublin girls” or “Dublin bitches” and refused to give them prison jobs, according to interviews and court papers. Elsewhere, other prisoners viewed them as snitches and held their decision to come forward against them. ** **

The women also continued to face sexual abuse. After getting shipped out of Dublin, the survivors reported almost 40 instances of abuse at their new prisons during the first six months of the court-appointed monitoring, according to monthly reports filed in federal court.

Abuse allegations continue to extend far beyond Dublin survivors. In interviews and legal filings, ProPublica and The Marshall Project uncovered accusations of sexual abuse at a prison camp in California, a low-security prison in Wisconsin and a [notoriously troubled facility](https://www.nytimes.com/2018/11/30/us/whitey-bulger-murder.html) in West Virginia.

And earlier this year, the FBI showed up at Carswell, a facility so troubled that one woman described it in court filings as “a federal prison that became a hunting ground.”

Investigators uncovered a cluster of allegations against paramedic Preston Emert, who was removed from his job after 18 women accused him of sexually abusive behavior, according to court filings and internal bureau correspondence. Emert targeted women with addiction issues and medical problems, demanding sex in exchange for drugs and medical treatments, according to several women, their attorneys and a top bureau official.

“I have seizures and would need help and in order to get it I would have to have sex with him,” Olivia Floyd said in a letter to reporters. Emert is one of 12 Carswell employees accused of sexual assault in the last five years. He has not been charged, and bureau officials said in November he is still employed as a paramedic at Carswell.

Last month, his boss — the health services supervisor who records show fielded at least one of the early complaints about the paramedic’s behavior — was arrested after he admitted to investigators that he was having sex with a woman incarcerated there. He has not yet entered a plea.

### “No Substantive Long-Term Changes”

Despite evidence of persistent abuse throughout the system, the Bureau of Prisons now appears poised to have less oversight than ever. The landmark consent decree is set to expire early next year. The Office of Inspector General, the Justice Department’s watchdog that has the power to investigate and recommend reforms, has suffered staffing shortages in recent years as the [Trump administration has pushed](https://www.govexec.com/oversight/2026/04/inspectors-general-targeted-funding-cuts-trumps-fy27-budget/412912/) to slash its budget. Meanwhile, hoping to shore up its staffing levels, [the bureau recently announced](https://www.facebook.com/BOPCareers/posts/pfbid02BFWHJkivsgKdF5zGVV8PJccMUU1WWwz8UWaVneCH3fcSxRE8MMYooWotEwHwbmCGl) it would allow new officers to start with fewer qualifications and lower pay.

“It’s almost as if they’ve learned nothing,” said Shanna Rifkin, general counsel for FAMM, a nonpartisan organization that advocates for criminal justice reform. “They need staff who are well-trained and well-compensated, and to lower the qualifications when you already have rampant sex abuse and drugs being brought in — what do they think is going to happen?”

Two years after [Congress passed the Federal Prison Oversight Act](https://www.congress.gov/bill/118th-congress/house-bill/3019/text), the ombuds office it mandated still does not exist. The Trump Department of Justice has failed to release a projected budget and progress report, even after[both chambers](https://www.congress.gov/committee-report/119th-congress/house-report/272/1)[of Congress](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CRPT-119srpt44/html/CRPT-119srpt44.htm) [directed it](https://www.famm.org/press-release/famm-responds-to-passage-of-h-r-6938-to-establish-ombudsman-office/) to do so by April of this year. And lawmakers have yet to appropriate any money for it.

Within the Bureau of Prisons, the effects of the intended reforms have been minimal. The agency has installed more cameras and restructured its Office of Internal Affairs, though under the new structure, staff at individual prisons typically still investigate their coworkers. “I think small things were changed — like the signage about how to report [abuse] needed fixing,” said former Justice Department attorney Marnie Shiels. “There were no substantive long-term changes from this that I know of.”

Lawyers say it’s also becoming harder for civil cases to succeed. So far, the federal government has agreed to pay $116 million to settle lawsuits with the first 103 victims of Dublin. Roughly 300 more cases are working their way through the legal system, including the one brought by Ana, who has since been released from prison. The man who abused her was never criminally charged, and he died while under investigation.

Ana, above, emboldened Ela, her younger cellmate at Aliceville, to speak out.

Trump’s Justice Department has offered paltry payouts in some cases and reneged on signed agreements that could have avoided protracted litigation in others, according to sources familiar with the situation. Lauren Bis, a spokesperson for the White House, referred questions to federal prison officials.

Legal experts also point to a recent, troubling precedent. In 2024, a federal judge in Alabama threw out a lawsuit brought by a woman at Aliceville who had been raped by an officer. The judge, Scott Coogler, sided with the Justice Department in ruling that the prison system wasn’t liable because the officer “was acting outside the scope of his employment” when he sexually assaulted her while on duty. The decision is pending appeal.

“This case could make it incredibly hard for anyone abused in government custody to seek accountability from the BOP,” said Deborah Golden, who is representing dozens of women in cases about their sexual abuse at federal prisons. “I hope that doesn’t happen.”

To the lawyers at the forefront of this fight, the fallout from Dublin has come to a disappointing conclusion. “It should not be hard to go to work and not force someone to give you a blow job,” Janssen said. “That is an extremely easy rule to follow. And I can only think that it’s just a complete lack of accountability.”

As for the Bureau of Prisons, it’s already returning to a familiar playbook. Earlier this year, the bureau announced plans to stop housing women at Aliceville and turn the facility into a men’s prison. Ela has since been released. But the rest of the women will, once again, be scattered across the country.

### How We Counted Abuse Cases

Reporters searched federal court records and civil lawsuits and interviewed currently and formerly incarcerated survivors of sexual abuse, prison officials, and civil rights attorneys to compile a list of allegations that met the criteria for “[sexual abuse](https://www.prearesourcecenter.org/standard/115-6)” under the Prison Rape Elimination Act. They included only abuse allegedly committed by a BOP staffer against prisoners at women’s facilities operated by the Bureau of Prisons. There were 172 cases involving women and 15 in which the victims were transgender men. Allegations were sourced from an official record — including tort claims, lawsuits, criminal filings and internal agency documents — or the individual themselves, in which cases reporters corroborated their accounts with contemporaneous witness statements, journal entries, or letters; court filings; sworn statements; and other documentation.

items.articleBody: Scientists have developed a new carbon capture material that turns moisture from an obstacle into an advantage, potentially solving a major problem with removing CO2 from industrial emissions. The material works even in extremely humid conditions and can be reused repeatedly, offering a promising path toward cheaper, more effective carbon capture.

items.title: When Jorge Luis Borges Co-Wrote a Surreal Sci-Fi Noir Film: Invasión (1969)

items.articleBody:
“ *La ciudad es más que la gente.* ” So declares a character called Don Porfirio in *Invasión*, the debut feature by Argentine director Hugo Santiago. The line is the film’s most memorable, not least because of the reversal it pulls on our expectations. Saying that a city is really its people must have been a somewhat banal observation even in 1969, when *Invasión* came out, but saying that a city is more than its people still sounds contrarian enough to be intriguing. It’s even more compelling coming from Don Porfirio, a mastermind whose intensely abstracted manner and refined literary diction will remind some viewers of no figure so much as[Jorge Luis Borges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jorge_Luis_Borges) — and as well he might, since Borges co-wrote the script.

Another major contributor to *Invasión* ’s screenplay was Borges’ longtime friend, occasional collaborator, and junior colleague in letters [Adolfo Bioy Casares](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adolfo_Bioy_Casares). Anyone who’s read about their relationship (as detailed in Bioy Casares’ tome of published diaries, simply titled [Borges](https://link.amazon/B0dw5EXR9)) knows how deeply entangled it was with the streets of Buenos Aires, where both of them were born and raised. And anyone who knows Buenos Aires will recognize those streets onscreen in this film, despite the title card that calls it Aquilea. Echoing the name of Achilles, it offers a clue as to Borges and Bioy Casares’ classical inspiration for this project, which transposes the city under siege of Homer’s Troy into mid-century Latin America, where a small group of resistance members organize against an arriving army of menacing white-coated invaders.

Though Borges wasn’t exactly one for topicality in his own *ficciones*, it wouldn’t be wholly unreasonable to make an allegorical reading of the film. It’s set in the year 1957, when Argentina was ruled by Pedro Eugenio Aramburu, one of several dictators in the country’s twentieth-century history. It came out during the dictatorship of Juan Carlos Onganía Carballo. And the 1976 military coup that put Jorge Rafael Videla in power banished it to an official non-existence, seen only in the most underground screenings. It wasn’t until the nineteen-nineties that *Invasión* was rediscovered and made whole out of partial prints found in France, the country to which Santiago had long since decamped. Now it can be seen on YouTube in [one version](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JbJZHB8Ce4E) with optional English and French subtitles, and [another, higher resolution version](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QxP1ftEepoE) with French subtitles only.

Viewers today may be quick to notice the obvious budgetary limitations, manifest in odd-sounding [foley work](https://www.openculture.com/2018/05/how-the-sounds-you-hear-in-movies-are-really-made-discover-the-magic-of-foley-artists.html) and theatrical death scenes, but the cinematic vitality of its mixture of film noir, *Nouvelle* *Vague*, political thriller, and even science fiction remains undeniable. (With the chases and explosions it manages, it may even partially qualify as an action movie.) So does the atmosphere of the real locations — the streets Borges and Bioy Casares walked, as well as cafés, rail yards, and the climactic football stadium — that constitute its alternately stately and desolate setting. It would be clichéd to say that the city itself becomes a character, but it would also prompt us to ask, which city, Buenos Aires or Aquilea? As with so many other questions about *Invasión*, there is no one answer.

items.articleBody:
Auf welche Art und Weise beziehen sich Parteien auf Wissenschaft? Welche Themen und Argumente spielen dabei eine Rolle? Das hat der Politikwissenschaftler Daniel Wiesner von der Universität Wien untersucht. Es zeigt sich: Rechtspopulist*innen nutzen am seltensten wissenschaftliche Bezüge, Grüne und Liberale am häufigsten.

**Sie haben mit** **Jakob-Moritz Eberl und Sophie Lecheler von der Universität Wien [untersucht, wie Parteien in österreichischen Parlamentsdebatten](https://jcom.sissa.it/article/pubid/JCOM_2506_2026_A09/) auf Wissenschaft Bezug nehmen. Wie sind Sie darauf gekommen, dass das ein lohnendes Forschungsthema wäre?**

**Daniel Wiesner** ist Doktorand in der Forschungsgruppe für Politische Kommunikation (POLCOM) an der Universität Wien. In seiner Dissertation befasst er sich mit der Rolle von Wissenschaft in politischen Diskursen. Foto: Jakob-Moritz Eberl

In meiner Dissertation geht es darum, wie Wissenschaft im politischen Diskurs eingesetzt und repräsentiert wird. Parlamentsdebatten sind spannend, weil in dieser Arena die unterschiedlichen Parteien miteinander kommunizieren. Es gibt ein argumentatives Hin und Her, das man in anderen Kanälen nicht findet. Gleichzeitig sind diese Debatten sehr nah am Policymaking-Prozess, also an konkreten politischen Gestaltungsprozessen. Man kann daran erkennen, welche Partei Wissenschaft wie zitiert, um ihre Entscheidungen zu rechtfertigen.

**Welche Verbindungen haben Politik und Wissenschaft idealerweise?**

Grundsätzlich ist beides stark miteinander verbunden. Wissenschaft ist wichtig für politische Entscheidungen, aber natürlich hat auch Politik Einfluss auf Wissenschaft – zum Beispiel über die Finanzierung oder eine bestimmte Agenda, die vorgegeben wird. Im konkreten Kontext der parlamentarischen Arbeit gibt es diese Idealvorstellung des evidenzbasierten Policy-Makings im Sinne von „Follow the Science“. Dieses Idealbild hat etwas mit der kultivierten Vorstellung von Wissenschaft als objektiver, rationaler und überlegener Wissensquelle zu tun, die sowohl in der Gesellschaft vorherrscht, aber auch von Politiker*innen vermittelt wird. Dahinter steckt die Idee, dass man dringende soziale und politische Probleme durch wissenschaftliche Evidenz lösen kann. Oft funktioniert das aber nicht ganz so einfach. Am Ende ist es doch oft eine politische Entscheidung, verschiedene Pro- und Contra-Argumente abzuwägen und eine Entscheidung zu treffen, die positive, aber gleichzeitig auch negative Folgen in unterschiedlichen Lebensbereichen der Bürger*innen haben kann. Dieses Spannungsfeld ist interessant.

**Sie haben**mehr als 100.000 Reden**des österreichischen Nationalrates von 1996 bis 2018 analysiert. Dazu mussten Sie erst einmal festlegen, was als Bezug zur Wissenschaft gewertet wird. Wie haben Sie das gemacht?**

Ja, das war eine Herausforderung. Wir haben zwei Hauptkategorien festgelegt. Die erste war „wissenschaftliche Akteur*innen“, also Wissenschaftler*innen und wissenschaftliche Institutionen. Die sind relativ einfach zu erkennen, weil sie meistens namentlich genannt werden. Bei der zweiten Kategorie, „wissenschaftliche Evidenz“, war das ein bisschen schwieriger. Es gibt konkrete Verweise auf spezifische Studien, aber auch abstraktere Konstrukte wie „die Wissenschaft sagt“. Wir haben deshalb ein breites Wörterbuch mit Schlüsselbegriffen erstellt. Large Language Models haben dann kodiert, ob ein Bezug zu einer spezifisch genannten Person, Institution, zu Studien oder Wissenschaft und wissenschaftlichen Erkenntnissen im abstrakten Sinn vorkommen.

### „Es gab keinen allgemeinen Trend zu mehr oder weniger Referenzen zur Wissenschaft. Vor allem während der Covid-19-Krise hätten wir erwartet, dass wissenschaftliche Bezüge deutlich häufiger vorkommen. Aber es war fast ausschließlich in Gesundheitsdebatten der Fall.“

Daniel Wiesner

**Art und Qualität der zitierten wissenschaftlichen Belege haben Sie nicht untersucht. Sie können also nicht ableiten, wer die „bessere“ Evidenz hat? **

Wir haben nicht erhoben, um welche Studien es geht, ob es seriöse wissenschaftliche Arbeiten sind und ob die Studien richtig zitiert wurden. Worauf wir uns konzentriert haben, ist das Selbstverständnis der Parteien – also wie sie Wissenschaft für ihre politischen Positionen verwenden und welches Selbstbild sie transportieren. Sind sie besonders wissenschaftshörig oder besonders kritisch?

**Haben Sie die Ergebnisse überrascht?**

Es gab überraschendere und weniger überraschende Aspekte. In etwa 20 Prozent der untersuchten Debatten kam irgendein Bezug zu Wissenschaft vor. Das ist nicht besonders viel oder wenig, das hatten wir ungefähr erwartet. Spannender war die zeitliche Komponente. Es gab keinen allgemeinen Trend zu mehr oder weniger Referenzen zur Wissenschaft. Vor allem während der Covid-19-Krise hätten wir erwartet, dass wissenschaftliche Bezüge deutlich häufiger vorkommen. Aber es war fast ausschließlich in Gesundheitsdebatten der Fall – zum Beispiel in Form von Studien zur Wirksamkeit von Impfungen und zu Auswirkungen von Kontaktbeschränkungen. Aber das hat nicht auf andere Politikfelder abgefärbt, in denen die Debatten so weitergeführt wurden wir bisher.

**Während es im Zeitverlauf kaum Veränderungen gab, haben Sie durchaus Unterschiede zwischen den Parteien gefunden. Welche waren die deutlichsten?**

Zum einen haben wir gesehen, dass die kleineren Parteien häufiger auf Wissenschaft verweisen als die großen, etablierten Parteien. Das könnte damit zusammenhängen, dass sie bei bestimmten Themen noch kein eindeutiges Profil haben und deswegen stärker auf Wissenschaft verweisen.

Zum anderen haben wir gesehen, dass es inhaltliche Unterschiede gibt, wie die Parteien Wissenschaft interpretieren. Die rechtspopulistische FPÖ zeigte die geringsten Referenzen zur Wissenschaft. Aber nicht nur in Bezug auf die Häufigkeit, sondern auch auf die Frage, wie eine Partei über Wissenschaft spricht, zeigten sich Unterschiede. Bei der FPÖ sahen wir, dass sie eine starke konfrontative Logik in den Reden verfolgt, in denen Wissenschaft vorkommt. Es wird häufig eine Outgroup benannt – zum Beispiel politische Gegner*innen oder Migrant*innen, von denen man sich abgrenzt.

### „Bei der FPÖ sahen wir, dass sie eine starke konfrontative Logik in den Reden verfolgt, in denen Wissenschaft vorkommt. Es wird häufig eine Outgroup benannt – zum Beispiel politische Gegner*innen oder Migrant*innen, von denen man sich abgrenzt.“

Daniel Wiesner

**Es wird also regelmäßig auf Wissenschaft Bezug genommen – jedoch selektiv und passend zur eigenen Parteilinie?**

Ja, genau. Wir haben uns im zweiten Teil unserer Analyse die „typischen“ und „untypischen“ Wörter im Wissenschaftsdiskurs der jeweiligen Parteien angesehen. Dadurch werden die Themen und Terminologien deutlich, die eine Partei etablieren möchte. Bei den Grünen wurde das Wort „ökologisch“ beispielsweise häufig verwendet und bei den Sozialdemokraten der Begriff „Arbeitnehmer*innen“. Typisch für den FPÖ-Diskurs war der Bezug auf „Linke“ als politische Gegner*innen und „Ausländer“. Begriffe wie Umweltpolitik, Klimaschutz und Energiefonds wurden bei der FPÖ hingegen sehr selten verwendet.

Auffällig war bei den Grünen, aber vor allem auch bei den liberalen Neos, dass sie Begriffe wie „Evidenz“ und „evidenzbasiert“ verwendeten, was der Follow-the-Science-Logik entspricht, weil Politik dadurch wissenschaftlich begründet wird. Die FPÖ verwendete diese Begriffe selten und hatte stattdessen meist einen konfrontativen Claim, den die Ergebnisse einer Studie untermauern sollten – beispielsweise, dass Migrant*innen laut Forschungsergebnissen zu viele Sozialleistungen in Anspruch nehmen würden.

Anteil der verschiedenen Darstellungsweisen von Wissenschaft an der Gesamtzahl der Reden der jeweiligen Partei (1996–2022). Abbildung: [Wiesner et al. (2026)](https://jcom.sissa.it/article/pubid/JCOM_2506_2026_A09/)

**Bei welchen politischen Themen spielte Wissenschaft eine Rolle?**

Vor allem bei Gesundheit, aber auch bei Umwelt, Technologie, Energie und bis zu einem gewissen Grad auch Bildung. Diese fünf Themen kamen am häufigsten vor. Es gab einige Themenbereiche, bei denen Wissenschaft eine sehr geringe Rolle spielte, was uns zum Teil überrascht hat – zum Beispiel bei Wirtschaft und Arbeit. Die wissenschaftlichen Referenzen waren hier selten, obwohl es viele Studien zu wirtschaftlichen und sozialen Themen gibt. Möglicherweise gibt die Parteiposition in diesen Bereichen stärker die Richtung vor, sodass es Wissenschaft schwerer hat, zitiert zu werden als beispielsweise bei Gesundheitsfragen.

**Wissenschaft hat es demnach bei bestimmten Themen schwerer, in parlamentarischen Debatten vorzukommen. Haben Sie überlegt, wie sich das ändern ließe?**

Die Ergebnisse zeigen, dass sich die Politik auf ihre Muster verlässt und die Themen gewissermaßen den Bezug zur Wissenschaft vorgeben. Aber ich denke, dass sich einiges ändern ließe. Es zeigt sich zum Beispiel, dass Institutionen wie Scientific Advisory Boards innerhalb der Parlamente einen positiven Effekt haben. 1 Wenn Wissenschaft für Entscheidungsträger*innen aufbereitet und verfügbar gemacht wird, hat das einen positiven Effekt auf evidenzbasiertes Policy-Making. In einem anderen Forschungsstrang schaut man, wie wissenschaftliche Argumente, die politische Implikationen haben, formuliert sein könnten. In der Honest-Broker-Diskussion („ehrliche Vermittler*innen“, Anm. d. Red.) nach Roger A. Pielke 2 lautet eine Annahme, dass es besonders vorteilhaft wäre, wenn Wissenschaftler*innen Evidenz präsentieren, ohne dabei politische Positionen oder Richtungen vorzugeben. Empirische Forschung hierzu zeichnet jedoch kein einheitliches Bild. Die Alternative wäre ein Advocacy-Modell, in dem Wissenschaftler*innen verstärkt Policy-Empfehlungen abgeben. Das ist ein spannendes Feld, und eine Frage, die uns wohl auch in Zukunft noch weiter beschäftigen wird.

### „Es gab einige Themenbereiche, bei denen Wissenschaft eine sehr geringe Rolle spielte, was uns zum Teil überrascht hat – zum Beispiel bei Wirtschaft und Arbeit.“

Daniel Wiesner

**Gibt es ähnliche Studien aus anderen Ländern – beispielsweise Deutschland?**

Zu parlamentarischen Reden gibt es relativ wenig. Eine Ausnahme ist eine Studie 3, in der über einen langen Zeitraum die Rhetorik im US-Kongress analysiert wurde. Es ging um die Frage, ob eher eine evidenzbasierte oder intuitionsbasierte Sprache verwendet wurde. Ansonsten gibt es ein breites Forschungsfeld, dass sich den Policy-Making-Prozess anschaut – also politische Dokumente, in denen bestimmte Quellen zitiert werden. Aber zum parlamentarischen politischen Diskurs gibt es relativ wenig.

**In welche Richtung würden Sie gerne weiterforschen?**

Zum einen zur angesprochenen Frage: Wie akkurat sind diese Darstellungen von Wissenschaft, also mehr im Sinne eines Fact Checkings, ob wissenschaftliche Argumente korrekt repräsentiert werden und welche Arten von Quellen innerhalb des politischen Diskurses herangezogen werden. Auf der anderen Seite interessiert mich auch: Was denken Bürger*innen über diese Argumente? Haben sie eher eine Follow-the-science-Erwartung oder wünschen sie sich abwägende politischen Prozesse, in denen Wissenschaft einbezogen wird, aber die Entscheidung am Ende doch bei der politischen Ebene liegt?

items.body: Welche Themen und Argumente spielen dabei eine Rolle? Das hat der Politikwissenschaftler Daniel Wiesner von der Universität Wien untersucht. Es zeigt sich: Rechtspopulist*innen nutzen am seltensten wissenschaftliche Bezüge, Grüne und Liberale am häufigsten. Sie haben mit Jakob-Moritz Eberl und Sophie Lecheler von der Universität Wien untersucht, wie Parteien in österreichischen Parlamentsdebatten auf Wissenschaft Bezug nehmen. items.articleBody: When U.S. President Donald Trump lands in Shenzhen later this week for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, he will sit down with Chinese leader Xi Jinping for the fourth time amid an unexpected détente between Washington and Beijing. The trade war of 2025 is in abeyance, the two governments have announced a relationship of “constructive strategic stability,” and, to the alarm of American allies, Trump and Xi are planning to meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin. Beneath the surface, however, the détente is beginning to crack.

APOD

Astronomy Picture of the Day

Discover the cosmos! Each day a different image or photograph of our fascinating universe is featured, along with a brief explanation written by a professional astronomer.

Original Annotated

## Milky Way versus Aurora

**Explanation:** Are these two giant arches battling for control of the sky? No, but it sure looks like it! The arch on the left is the central band of our [Milky Way Galaxy](https://science.nasa.gov/resource/the-milky-way-galaxy/), an ancient system of stars, gas, and dust that predates [our Earth](https://science.nasa.gov/resource/planet-earth-through-the-ages/) and is very far away. The arch on the right, by contrast, is an [auroral ribbon](https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2004-november-12-missouris-green-ribbon-sky/) that is only hours old, composed of energized [atoms and molecules](https://www.bbc.co.uk/bitesize/articles/zc86m39#zygjdp3), and is close by — right in [Earth’s upper atmosphere](https://www.nasa.gov/image-article/properties-of-earths-upper-atmosphere/). These chance-superposed [titan](https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2025-november-30-the-surface-of-titan-from-huygens/)s have [our Sun](https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2024-june-15-prominences-and-filaments-on-the-active-sun/) in common, a [stellar member](https://www.reddit.com/media?url=https%3A%2F%2Fpreview.redd.it%2Fthis-is-the-most-cute-thing-i-ever-seen-v0-mpx697lakcue1.jpg%3Fwidth%3D1080%26crop%3Dsmart%26auto%3Dwebp%26s%3Da5d18b145135737912b5caa61fcc56766726f6cb) of the Milky Way that ejects energetic particles which create [aurora](https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2026-february-10-in-green-company-aurora-over-norway/)s. Far behind the middle of the [auroral arch](https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2021-january-13-arches-across-an-arctic-sky/) is the [Big Dipper](https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2013-april-21-the-big-dipper/). Even farther in the distance is the [Andromeda galaxy](https://svs.gsfc.nasa.gov/11675/) — the bright spot near the top of the frame, just left of center. The [featured image](https://www.instagram.com/p/DfAZEgmIDIq/) was taken about a month ago from [Kvaløya](https://youtu.be/4VlzJh3WBGU) in northern [Norway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norway).

items.articleBody:
## Improving on a timeless recipe

The bezier curve is a staple of CAD and computer graphics. Like Bic pens, the design is decades old and they're everywhere. You'll often find them as the default or only choice in various illustration and animation tools.

Conceived by [Paul de Casteljau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_de_Casteljau) in 1959, and refined by [Pierre Bézier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Bézier) in the 1960s at Renault, the enduring appeal of the bezier curve lies in its simplicity. While more sophisticated curves have been invented, and [new ones continue to be proposed](https://linebender.org/blog/hyperbezier/), these are limited to specific domains, like high-precision CAD or road design. In general use, the bezier stubbornly refuses to be dethroned, despite its shortcomings.

Hence bezier curves are a piece of legacy tech we appear to be stuck with. As a software engineer, my question then is: can we make beziers better without invalidating all the tech built on and with them?

The answer is yes.

[↗ wallup.net](https://wallup.net/renault-4cv-classic-cars-french-73/)

## Lerp-a-derp

Drawing a bezier curve is a surprisingly simple and linear process:

*Tip: All the diagrams in this post are fully interactive.*

Given a series of control points, we connect them with lines. We then run along those lines simultaneously, to produce new points, which can be connected again. This process is repeated until we are left with a single point, which lies on the curve.

This construction makes beziers far more regular than they might first appear.

The linear interpolations (aka *lerps* ) can be summarized into a single compact formula, e.g. for 4 control points $ \left(A, B, C, D\right) $:

$$ \gamma \left( t \right) = A \cdot \left(1 - t\right)^3 + B \cdot 3 \left(1 - t\right)^2 t + C \cdot 3 \left(1 - t\right) t^2 + D \cdot t^3 $$

The rule is simple: descending powers of $\left(1 - t\right)$, ascending powers of $t$, with coefficients taken from the n'th row of Pascal's triangle:

$$
\ {ccccccccccccc}
&&&&&& 1 \\
&&&&& 1 && 1 \\
&&&& 1 && 2 && 1 \\
&&& 1 && 3 && 3 && 1 \\
&& 1 && 4 && 6 && 4 && 1 \\
&1 && 5 && 10 && 10 && 5 && 1 \\
... &&&&&&... &&&&&&... \\
\ $$

For curves in 2D and 3D, the formula is applied to the individual X, Y or Z coordinates.

While beziers can be constructed for any number of control points, the common practice is to only use cubic beziers with 4 control points. This is because the curve is only guaranteed to cross through the first and last control point, which makes higher degree beziers more difficult to shape.

Larger curves are instead constructed by joining together multiple cubic bezier segments, with the tangents lined up to create a segmented curve that appears smooth:

This is the cubic bezier *spline*, as commonly understood. The precision "pen tool" in most drawing apps then consists of drawing and editing the control points, rather than drawing curves directly.

## A Lie Told Everywhere

Pen tools typically have a few different modes for the control points:

Intuitively these represent various degrees of smoothness. Symmetric tangents are offered as the smoothest option, with some qualities of smoothness being lost as you relax the constraints.

In reality this is **completely wrong**, and this is easy to demonstrate.

Bezier curves can be split exactly, by reading off the new control points from the interpolation diagram:

The left and right segments are 100% identical to the original curve, and always join up perfectly at the seam. Yet the tangents in the middle will be asymmetric except for one split near the middle. This can be confirmed using a *curvature comb* which represents the (inverse) radius of curvature at every point:

The curvature comb remains continuous, with no jumps.

This means that whether or not adjacent tangents are of equal length, i.e. symmetric, is completely irrelevant. Attempting to draw smooth and intuitive bezier curves this way is a fool's errand.

A simple way to improve this is to treat the tangents as relative rather than absolute. e.g. We can make them proportional to the distance between the start and end of each segment:

This spline is easier to edit, because as you move each curve point around, the adjacent segments naturally flex to get out of the way. There are far fewer cusps created this way. Editing the tangents remains the same.

However if we plot curvature again, we can tell this isn't a great solution:

Scaling tangents proportionally doesn't guarantee that curvature is preserved as you edit, nor does curvature remain continuous from one segment to the next.

This also shows that offering users a curvature comb visualization as a "helpful tool" is really quite *mean*: adjusting the curvature on one end will also affect the other side, requiring repeated adjustments back and forth until it's close enough.

## Handle Carefully

A much more effective strategy is to work with curvature directly.

While this is a difficult problem in general, it turns out there are some surprising relationships here, which we can observe directly:

Consider the curvature at the start of segment $A-B-C-D$. This is affected only by the positions of $A$, $B$ and $C$. Point $D$ can be moved freely if it's detached from $C$.

Furthermore, because the tangent $A-B$ is horizontal, only the vertical position of $C$ matters. This is a result of the underlying linear interpolations, which end up cancelling out a lot of terms in the formulas.

The curvature at $A$ is therefor only affected by the length of $A-B$, and the perpendicular distance from $C$ to $A-B$. The same applies to $D$ on the other side with $C-D$ and $B$.

This isn't very useful by itself though. When we move a curve point ($A$ or $D$), typically the adjacent control point ($B$ or $C$) is moved as well to preserve the tangent. And when we turn a symmetric or asymmetric tangent, the adjacent tangent in the next segment is turned by the same angle, altering the curvature on that side.

Still, this shows that preserving curvature is not by itself a crazy idea and can be done simply by scaling the tangents appropriately. The rules would be simple:

- When we move a curve point, we have to preserve the start and end curvature in the adjacent segments
- When we move a tangent, we have to preserve the curvature on the opposite end of the current segment, as well as on both sides of the adjacent segment

This ought to produce an editing experience where the curve actually respects your intent. Except not quite:

Moving curve points works great, but when turning a tangent, the length of that tangent is itself a poor representation of the user's intent. Small changes can cause huge shifts in curvature, which can cause the curve to jump around and explode unexpectedly as it tries to find a matching solution.

Hence it's better to work with curvature handles instead, where the length corresponds directly to curvature:

Unlike the curvature comb, the length of the handles is the non-inverted radius of curvature, which is the more natural choice.

These handles are very stable and can be converted just-in-time to classic bezier control points, without needing to round-trip back and forth between the two representations. Helpfully, this also avoids numerical drift.

## Goldilocks

To actually pull this off, we need to solve for the lengths $l_0$ and $l_1$ of the tangents, given the desired curvatures $k_0$ and $k_1$, the start/end points $A$ and $D$, and the unit-length tangents at the start/end.

Given a curve $\gamma\left(t\right)$, we can express the unit tangent vector $\ \left(t\right)$ as the normalized derivative:

$$ \ \left(t\right) = \ {\displaystyle |γ'\left(t\right)|} $$

This can be used to find the curvature vector $\ \left(t\right)$ via two vector cross products using the first and second derivative:

$$ \ \left(t\right) = \ \left(t\right) \times \ {|\gamma'\left(t\right)|^2} \times \ \left(t\right) $$

The cross products ensure that $\ \left(t\right)$ is perpendicular to $\ \left(t\right)$, i.e. they extract the normal vector component of the middle term. Now we can solve for $\ \left(0\right) = k_0$ and $\ \left(1\right) = k_1$.

After working through the math, we end up with a quadratic system of equations in $l_0$ and $l_1$:

$$
\ a_0 \cdot l_0^2 + b \cdot l_1 + c_0 = 0 \\[0.3em]
a_1 \cdot l_1^2 + b \cdot l_0 + c_1 = 0
\ $$

Where:

$$
\ {lcl}
a_0 & = & ±|k_0| \\[0.3em]
a_1 & = & ±|k_1| \\[0.3em]
b & = & 2 \cdot |\ (0) \times \ (1)| \\[0.3em]
c_0 & = & 6 \cdot |\ (0) \times (D - A)| \\[0.3em]
c_1 & = & 6 \cdot |\ (1) \times (A - D)| \\[0.3em]
\ $$

This captures a few things:

- The sign of the curvature $k_i$ defines whether the curve turns clockwise or counterclockwise. When moving curve points around, the curve may be forced to flip, hence the $±$ is necessary, and both signs can change independently.
- The coupling between $l_0$ and $l_1$ is influenced only by $b$. If $b = 0$, then the two equations are independent and the problem is trivial to solve. This corresponds to the situation where the two tangents are parallel.
- The constant term $c_i$ is influenced only by the perpendicular distance $D - A$ (or $A - D$) to the tangent $\ $. This matches the earlier finding that only perpendicular distance affects curvature.

Hence, the problem is reduced to finding the intersection of two double-parabolas, one horizontal and one vertical:

The two sides of each double-parabola represent bending clockwise or counterclockwise. We have to solve 4 times, one for each sign combination $\left(+,+\right)$, $\left(+,-\right)$, $\left(-,+\right)$, $\left(-,-\right)$.

To solve this system, we can rewrite either of the equations to isolate $l_1$ or $l_0$:

$$
l_1 = \ {\displaystyle b} \\[0.5em]
l_0 = \ {\displaystyle b}
$$

Pick one, and square it to plug it into the other original equation as the $l_1^2$ or $l_0^2$ term. This produces a quartic equation in the other variable (resp. $l_0$ or $l_1$), which can be solved directly using the quartic formula.

We can then compute the other $l_i$, either:

$$
l_1 = \ {\displaystyle a_1}} \\[0.5em]
l_0 = \ {\displaystyle a_0}}
$$

Not all solutions of the quartic will be actual solutions to the system however, because of the squaring. So we have to double check that the original equations hold before accepting a solution for $\left(l_0, l_1\right)$.

We also want to reject solutions where $l_0 < 0$ or $l_1 < 0$, because these represent situations where the tangents have been flipped by 180º.

In most cases, there will only be one valid solution, and this works pretty well:

For corner-type points, one or both $k_i$'s are infinite. This is straightforward to solve as the matching $l_i$ is zero and the other can be computed directly.

## Grouper and Snapper

Unfortunately if there are multiple solutions, these each represent a different curve:

Having the curve jump around as you edit it would be a very bad editing experience, but there is no obvious way to pick the right one.

One strategy would be to remember the previous $l_0$ and $l_1$ as you edit, and pick the solution that is closest to the previous curve. However this would introduce path-dependence into editing, where the order and direction that you moved points around in affects which curve you end up with. For a drawing tool, this is quite frustrating and undesirable.

Different solutions to the equation can also appear and vanish suddenly, so this wouldn't eliminate popping either, merely reduce it.

Ideally the resulting curvatures should always change smoothly themselves. This can be accomplished by designing an appropriate weighting heuristic for the solutions, and calculating their weighted average.

1) The forbidden regions:

When a solution approaches either $l_0 < 0$ or $l_1 < 0$, it's about to vanish, so its weight should go to zero there.

2) When two opposite-bending parabolas are about to become tangent, two solutions will move towards each other, before both vanishing at the same time:

These solutions are unstable and should be avoided. To detect this, I calculate the gradient vector of each equation.

$$
\ = \ 2 \cdot a_0 \cdot l_0 & b\ \\[0.3em]
\ = \ b & 2 \cdot a_1 \cdot l_1\ $$

The angle between them can be found via their dot product, after dividing by their respective lengths:

$$
\cos \theta = \ \cdot \ }{\displaystyle |\ ||\ |}
$$

A value close to $-1$ means two opposite-bending parabolas, while a value close to $1$ means two aligned parabolas. The latter is not as bad, as this implies many almost-equivalent solutions.

3) When the radius of curvature is very big compared to the bezier itself, one of the possible solutions is for the curve to cross through itself, forming a loop. This should be discouraged:

We can divide by the length of $|\ |$ i.e. $\ $, preferring solutions that have shorter tangents.

Putting it all together, the weighting heuristic I chose is:

$$
\left(\ \right) = \left(\ {\displaystyle |\ |^2}\right)^2
$$

- By applying $\arccos \left(-\cos \theta\right)$, we remap the dot-product range $(-1..1)$ to $(0..π)$ which effectively neutralizes the unstable solutions
- Large $|\ |$'s represent undesirable solutions, so should be strongly penalized and only chosen if they are the only option
- When the entire heuristic approaches $0$, the influence should vanish smoothly, hence the overall squaring

Using this as the weight, the resulting bezier curves always change smoothly, even when the start and end are moved around and through each other.

But when multiple solutions are averaged together, the resulting $(l_0, l_1)$ is not necessarily a solution to the original system. This means the resulting curvatures are not always exact, even when there is an exact solution nearby.

To mitigate this, we can add an additional resampling step, where we re-weigh the solutions according to the inverse distance^4 to the weighted average:

$$
\left(\ \right) = \ {|\ - \ |^4}
$$

This causes the solution to snap smoothly to exact solutions when available.

## Migratory Curves

What's especially nice about this approach is that it can largely be slotted into existing systems with little modification required.

The UI of adjusting and editing bezier handles can be kept, including the notion of the 4 point types. Just the meaning of the lengths of the tangents changes. Converting an asymmetric point to a symmetric point will actually equalize the curvature of the left and right side, which is what the user actually wants.

The internal representation can mostly remain the same type, i.e. a series of points, just those points represent curvature tangents, not bezier tangents. Though it's better to explicitly store the unit length tangents and curvatures directly, which is more numerically stable. For the demos here I made pairwise conversion functions between curvature handles ↔︎ points/tangents/curvatures ↔︎ bezier handles.

Splitting a curvature bezier is a lot simpler than splitting a classic bezier, because the start and end handles don't change at all, and the newly created handles are symmetric:

There is one remaining flaw though. When splitting a curve with an S-bend, the splits near the bend are not exact:

The heuristic picks the wrong curve on one or both sides. This can be fixed by remembering the specific orientation of the curvature, and only flipping the curvature sign when necessary. Though this does introduce some minimal path-dependence into editing.

So really you would need to expose this in the UI as an extra orientation toggle for ambiguous control points. It would also mean that the internal representation has to be in tangent + signed curvature form to be fully stable, not just curvature handles.

Near the S-bend, the radius of curvature—and thus the handle size—effectively becomes infinite, because $|k|$ becomes $0$. The bezier control points lie on a straight line, as perpendicular distance to the tangent is zero.

So even when handled exactly, this can still create impractically large curvature handles. Perhaps what's needed is a 5th "Inflection" point type, for points with exactly zero $|k|$, though such points tend to be very unstable, and sometimes no solution exists:

To migrate a classic bezier to a curvature bezier, you can measure the unit tangents and curvature at the start and end. In the vast majority of cases this will result in the exact same curve. If it doesn't, then you must split the original bezier to avoid the ambiguity.

For complex operations on bezier curves, e.g. boolean union or intersection, these still have to be done in bezier form. This implies some amount of round-tripping between the two representations, which would introduce numerical drift. However, only the newly created points need to be converted back, because the curvature and tangents elsewhere remain the same.

* * *

This post started from the observation that "symmetric" bezier tangents aren't actually symmetric as you'd expect. Hopefully you found the resulting exploration enlightening.

The practice of showing curvature combs to diagnose problems with splines is really backwards. If we can show a curvature comb, we can also compute an appropriate spline to match the desired curvature.

So beziers as they commonly exist are quite inadequate. We can retrofit a better system to edit them without breaking the expectations of a smooth editing experience, or introducing a new class of curves that behaves very differently.

*The code for the diagrams and implementation can be found on [GitLab](https://gitlab.com/unconed/bezbox/-/blob/master/src/graph/bez.ts?ref_type=heads#L61).*
