items.articleBody:
arXiv:2611.18642v1 Announce Type: new
Abstract: Agents that work beyond a single context window, or in teams, hand their work to a successor as a short written summary. Evaluation has focused on whether an agent can solve a task, and relatively little is known about how much of what an agent has learned survives being written down. We study this in 56 interactive worlds with hidden rules, where an agent that is told nothing fails and an agent given a 300-character statement of the rules succeeds. We compare one agent that plays eight lives and keeps its whole history with a chain of eight agents that each play one life and inherit a 300-character note. All six models we test learn less in the chain: after eight generations it stands where the single agent stood after about four lives. Controlled variants of the chain decompose this handoff loss into three components: none from changing the agent, a smaller loss from compressing to 300 characters, and a larger loss from compressing repeatedly. When each note is written from the full record of earlier lives instead of from the previous note, the same 300 characters recover 70% to 82% of the loss. The loss is robust across model sizes and is not alleviated by instructing the writer to record evidence, to revise the inherited note, or to keep a structured ledger. In simpler terms, an agent cannot hand over what it has not yet understood: a note holds what its writer has worked out, and a rule that takes several lives to see is lost with the lives that were not passed on.

items.articleBody:
It is an anti-government ideology that began in the US and has spread across the world – wasting public resources and ruining lives. But why have the wild ideas of this movement become so appealing?

In the early morning of 20 June 2023, 13 police officers raided a five-bed barn conversion in rural Hampshire. The occupant, a 57-year-old man named Iain Clifford Stamp, was rudely awoken. The police informed him that they were executing a warrant on behalf of the Financial Conduct Authority, the body that regulates financial services in the UK. FCA raids are rare. They are only permitted when the regulator can persuade a judge that there are reasonable grounds for believing the person or firm that they are investigating will not cooperate. In this case, it seems, there was good reason to believe that Iain Clifford Stamp might cause trouble.

Stamp’s frosty relationship with financial authorities dated back to 2008, when his first company, a financial product provider called Integrity, imploded and was left facing claims from clients of up to an estimated £80m. Back then, Integrity had been publicly censured by the Financial Services Authority for not fairly communicating to customers the risks in the products it was selling. This time was more serious. Stamp was arrested for suspected breaches of the Financial Services and Markets Act: the FCA believed it had evidence he was offering financial services, such as debt and investment advice, without a licence. The day he was arrested, police also raided an industrial estate in Chessington, south-west London, where Stamp’s company had its offices, and seized dozens of computers and files.

items.articleBody:
When deploying deep learning models in high-stakes scenarios, researchers would like to understand how they work. Today, this requires unraveling an enormously complex network of internal processing nodes to understand what the model knows and how it will likely behave in practice.

Jacob Andreas would rather have the models explain themselves.

The newly tenured associate professor develops techniques that enable artificial intelligence models to communicate accurately about what they learned from their training data, in language humans can understand.

“Rather than needing to use all these external tools to try and understand what is going on under the hood, maybe we can train models to talk about themselves in a way that is accurate,” says Andreas, an associate professor in the Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science (EECS) and a member of the Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (CSAIL).

Ultimately, he and his group want to help people design more accurate and robust deep-learning models that are better suited for their intended application.

“We used to debug systems just by looking at their parameters and figuring out whether they make sense or not. Now, we need ‘mind-reading tools’ that can take this really complicated neural computation and translate it for us because it is just not in a language that we, as humans, know how to speak,” he says.

**A love of language**

Andreas’ fascination with language blossomed at a young age. As a child growing up in the San Francisco Bay Area, he was a voracious reader of any book he could get his hands on.

One such book, passed along to him by a family friend, contained a pivotal scene where the main character hacked into a computer system to save the day.

That piqued his interest in computers. A few years later, his father brought home a simple BASIC Engine that Andreas could run on their home computer, and he started immersing himself in the world of computer programming.

Andreas chose to major in computer science as an undergraduate at Columbia University but wasn’t sure if he wanted to pursue a career as a researcher, as a software engineer, or at a startup.

His friends signed up for research projects in faculty labs, so Andreas figured he would try that, too.

“I just blast emailed everyone in the computer science department who was working on anything vaguely AI-related, and the natural language processing faculty got back to me first. That is how I wound up in the field where I am now,” he says.

Working in the lab of Michael Collins, the Vikram S. Pandit Professor of Computer Science at Columbia University, Andreas completed an undergraduate thesis project on machine translation. His project involved adapting existing statistical techniques for representing the meaning of language into more powerful AI systems that could translate passages of text.

“I always felt like these deeper questions about how thought works or how to model the world were closer to the surface in language processing problems than in the other tasks that AI people were working on at the time,” he recalls.

**A seismic shift**

He wanted to keep exploring deep questions, so Andreas enrolled in graduate school at the University of California at Berkeley to pursue a career as an academic researcher.

Before starting his PhD studies, he spent a year earning a master’s degree at Cambridge University in England. In that historic environment, he was inspired to contemplate the nature of language learning as he worked on computational translation problems.

Those studies fueled his research when he joined the lab of Berkeley professor of computer science Dan Klein.

Andreas began his studies at the time when neural networks were starting to take off. The field of natural language processing was making a seismic shift from statistical methods to this new world of deep learning.

Statistical methods utilize transparent, mathematical formulas to analyze text, while deep learning techniques use opaque algorithms to automatically learn complex meanings from massive amounts of text data.

“It was fun to be there as we made this transition to the modern toolkit, and learning and inventing all of that stuff when it was still new,” Andreas says.

He began collaborating with scientists in computer vision labs to tackle increasingly complex questions about language learning. Together, they designed AI systems that excelled at generating natural language by teaching those systems to “see” and understand the world around them.

“This was all super-exciting because there really hadn’t been a common set of tools for working with both language and vision data. Then, all of a sudden, neural networks gave us this common language,” he recalls.

He completed a thesis project on the use of neural module networks, which are small fragments of neural networks that perform specific tasks, like localizing objects or logical reasoning, in a larger AI system. But it was the more speculative projects he tackled alongside his thesis, like interpretability and creating natural language descriptions of an AI model’s internal states, that would drive the focus of his group at MIT.

**Faculty focus**

After spending a year at the startup Semantic Machines (which spun out of his lab at Berkeley), Andreas joined the MIT faculty in 2019.

“It felt like this was a fantastic opportunity to be in the homeland of AI research and collaborate with all these amazing, established people, but also do something new and figure out what the modern era in machine learning was going to look like,” he says.

His group focuses on two main areas. First, they are studying the science of large language models to understand the algorithms these models deploy as they learn and process information.

The tools they develop help scientists and researchers better predict how a trained model will behave in the real world. For instance, one family of techniques they developed trains large language models to explain what is going on inside other neural networks using language a human could understand.

These techniques can assign a natural language description to every information-processing node in a massive neural network. For example, one such description might represent an individual node that identifies [“patches of grass near animals” in input images](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2201.11114).

“That work serves as a jumping off point for a bunch of higher-level questions we ask about how these models represent meaning,” he says.

On the other side, his team designs new algorithms for training machine-learning models, and for predicting how specific datasets or examples will affect different aspects of model behavior.

“We don’t have a good scientific theory of what is going to happen when you train a model on a particular dataset. This is a big challenge for the field right now,” he says.

**A changing environment**

The speed of AI advancement presents one of the biggest challenges his lab faces. The field seems to completely change every three to five years, Andreas says, forcing him to stay nimble and ready to learn something new.

That same dilemma carries over into the courses 6.461 and 6.861 (undergraduate and graduate Natural Language Processing), which Andreas co-teaches. He and his fellow instructors must redesign the course each year to keep up with the newest developments.

It’s also challenging to teach the technical pieces of machine learning in an era where every assignment could be completed by a large language model rather than a human pupil.

“I try to impress upon the students that having a really deep foundation in how all this technology works under the hood is the only way they are going to understand it, and will differentiate them in a world where everyone has access to a coding agent,” he says.

With so much change, it is difficult to predict where the field is headed next, Andreas says. He foresees that his group’s work on interpretability will become even more important for making advanced systems like AI agents safe enough to deploy in high-stakes situations.

This will be especially true as researchers design deep-learning models that can aid in scientific discovery. These models will be trained on troves of raw data from research labs that may not be well-understood by scientists yet.

“Figuring out how to enable these models to verbalize all of this hidden knowledge they have about things people have never written about explicitly will be a huge challenge and opportunity for people who work in machine learning,” he says.

In addition to tackling challenges in the lab, Andreas enjoys pushing himself as a hiker and backpacker. He has loved spending time in the outdoors since his childhood in California and goes on at least one or two backpacking trips each summer.

He and a colleague in the Department of Mathematics are working their way across all the 4,000-foot peaks in the White Mountains of New Hampshire, making slow but steady progress.

And now that he has earned tenure, Andreas is looking forward to getting back into an old hobby — singing in a chamber choir. He’s always enjoyed music and became enamored with chapel choirs and bell ringing during his time at Cambridge University.

items.title: Fact Check: FAKE Video From 'SUETA' Shows Damage To Kerch Strait Bridge After Ukrainian Drone Attack -- Video Is AI-Generated
items.subtitle: Does a real video from "Sueta" show damage to the Kerch Strait Bridge after a Ukrainian drone attack on Nov.
items.feedText: 16, 2026? No, that's not true: The video was created using Google AI and contains a SynthID watermark. A second AI detection tool rated the video as "likely to be AI-Generated." items.articleBody:
Does a real video from "Sueta" show damage to the Kerch Strait Bridge after a Ukrainian drone attack on Nov. 16, 2026? No, that's not true: The video was created using Google AI and contains a SynthID watermark. A second AI detection tool rated the video as "likely to be AI-Generated." Lead Stories found no matching reports from established news outlets showing the video or images depicting the same damage, however more recent media reports now appear to show the complete collapse of the road bridge after a follow-up attack.

The claim appeared in [a video](https://www.instagram.com/reels/Dfz1TqAt3W2/) (archived [↗ web.archive.org](https://web.archive.org/web/20261117004404/https://www.instagram.com/reels/Dfz1TqAt3W2/) ) by the @suetanews account on Instagram on Nov. 16, 2026. Translated from Ukrainian, it read:

> After the drone attack, the traffic on the Crimean Bridge was completely blocked.
> Significant damage to the road surface in at least two places and the deformation of the arch of the shipping passage.
> The arch is an important element of the bridge's construction, so its damage raises concerns about the stability of the structure.
> [#КримськийМіст](https://www.instagram.com/explore/tags/%D0%BA%D1%80%D0%B8%D0%BC%D1%81%D1%8C%D0%BA%D0%B8%D0%B9%D0%BC%D1%96%D1%81%D1%82/) [#Крим](https://www.instagram.com/explore/tags/%D0%BA%D1%80%D0%B8%D0%BC/) [#АтакаДронів](https://www.instagram.com/explore/tags/%D0%B0%D1%82%D0%B0%D0%BA%D0%B0%D0%B4%D1%80%D0%BE%D0%BD%D1%96%D0%B2/) [#Україна](https://www.instagram.com/explore/tags/%D1%83%D0%BA%D1%80%D0%B0%D1%97%D0%BD%D0%B0/) [#Новини](https://www.instagram.com/explore/tags/%D0%BD%D0%BE%D0%B2%D0%B8%D0%BD%D0%B8/)

This is what a screenshot of the video in the post looked like at the time of writing:

*(Image source: post by @suetanews on Instagram.)*

The post is embedded below:

> [View this post on Instagram](https://www.instagram.com/reel/Dfz1TqAt3W2/?utm_source=ig_embed&utm_campaign=loading)
> [A post shared by SUETA (@suetanews)](https://www.instagram.com/reel/Dfz1TqAt3W2/?utm_source=ig_embed&utm_campaign=loading)

#### Current situation

The above footage was published before a second wave of attacks hit the bridge during the night between November 16 and November 17, 2026. Media reports after that attack, for example in T[he Guardian](https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/17/ukraine-strikes-critical-damage-russia-kerch-bridge-crimea) (archived [↗ web.archive.org](https://web.archive.org/web/20261117075708/https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/17/ukraine-strikes-critical-damage-russia-kerch-bridge-crimea) ) appear to now show the complete collapse of the arches and the deck of the road bridge.

#### Video analysis

Lead Stories ran the video through the [Hive Moderation AI-Generated Content Detection tool](https://hivemoderation.com/ai-generated-content-detection) (archived [↗ web.archive.org](https://web.archive.org/web/20261116232134/https://hivemoderation.com/ai-generated-content-detection) ), which concluded that it was 99.8% "likely to be [an] AI-generated video":

*(Image source: Hive Moderation.)*

Lead Stories also ran the video through [SynthID Detector](https://synthid.com/) (archived [↗ web.archive.org](https://web.archive.org/web/20261116232819/https://synthid.com/video-detection) ). The tool detected [SynthID](https://deepmind.google/models/synthid/) (archived [↗ web.archive.org](https://web.archive.org/web/20261027152928/https://deepmind.google/models/synthid/) ), indicating the video was made or edited using [Google AI](https://gemini.google.com/app/093a5d6e6564b103?utm_source=deepmind.google&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=gdm&utm_content=) (archived [↗ web.archive.org](https://web.archive.org/web/20261116233056/https://gemini.google.com/app/093a5d6e6564b103?utm_source=deepmind.google&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=gdm&utm_content=) ):

*(Image source: SynthID Detector.)*

Lead Stories compared an [Associated Press photo](https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/16/ukraine-drone-kerch-bridge-russia-occupied-crimea) (archived [↗ web.archive.org](https://web.archive.org/web/20261117020030/https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/16/ukraine-drone-kerch-bridge-russia-occupied-crimea) ) of the bridge with the AI-generated version. Not only does the railroad bridge on the right have a different structure (circled in red) from the one shown in the fabricated image, but the AI-generated bridge is not a railroad bridge at all. Instead, it appears to be designed to carry vehicular traffic:

*(Image sources: Associated Press and a post by @suetanews on Instagram.)*

Additionally, scenes in the short AI-generated video are inconsistent with one another. The damage shown in the top image differs from what appears in the image below, as the highlighted screenshots demonstrate:

(Image source: post by @suetanews on Instagram.)

#### News searches

Lead Stories searched [Google News](https://news.google.com/search?q=%22Kerch%2C%22%20%22bridge%2C%22%20%22drone%2C%22%20and%20%22Sueta.%22&hl=en-US&gl=US&ceid=US%3Aen) (archived [↗ web.archive.org](https://web.archive.org/web/20261117000730/https://news.google.com/search?q=%22Kerch%2C%22%20%22bridge%2C%22%20%22drone%2C%22%20and%20%22Sueta.%22&hl=en-US&gl=US&ceid=US%3Aen) ) and [Yahoo News](https://news.search.yahoo.com/search;_ylt=A2RRUdbwmvtqjQIAG3nQtDMD;_-?fr=uh3_news_web&.tsrc=uh3_news_web&fr2=sb-top&p=%22Kerch%2C%22+%22bridge%2C%22+%22drone%2C%22+and+%22Sueta.%22) (archived [↗ web.archive.org](https://web.archive.org/web/20261117000906/https://news.search.yahoo.com/search;_ylt=A2RRUdbwmvtqjQIAG3nQtDMD;_-?fr=uh3_news_web&.tsrc=uh3_news_web&fr2=sb-top&p=%22Kerch%2C%22+%22bridge%2C%22+%22drone%2C%22+and+%22Sueta.%22) ) and found no matching reports about the claim from established news outlets using the search terms: "Kerch," "bridge," "drone," and "Sueta."

The Kerch Strait Bridge, also known as the Crimean Bridge, is a 12-mile crossing connecting Russia to Crimea, a Ukrainian peninsula Russia annexed in 2014 in a move not recognized by most of the international community. The bridge is an important route for moving military and civilian supplies and has been targeted in previous Ukrainian attacks. On Nov. 16, 2026, Ukrainian drones struck the bridge overnight. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov described the damage as "insignificant," and bridge authorities said vehicle traffic resumed later that day, the [Associated Press reported](https://apnews.com/article/russia-ukraine-war-drone-attacks-oil-refineries-242cb3fd47fc79293cf264c321b93800) (archived [↗ web.archive.org](https://web.archive.org/web/20261116235119/https://apnews.com/article/russia-ukraine-war-drone-attacks-oil-refineries-242cb3fd47fc79293cf264c321b93800) ).

#### Read more

At the time this was written, videos posted by Sueta News had previously been flagged as AI-generated by other fact-checking organizations, including [Myth Detector](https://mythdetector.com/en/ai-generated-video-of-a-ukrainian-respondent/), [Provereno Media](https://provereno.media/blog/2026/02/20/pravdivo-li-video-na-kotorom-ukrainec-po-russki-govorit-chto-nastoyashie-ukraincy-dolzhny-govorit-tolko-po-ukrainski3/), [Re:Baltica's Re:Check](https://ru.rebaltica.lv/archives/7301), and [15min.lt](https://www.15min.lt/naujiena/aktualu/pasaulis/vartoti-ukrainieciu-kalba-rusiskai-ragina-ne-nutukes-deputatas-o-dirbtinis-intelektas-57-2630790).

items.articleBody:
From an early mishmash of chaotic lines and misspelled words to the loose lilt of a signature scribbled for decades, “Paper Trail” is a moving animation that shows the evolution of a young mind and what we can glean from a life through notes and lists. The latest project by [Don Hertzfeldt](https://www.bitterfilms.com/), the short film follows the protagonist Steven Richardson as he makes his first marks, learns to write his name, doodles, and later completes the perfunctory math problems of elementary school. We witness his cursive lessons and adolescent love letters to a girl named Lindsey before observing grocery lists and remnants of his professional life.

Based in Austin, Texas, Hertzfeldt is known for his poetic animations that harness the indelible intimacy of hand-drawn scenes. “Paper Trail” has been on the festival circuit where it’s garnered top honors at Annecy, Sundance, SXSW, and many others. The film is available for streaming for a limited-timed on [Vimeo](https://vimeo.com/donhertzfeldt), along with more of Hertzfeldt’s work.

items.articleBody:
I’m seeing some people object to these settings as being scarier “scare sheets”, and while I disagree, I think that’s a reasonable debate. But I think it’s indisputable that Apple put a lot of thought into these new settings and permissions. Again, you might disagree with their intentions and assumptions here, but given their stated intentions and assumptions — to wit: that many Mac users were granting Full Disk Access permissions to too many apps without realizing just how much access that entails — I think this is a very considered design. The previous settings for these permissions seem slapdash in comparison — like a lot of the “new” Mac System Settings panels.

Even this new support document seems very considered. A lot of times Apple doesn’t have support documents ready to go while the software is still in beta — here they have a good support document for the first beta with the new stuff.

*See Also:* * This [Apple Developer News article](https://developer.apple.com/news/?id=oqng0zjk), which states:

> Developers should be prepared to adjust how they onboard users
> and make sure their apps can gracefully handle having access to
> only a limited set of folders or apps when utilizing these APIs.
> Users will see these updates when approving new app permission
> requests. All app permissions previously granted by users will
> remain in effect.

So if you’ve already OK’d an app in MacOS 27.2 or earlier, you shouldn’t be prompted again after upgrading to 27.3.

items.articleBody:
What if The Orb’s Adventures Beyond the Ultraworld were beamed 35 years forward, accumulating the detritus of breakbeat, IDM and other genres along the way?  It might sound a lot like xicada‘s debut album. The impression is solidified by the journal entries that run through the ten-minute title track, xicada’s old self channeled through her present self, an interastral communication.

The laser beam sounds that launch the track mark it as sci-fi, while the layered voices suggest a heavenly chorus.  One can dance to the track, but one might also contemplate.  After displaying a futuristic sheen, the track delves into philosophy, phrase by phrase. Who was this younger self?  Was she transferred intact across the years, or has she been altered?  Looped flute suggests ritual, while rapid drum patterns imitate the flow of time.  Connecting universe and mind, the piece makes a metaphor of the human quest for meaning.  “Is there another body out there suspended in this darkness?”  The thought alone is a comfort.

Ilyse Krivel is not alone here.  Eyin Sof guest stars on “Time Bent,” the first single and opening track.  The guest’s name references the Kabbalistic concept of infinity.  The combination of spoken word, ethereal wordless voices and rapid beats creates its own form of trance.  In the hard-hitting “Original Face,” Y.F. Tamashi contributes to a maelstrom of sonic activity recalling the chaos before creation.  At 2:58, we expect it to be the second single, the primal scream at the end serving as a cry into – or out of – the abyss.  And the pairing of “Remember” and “Reflection” offers its own wisdom, the former beginning with clock-like timbres before tumbling forward, transferring its energy mid-track to a new set of patterns and observations, “time spiraling back.”  The percussive ending is particularly powerful.

The birds at the beginning of “Mirror Like Vision” connect to the very act of creation, playful synth eventually dissolving into echoes of voice and drone, with the suggestion of “spiritual death.”  Past, present and future are sucked into a black hole of sound.  The set ends in a whisper, an inversion of the creation story in which voice brings the world into existence.  What manner of creature might step forth after the walls of self collapse?  (Richard Allen)

items.title: Q&A: Why building math muscles remains important in the AI era

items.articleBody:
John Urschel PhD ’21, the Class of 1956 Career Development Assistant Professor in the MIT Department of Mathematics, is no stranger to building muscle: Before earning his PhD at MIT, Urschel strengthened his offensive muscles as a lineman for the Baltimore Ravens. He remains committed to helping his students exercise, but now his focus is on critical thinking skills. In the classroom, Urschel shares with his students his lifelong love for solving puzzles, while honing their abilities to be strong qualitive thinkers — skills he argues will be essential in an artificial intelligence-enabled world.

*Urschel recently published two preprints on arXiv, one on the* [growth factor of random matrices](https://math.mit.edu/~urschel/preprints/random_growth.pdf) *, the other on worst-case behavior in* [Gaussian elimination](https://math.mit.edu/~urschel/preprints/entrygrowth.pdf), in which he used a combination of human insight and AI tools to solve problems that had stumped mathematicians for decades. That experience provided Urschel with new insights into the future of mathematics and higher education, and the enduring importance of the in-person, residential education offered on college campuses, where students can experience the importance of struggle, problem solving, and human connection. Urschel recently chatted with MIT News *about education, AI, and mathematics; excerpts from the conversation follow.*

**Q**: What is it about studying math that you hope to share with your students?

**A**: When I was very little, I loved solving puzzles, whether that’s Sudoku puzzles or Martin Gardner math puzzles or crossword puzzles. I think there’s something really enjoyable about being faced with some problem that you don’t quite understand, trying to get your bearings, trying to make your way through it, and finally gleaning some sort of understanding from it. That’s a process that I’ve enjoyed for as long as I can remember, and that’s the thing that I’ve really enjoyed most about math.

When it comes to teaching, first, I want to help our students train themselves and hone their ability to solve problems and their ability to be strong quantitative thinkers.

The second part, which is more specific to whichever course I’m teaching, is to help them assimilate the big ideas or tools or techniques or themes that help them become better problem solvers in that specific discipline. If they’re taking a course on a specific subject, the idea is for me to try to convey important fundamentals so that they can use that learned expertise to become better problem solvers out in the world.

**Q**: You recently used AI to assist in solving two proofs. Can you talk a bit about the experience?

**A**: These are the first two papers where I’ve ever touched the machine, and it does feel different. It’s not unlike having a collaborator, but it’s a collaborator who has access to unlimited resources, seemingly, and does certain things much, much faster than I ever could.

In the same way that computers can do calculations much faster than any of us can, I think at this point it’s very clear that artificial intelligence systems can do certain types of mathematics much, much more efficiently than any of us can.

**Q**: What was it like using AI to solve math problems? Was it just as rewarding?

**A**: For me, personally, I would say that the feeling that I talked about of problem solving, of thinking your way through a problem, I find that that’s most joyful for me when I do that by myself, without AI.

One thing that I think is really important is to have an independent sense of problem-solving ability, a sense of curiosity — this idea of building those mathematics muscles, which I think are important, even in the era of AI.

Especially when you are talking with a machine, asking the machine for things, I think it’s very important to elevate the idea of understanding. If you’re talking to a machine, let’s say, and it gives you a proof of some mathematical fact, I think the true value in that proof comes from a human understanding and assimilating the way in which the machine combines certain mathematical ideas, and then internalizing that and communicating that knowledge to others.

Understanding is the big thing that I stress to my students who use AI systems. And then for the students who do not use AI systems, I focus on building their problem-solving abilities, which is what we’ve done for centuries in mathematics.

I think in the age of modern AI machines, as long as there is a role for humans to think and try to solve problems, which I believe there is, then building these skills remains important.

**Q**: The recent [report from MIT’s Ad Hoc Committee on AI Use in Teaching, Learning and Research Training](https://aiandeducation.mit.edu/) stressed the importance of experiencing the necessary and productive struggle of learning, along with the collaborative aspect of learning. I’m curious what you think about the role of AI in math education going forward.

**A**: On one hand, the development of AI technologies should be viewed as a giant win for education, a giant win for leveling playing fields when you have technology that’s easily accessible, that gives you access to vast amounts of knowledge.

Neither of my parents are professors; I remember when I was a kid, I didn’t know what a mathematician was until I got to college. And the way I learned about advanced mathematical concepts in high school, but also when I got to college, was with a laptop, and with Google. I was able to Google some topic I want to learn about, and it was amazing that I could find papers written by some of the world’s leading experts, just freely available online at my fingertips to learn from. That was really important for me and so helpful for my education.

But I think we’re at a point where modern technology is a bit of a double-edged sword. Because on one hand, with AI systems you can learn something faster than ever, and the resources I had when I was a kid would seem like small potatoes compared to the sorts of things you can do to help yourself learn nowadays.

But the issue is that this also can take away your ability to think and learn for yourself. I think it’s hard if you’re a high school student or you’re a college student. You have a lot going on, you’re tired, and thanks to AI, you can just finish your homework with the push of a button. You can write your 10-page essay with the push of a button. Also, you can get the false impression that you more or less understand what’s going on when you really don’t. I think that’s one of the big dangers when you don’t try to learn things for yourself.

People don’t like the word “struggle.” But when you don’t struggle with a certain material on your own, I think you can get the impression of learning without actually learning. Connecting with the material and really pushing yourself, that’s quite an important skill.

Certainly, there’s work to do from the faculty and instructor side: to make sure that our recitations are maximally useful; to make sure that our office hours are serving students in the best way possible; to encourage the students and try to remind them that they have some responsibility for their education, and that the best way is to come and show up and interact with the material. But we should also recognize our responsibility to the students to deliver them the best learning experience possible and to give them an educational system that challenges them but also is a quality product they want to come and take part in.

**Q**: Why would you still encourage students to pursue studies in mathematics given the advances AI technologies have made? Do you still see the future of mathematics as exciting?

**A**: Yes, for a multitude of reasons. The act of learning how to think is going to be more important than ever. This idea of being an expert, of knowing all these things, which are easily available and at your fingertips, is perhaps a little less important when you have a machine that has all these resources. I think something that may become even more important is the ability to think for yourself. Because with the existence of these machines, I think a natural fear is that that skill set is going to lessen in the general population as generations move on and on, and so I think that ability will be at a premium. I think training in mathematics and quantitative sciences more generally is quite important for that.

The second thing is community. I think learning, not by yourself, but with a group of peers, greatly improves the overall experience. It’s an integral part of the experience. I would say those two things are the reason why I think it’s still important to study math, to study quantitative sciences, and also why it’s still important to come and go to class.

The world is changing fairly rapidly. I think we as an institution have a responsibility to prepare students for that. We’re having lots of conversations about this right now because the ability to think, reason, and solve problems are core skills that our students, I think, will need now more than ever. I also think we need to make sure that we’re preparing our students for the world that they’re about to enter into. The exact way that we teach our students, or prepare our students for the world, absolutely cannot look like what it was 10 years ago. Because this world simply looks quite different.

items.articleBody: This study evaluates the performance of a fully integrated in-ear EEG device by comparing it with simultaneous clinical-grade scalp EEG recordings in 29 healthy adults. The analysis focused on two electrophysiological markers: resting-state alpha activity (8–12 Hz) and auditory steady-state responses (ASSRs). ASSRs were tested using both single-frequency stimulation (40 Hz and 80 Hz) and more complex multi-frequency chirp configurations. A significant alpha peak was detected in the in-ear recordings of 15 of 29 participants (52%), compared with 83–100% for the scalp derivations. In-ear alpha peak power and signal-to-noise ratio were significantly correlated with scalp EEG at all six scalp derivations, indicating that the device preserves inter-individual differences in alpha strength despite reduced signal amplitude. The in-ear device recovered the group-level alpha frequency, but agreement with scalp EEG for individual alpha frequency (IAF) was limited. ASSR performance depended strongly on the stimulation paradigm. In-ear ASSR detection rates were lower than scalp rates at both modulation frequencies; at the two highest intensities, they reached 39–44% of the rate of the ipsilateral temporal scalp derivations at 40 Hz and 74–75% at 80 Hz. More complex multi-frequency stimulation resulted in a marked reduction in detection performance in both recording modalities. Overall, in a short controlled laboratory session, the fully integrated in-ear EEG system captured resting-state alpha activity and detected auditory steady-state responses under simple stimulation conditions in a subset of participants.

items.articleBody: Green tea catechins protect tea plants from biotic stressors. Among herbivorous mites, the generalist Tetranychus urticae has not been reported as a tea pest. In contrast, some populations of Tetranychus kanzawai thrive on tea plants. Here, we investigated the mechanism of this adaptation. Green tea catechins were repellent and toxic to T. urticae and tea non-adapted T. kanzawai and had an antifeedant effect on the latter. We identified an intradiol ring-cleavage dioxygenase DOG15, a gene horizontally transferred from fungi, as required for the adaptation of T. kanzawai to tea plants. Tea feeding strongly induces DOG15 expression in tea-adapted T. kanzawai, with mRNA and protein levels up to 31.6 and 12.1 times higher than in tea-fed T. urticae. We also identified two amino acid substitutions in DOG15 between the two Tetranychus species that increased the catechin-cleaving activity of the T. kanzawai enzyme. These substitutions predispose T. kanzawai but not T. urticae for the adaptation to tea plants. Inducible expression of modified DOG15 then enables T. kanzawai to efficiently detoxify green tea catechins. Our findings reveal how a horizontally transferred gene can be co-opted through structural and regulatory changes to overcome plant chemical defenses.

items.subtitle: Within the sprawling grounds of Mantua's Ducal Palace lies Piazza Pallone (now officially Piazza Lega Lombarda), a quiet, tree-lined square, few to…

items.articleBody:
Within the sprawling grounds of Mantua's Ducal Palace lies Piazza Pallone (now officially Piazza Lega Lombarda), a quiet, tree-lined square, few tourists notice the simple stone plaque mounted on the perimeter wall enclosing the space.

The plaque commemorates one of the darkest episodes of Mantuan Renaissance history: the beheading of Agnese Visconti on February 7, 1391.

Agnese, daughter of the Lord of Milan, Bernabò Visconti, was married at just fourteen years old to Francesco I Gonzaga, Lord of Mantua. Twelve years later, her husband accused her of adultery with the knight Antonio da Scandiano (also known as Vincenzo da Scalona). Her alleged lover was hanged in the square, while Agnese was beheaded at the age of 28 in the very same spot.

Historians generally agree that the accusation was a political setup orchestrated by Francesco I Gonzaga to sever ties with the Visconti family and forge a new alliance with the Republic of Venice. The bodies of both executed lovers were buried without ceremony in unconsecrated ground within the square.

Over the centuries, the injustice suffered by Agnese seemed to permeate the stones of the square, giving rise to one of Lombardy's most famous ghost stories.

It is said that on cold winter nights—particularly around the anniversary of her death in February—when dense fog from the Mincio River rolls over the palace courtyards, the shadowy figure of Agnese reappears near the plaque.

Local lore claims her headless spirit wanders desperately around the perimeter of the square searching for her severed head or clutching a stained shroud to her chest. Over the years, passersby have reported hearing heavy footsteps on the ground, the rustle of period garments, and a quiet weeping that cuts off abruptly right in front of the stone tablet.

Funnyly the XIX century plaque lists an incorrect age for the noblewoman at the time of her execution—a historical error preserved on the marble during restorations.

items.articleBody: BackgroundParkinson’s disease (PD) is recognized as a multisystem disorder involving central neuroinflammation and peripheral immune dysregulation. Reported alterations in circulating lymphocyte subsets remain inconsistent, owing to small study sizes, heterogeneous marker definitions, and variable reporting of absolute counts versus percentages.ObjectiveTo evaluate peripheral lymphocyte subset alterations in PD versus controls, analyzing absolute-count and percentage outcomes separately.MethodsEligible case–control and observational studies reporting peripheral blood lymphocyte data were included. Standardized mean differences (Hedges’ g) for CD3+, CD4+, CD8+, B-cell, CD56+, and NK-cell outcomes were pooled using random-effects meta-analyses. Absolute counts and percentages were analyzed separately, never pooled, and the between-scale difference tested formally. Heterogeneity (Cochran’s Q, I2, τ2), subgroup, meta-regression, funnel, leave-one-out, Baujat, and influence analyses were performed where feasible.ResultsEighteen studies (1,807 patients; 1,729 controls) were included. After a study-level audit correcting standard-error, interquartile-range, sample-size, and measurement-scale discrepancies, the strongest adaptive finding was a modest, significant CD4+ absolute-count reduction (k = 3; g = −0.40, 95% CI −0.71 to −0.09; p = 0.011; I2 = 39%). CD8+ absolute counts were also significantly reduced (k = 2; g = −0.40, −0.68 to −0.12; p = 0.005), whereas CD3+ absolute counts met inclusion rules in only one cohort (not pooled). The CD3+ percentage was modestly but significantly reduced (k = 11; g = −0.37; p = 0.025), whereas percentages showed no significant association for CD4+ (g = 0.07; p = 0.615), CD8+ (p = 0.439), or B cells (p = 0.203). NK-cell percentage was not significantly altered once repeated within-cohort gating and marker-definition differences were addressed (k = 4; g = 0.12, −0.30 to 0.55; p = 0.572); NK-cell absolute count was positive but non-significant (k = 2; g = 0.16; p = 0.148), and CD56+ was not poolable after excluding a biologically implausible gate. Several analyses were limited by small study number, heterogeneity, and variable marker definitions.ConclusionPD is associated with peripheral lymphocyte alterations, most notably modest, low-heterogeneity reductions in CD4+ and CD8+ absolute counts and a modest reduction in the CD3+ percentage; the NK-cell percentage increase reported in earlier studies was not reproduced once within-cohort dependence and marker definitions were accounted for. These findings support peripheral immune remodeling and underscore distinguishing counts from percentages and accounting for correlated estimates. Larger, longitudinal studies using standardized flow-cytometry panels are needed to validate these subsets as biomarkers of PD immune dysregulation, severity, and progression.

items.articleBody: Narratives are a universal part of natural human experience. As experimental stimuli, narratives allow scientists to study complex mental processes with direct relevance to everyday experience. These analyses typically require manual labeling of key event features. Such characterization of narrative stimuli are extremely labor-intensive and prone to subjectivity. Automated tools could reduce these difficulties and enable scaling to longer, varied stimuli by exposing the exact quantities computed. We address this by introducing a metric that uses open-weight LLMs to compute contextual information gain. Our metric correlates with human ratings of event importance and causal centrality, critically distinguishing the latter from semantic centrality, thus overcoming limitations of existing automated tools. The metric similarly captures shared coactivation in the default mode network, a network implicated in narrative comprehension. Taken together, these results validate an automated, empirically-grounded tool that researchers can use to identify behaviorally- and neurally-relevant computational quantities in naturalistic stimuli.

items.articleBody:
“I have been trying so hard to capture the smell of rain for you,” an unseen narrator with a British accent explains in Abi Palmer Invents the Weather (2023), as cats slink across the screen. “But being as I am no god or scientist,” the voice continues, as human hands wring out a cloth soaking in a jar of dirty water, “I am forced to work backward.” Soon, dripping white fabric is seen hanging from twine inside a cardboard box, clumped like a cloud.

Abi Palmer: Abi Palmer Invents the Weather, 2023.

Courtesy Abi Palmer

This non-god, the artist Abi Palmer, is recreating the weather for her two indoor cats, mixing rainwater with moss and earth. All the while, she muses on how chronic illness keeps her inside, catlike, yet also binds her intricately to meteorological variation. Palmer alludes to the ways joint pain can flare when pressure drops or smoky skies are felt by some in the lungs or in the back of the throat.

As it happens, Palmer got her start making art in the form of wet white wads. As an “unsupervised child,” as she told me from her London apartment, she’d combine water and tissue into globby sculptures—“blob creatures”—then let them dry. Recently, making massive slug sculptures inspired by the way the species survives by ugliness, she realized how consistent her materials and methods remained. At the University of Cambridge, she studied literature, as is evident in her voice-overs and her two books: Sanitorium (2020) and Slugs: A Manifesto (2024). But soon, she found her hands hurt too much to type—though her muscles were “really bendy” and thus “good at squeezing things into quite unusual shapes,” as she had intuited at a very young age.

It’s not so common, Palmer told me, for cats to live indoors in the UK: Some pet people even consider keeping them inside cruel. But her housing and health situations didn’t allow for her animals to roam freely, never mind that domestic cats kill billions of birds each year. So her video was born of a bit of guilt, an attempt at “navigating the imperfection of the world, but also the magic and beauty of it.” She admitted: “It’s absurd.”

Abi Palmer: Abi Palmer Invents the Weather, 2023.

Photo Gina Folly

For Palmer, retaining a childlike sense of play is essential. She came to art with little technical training. As she started to receive institutional recognition and awards—she’s been in group shows at the National Museum of Contemporary Art (EMST) in Athens, Goldsmiths in London, EMAP in Seoul, and elsewhere, in addition to receiving the 2025 Heny Moore Foundation Award—she was struck by the haunting sense that she ought to be doing things more “properly.” But she realized: “The moment I start taking things too seriously, it’s a trap.” The external rewards come and go, often without much in the way of remuneration—so it helps to have fun with art. “I take play very seriously,” Palmer said.

Her work attests: In Abi Palmer Invents the Weather she not only elaborately simulates meteorological conditions but shows the video within playful cardboard constructions that she reconfigures for each exhibition: a feline paradise. In a world that tends to address disability and illness in the gravest of tones, Palmer infuses humor. For disabled people, humor can be a survival tactic, a way of putting others at ease with difference—often, not without some resentment. But it is also simply true that life is never one-note.

items.articleBody: Human learning is a dynamic cognitive process in which latent knowledge and competency states evolve through sequential interactions. However, existing generative AI learning-support systems often separate learner-state modeling, resource recommendation, knowledge-grounded generation, and pedagogical planning, limiting adaptive performance and interpretability. This study proposes ICG-AGLS, an interdisciplinary competency graph-guided adaptive generative AI learning support framework. It models learner states from historical interactions, projects them into a competency space, and constructs an interdisciplinary competency graph linking courses, concepts, resources, assignments, and competency dimensions. The framework integrates competency-gap-guided recommendation, graph-guided retrieval-augmented generation, adaptive reasoning routing, and multi-agent pedagogical coordination. Experiments on MOOCCubeX, OULAD, and EdNet demonstrate consistent improvements across learner-state modeling, recommendation, knowledge-grounded generation, and multi-agent planning. ICG-AGLS achieves an AUC of 0.871, Recall@10 of 0.812, ROUGE-L of 0.772, and a task completion rate of 0.839, outperforming representative task-specific baselines. These findings suggest that competency-structured latent-state modeling provides an interpretable computational bridge between evolving human learning states and adaptive generative AI at the behavioral and computational-representation levels, rather than establishing direct neural correspondence. The framework offers practical potential for personalized learning support in higher education.

items.feedText: Safari on visionOS 27.3 comes with an important update: a limited feature preview of the proposed [spatial CSS API](https://drafts.csswg.org/css-spatial-1/), with an initial focus on working with 3D objects through the element. While it’s a big conceptual jump, spatial CSS itself is made of a lot of small tweaks to existing syntax. However, the web is at its best when it allows the **composition and configuration**of content based on author intentions and user context.
items.articleBody:
Safari on visionOS 27.3 comes with an important update: a limited feature preview of the proposed [spatial CSS API](https://drafts.csswg.org/css-spatial-1/), with an initial focus on working with 3D objects through the <model> element. While it’s a big conceptual jump, spatial CSS itself is made of a lot of small tweaks to existing syntax. Read on for more details, but here’s a list of each of the features covered in the update:

- Collecting multiple elements inside a spatial: portal
- transform to move multiple models independently
- position-anchor to snap models together
- @environment-map syntax to reuse and manage different lighting,
- Enabling orbit over the portal scene with portal-action:orbit,
- Using requestVolumetricScene() to launch a connected volumetric scene.

To enable the features for yourself on Vision Pro, or to check it out in the visionOS Simulator, go to

**Settings**>**Apps**>**Safari**>**Advanced**>**Feature flags**>**CSS Portals**.

You can [experience the spatial CSS demo page here.](https://webkit.org/demos/webkids-puzzle-playground/index.html) You can also learn more about [installing additional simulators from Xcode here.](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/safari-developer-tools/installing-xcode-and-simulators)

## The big picture

The 3D <model> element, now available in Safari 27 on all platforms, allows you to present intrinsically 3d objects on their own, in their own space. However, the web is at its best when it allows the **composition and configuration**of content based on author intentions and user context. These context cues can include the device display capabilities, window size, and color theme. These requirements will remain**even as we include spatial content** — and ideally, authors should be able to use the same kinds of patterns to build for the spatial web.

And spatial *content* should not just be designed for spatial *devices*. The last few years have seen a dramatic rise in the number of websites showing 3D content – on phones, tablets and computers as well as headsets. Spatial web standards should support designing **for browsers wherever they run**.

### New web features, classical CSS

Even better, the numerical parameters can be animated and transitioned in the same way that any other value can be changed on the page.

visionOS 27.3 offers the first components of spatial CSS in a developer preview, and this article demonstrates how to use them through the case study of a simple set of children’s blocks.

## Feature breakdown

### spatial: portal

The feature that kicks this all off is the declaration that an element is acting as a *portal*, through the new spatial:portal syntax. Elements that can contain other elements – think <figure>, <div> – can act as a portal, and will then act as a space that all of the child elements nested inside it share. This preview focuses on model elements, but the specification is written so that this approach should work for all content.

### spatial transform:

Once the models are collected inside a shared space, you can then move, rotate, and scale them using their standard transform attribute. This takes the same DOMMatrix class that creates 2D and pseudo-3D transforms in other contexts, but can now act as a *true* 3D transform to objects inside the portal context.

A simple scene of shaped blocks and a board to slot them in.

< div class = "world" style = "spatial:portal;" >
< model id = "board" src = "board.usdz" > </ model >
< model id = "octagon" src = "octagon.usdz" > </ model >
< model id = "star" src = "star.usdz" > </ model >
</ div >
< style >
</ stye >

The code for presenting this scene and setting the blocks off to the sides.

The board and the block objects can be moved and rotated independently — an expanded settings panel shows different values. While a model’s animation timeline could manage single sequence of action, this adds the degrees of freedom required for more sophisticated interaction or configuration.

### position-anchor

Fitting 3D objects together can get complicated. We need a way to attach models to specific places on other models — think of putting together pieces of furniture. Model is a [void element](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Glossary/Void_element), which means it means we can’t nest models *inside* other model elements the same way that other DOM is nested. Instead, we’re borrowing from the CSS concept of position-anchor and adding a way to align and orient objects according to their anchors. position-context: anchor is the way to make it work.

#### See it in action

The scene presented earlier with the octagonal block slotted exactly into place.

< div class = "world" >
< model id = "board" src = "board.usdz" > </ model >
< model id = "octagon" src = "octagon.usdz" > </ model >
< model id = "star" src = "star.usdz" > </ model >
</ div >

< style >
</ style >

The code for using position-anchor to achieve the correct placement for the block.

The board used in the example consists of three separate objects inside the 3D program it was built within: The visible shape of the board itself, and two *reference* positions — often called “null objects” or “empties” in 3D editors. These correspond to the correct position for each of the shape blocks to slot into when they’re on the board. Here’s the scene and its contents inside Blender:

The default view of the block scene presented inside Blender. Note both the block objects and the target objects in-place on the board.

Rather than copy-pasting values from your 3D editor, or having to guess at the right transform, you can nominate specific anchor points — just like in the 2D equivalent of the feature — to place an object in the right location. These anchor points can be animated, too, making it easier to compose elements even when they’re moving around.

### @environment-map

An environment map is the lighting that is reflected off of an object — think of it as the room that an object appears within.

We introduced environment maps as an HTML attribute on the model element, because it was the only element that would be able to use it. Now that there is a broader range of elements that will be able to *share* environment maps. Taking inspiration from @keyframes for animation, we leverage @environment-map to facilitate this. This preview provides support for 360º HDR images and adds the clarifying syntax to indicate what they are and how to work with them.

#### See it in action

The scene showing a spooky-colored underlighting effect.

< div class = "world spooky" >
<!--... -->
</ div >
@ .world The code for setting up the spooky environment lighting.

### portal-action:orbit

One of the main things that users want to do with 3D content is to look around it by rotating the scene in-place. In 3D programs this is often called an ‘orbit’, and spatial CSS enables it with the new portal-action attribute. It may be useful to add more modes in the future like pan-x or pan-y. This mirrors the model element’s stagemode attribute on the HTML element, but by configuring it in CSS it becomes more flexible.

### requestVolumetricScene()

In addition to showing a spatial arrangement inside a portal, visionOS has the ability to show these scenes *outside* of the browser window in what we’re calling a Connected Volumetric Scene. Launch a request from a user action to remove the spatial content from its portal and present it in the user’s space:

launchSpaceButton. addEventListener ( "click", event = > {
const world = document. querySelector ( ".world" );
world. requestVolumetricScene ();
});

The code to launch the volumetric scene.

Users can place the volumetric scene anywhere in their space, and the live link between the web page and the volumetric scene will let you update the scene — add or remove objects, or move them based on your needs.

### Your feedback is essential

There is a long journey ahead, and a lot more to get to in the [proposed spatial CSS specification](https://drafts.csswg.org/css-spatial-1/). While this feature preview is limited to visionOS, we thought it was important to release along with the full specification as an indication of how to approach bringing spatial concepts to the web. Along with the general release of the <model> element on Safari 27, we hope this gives authors enough to think about the opportunities — and requirements — that lie ahead in the spatial web. That’s also why it’s so important for authors to **explore the feature preview** and tell us about their experience of using it. You can download the visionOS simulator with Xcode. If you don’t already have Xcode, you can [download Xcode from the Mac app store.](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/xcode/id497799835?mt=12)

To share your thoughts on the Spatial CSS feature preview, find us on Mastodon at [@jensimmons@front-end.social](https://front-end.social/@jensimmons), [@jondavis@mastodon.social](https://mastodon.social/@jondavis), or on X at [@zachernuk](https://x.com/zachernuk). Or send a reply on X to [@webkit](https://x.com/webkit). You can also follow [WebKit on LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/in/apple-webkit/). If you run into any issues, we welcome your feedback about WebKit at [bugs.webkit.org](https://bugs.webkit.org/). Filing issues really does make a difference. Thanks.
items.body:
# Introducing spatial css a developer preview

Safari on visionOS 27.3 comes with an important update: a limited feature preview of the proposed [spatial CSS API](https://drafts.csswg.org/css-spatial-1/), with an initial focus on working with 3D objects through the element. While it’s a big conceptual jump, spatial CSS itself is made of a lot of small tweaks to existing syntax. Read on for more details, but here’s a list of each of the features covered in the update: - Collecting multiple elements inside a spatial: portal - transform to move multiple models independently - position-anchor to snap models together - @environment-map syntax to reuse and manage different lighting, - Enabling orbit over the portal scene with portal-action:orbit, - Using requestVolumetricScene() to launch a connected volumetric scene. To enable the features for yourself on Vision Pro, or to check it out in the visionOS Simulator, go to **Settings**>**Apps**>**Safari**>**Advanced**>**Feature flags**>**CSS Portals**. You can [experience the spatial CSS demo page here.](https://webkit.org/demos/webkids-puzzle-playground/index.html) You can also learn more about [installing additional simulators from Xcode here.](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/safari-developer-tools/installing-xcode-and-simulators) ## The big picture The 3D element, now available in Safari 27 on all platforms, allows you to present intrinsically 3d objects on their own, in their own space. However, the web is at its best when it allows the **composition and configuration**of content based on author intentions and user context. These context cues can include the device display capabilities, window size, and color theme. These requirements will remain**even as we include spatial content** — and ideally, authors should be able to use the same kinds of patterns to build for the spatial web. And spatial *content* should not just be designed for spatial *devices*. The last few years have seen a dramatic rise in the number of websites showing 3D content – on phones, tablets and computers as well as headsets. Spatial web standards should support designing **for browsers wherever they run**. ### New web features, classical CSS By routing functionality for spatial content through declarative CSS, a page can use media queries targeting aspect ratio, color theme and reduced motion to adapt spatially as well. This adds much more flexibility to your website without having to do as much in your JavaScript, and removing the need to keep track of any complicated state. Even better, the numerical parameters can be animated and transitioned in the same way that any other value can be changed on the page. visionOS 27.3 offers the first components of spatial CSS in a developer preview, and this article demonstrates how to use them through the case study of a simple set of children’s blocks. ## Feature breakdown ### spatial: portal The feature that kicks this all off is the declaration that an element is acting as a *portal*, through the new spatial:portal syntax. Elements that can contain other elements – think , – can act as a portal, and will then act as a space that all of the child elements nested inside it share. This preview focuses on model elements, but the specification is written so that this approach should work for all content. ### spatial transform: Once the models are collected inside a shared space, you can then move, rotate, and scale them using their standard transform attribute. This takes the same DOMMatrix class that creates 2D and pseudo-3D transforms in other contexts, but can now act as a *true* 3D transform to objects inside the portal context. A simple scene of shaped blocks and a board to slot them in. The code for presenting this scene and setting the blocks off to the sides. The board and the block objects can be moved and rotated independently — an expanded settings panel shows different values. While a model’s animation timeline could manage single sequence of action, this adds the degrees of freedom required for more sophisticated interaction or configuration. ### position-anchor Fitting 3D objects together can get complicated. We need a way to attach models to specific places on other models — think of putting together pieces of furniture. Model is a [void element](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Glossary/Void_element), which means it means we can’t nest models *inside* other model elements the same way that other DOM is nested. Instead, we’re borrowing from the CSS concept of position-anchor and adding a way to align and orient objects according to their anchors. position-context: anchor is the way to make it work. #### See it in action The scene presented earlier with the octagonal block slotted exactly into place. The code for using position-anchor to achieve the correct placement for the block. The board used in the example consists of three separate objects inside the 3D program it was built within: The visible shape of the board itself, and two *reference* positions — often called “null objects” or “empties” in 3D editors. These correspond to the correct position for each of the shape blocks to slot into when they’re on the board. Here’s the scene and its contents inside Blender: The default view of the block scene presented inside Blender. Note both the block objects and the target objects in-place on the board. Rather than copy-pasting values from your 3D editor, or having to guess at the right transform, you can nominate specific anchor points — just like in the 2D equivalent of the feature — to place an object in the right location. These anchor points can be animated, too, making it easier to compose elements even when they’re moving around. ### @environment-map An environment map is the lighting that is reflected off of an object — think of it as the room that an object appears within. We introduced environment maps as an HTML attribute on the model element, because it was the only element that would be able to use it. Now that there is a broader range of elements that will be able to *share* environment maps. Taking inspiration from @keyframes for animation, we leverage @environment-map to facilitate this. This preview provides support for 360º HDR images and adds the clarifying syntax to indicate what they are and how to work with them. #### See it in action The scene showing a spooky-colored underlighting effect. @ .world The code for setting up the spooky environment lighting. ### portal-action:orbit One of the main things that users want to do with 3D content is to look around it by rotating the scene in-place. In 3D programs this is often called an ‘orbit’, and spatial CSS enables it with the new portal-action attribute. It may be useful to add more modes in the future like pan-x or pan-y. This mirrors the model element’s stagemode attribute on the HTML element, but by configuring it in CSS it becomes more flexible. ### requestVolumetricScene() In addition to showing a spatial arrangement inside a portal, visionOS has the ability to show these scenes *outside* of the browser window in what we’re calling a Connected Volumetric Scene. Launch a request from a user action to remove the spatial content from its portal and present it in the user’s space: launchSpaceButton. addEventListener ( "click", event = > { const world = document. querySelector ( ".world" ); world. requestVolumetricScene (); }); The code to launch the volumetric scene. Users can place the volumetric scene anywhere in their space, and the live link between the web page and the volumetric scene will let you update the scene — add or remove objects, or move them based on your needs. ### Your feedback is essential There is a long journey ahead, and a lot more to get to in the [proposed spatial CSS specification](https://drafts.csswg.org/css-spatial-1/). While this feature preview is limited to visionOS, we thought it was important to release along with the full specification as an indication of how to approach bringing spatial concepts to the web. Along with the general release of the element on Safari 27, we hope this gives authors enough to think about the opportunities — and requirements — that lie ahead in the spatial web. That’s also why it’s so important for authors to **explore the feature preview** and tell us about their experience of using it. You can download the visionOS simulator with Xcode. If you don’t already have Xcode, you can [download Xcode from the Mac app store.](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/xcode/id497799835?mt=12) To share your thoughts on the Spatial CSS feature preview, find us on Mastodon at [@jensimmons@front-end.social](https://front-end.social/@jensimmons), [@jondavis@mastodon.social](https://mastodon.social/@jondavis), or on X at [@zachernuk](https://x.com/zachernuk). Or send a reply on X to [@webkit](https://x.com/webkit). You can also follow [WebKit on LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/in/apple-webkit/). If you run into any issues, we welcome your feedback about WebKit at [bugs.webkit.org](https://bugs.webkit.org/). Filing issues really does make a difference. Thanks.

items.articleBody:
The Intercept and Freedom of the Press Foundation sued Pete Hegseth’s Pentagon in a pair of lawsuits demanding the release of documents related to the number of U.S. casualties in its war on Iran and the Department of Defense’s secretive blacklist of journalists.

One [lawsuit](https://democracyforward.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/26-9964-Intercept-Iran-War-Complaint.pdf), filed on Friday, responds to the department’s “repeated, unexplained changes” to its publicly available tracker showing U.S. service members killed or injured in the conflict with Iran — including a [failure to acknowledge](https://theintercept.com/2026/10/12/iran-war-casualties-death-toll-accuracy/) one soldier’s death for the six months after he died — that were [documented](https://theintercept.com/2026/08/04/us-military-casualties-count-iran-war/) by Intercept reporter Nick Turse. The shifting figures led one defense official to call the undercount a “[casualty cover-up](https://theintercept.com/2026/04/01/iran-war-us-casualty-numbers-trump-hegseth/).”

In August, Turse requested from the Pentagon, through the Freedom of Information Act, casualty-related records and briefing materials presented to Defense Secretary Hegseth and his chief of staff, directives and guidance on casualties, as well as communications related to casualties between Hegseth and his staff of advisers. A later request filed by The Intercept in September sought the [financial costs](https://theintercept.com/2026/05/12/hegseth-pentagn-budget-defense-iran-war-cost/) of the [Iran war](https://theintercept.com/2026/10/01/trump-military-true-cost-budget-pentagon-trillions/) since its start in February. In all cases, the government stopped responding to The Intercept and has failed to provide any documents.

> “They need to come clean to the American people.”

A [second lawsuit](https://www.documentcloud.org/documents/28913341-fpf-intercept-media-v-dod-26-4041-compl/) against Hegseth’s DoD, filed on Monday, follows a July conversation with The Intercept in which a spokesperson for U.S. Central Command admitted the military post keeps [a blacklist of media members](https://theintercept.com/2026/08/24/pentagon-military-journalist-blacklist-press-media/). While reporting on the shifting U.S. soldier casualty figures, the CENTCOM spokesperson, Richard Allee, threatened Turse that he would be “put on a list of people to disregard” for calling the command too often.

[Related Pentagon Spokesperson Admits There’s a Secret Blacklist of Journalists](https://theintercept.com/2026/08/24/pentagon-military-journalist-blacklist-press-media/)

CENTCOM later denied the existence of such a list. But Turse spoke with an unnamed U.S. official who confirmed that “Hegseth’s office had a standing order not to engage with [Turse] and would deny it if challenged.” During the first Trump administration, Turse had been placed on a [separate blacklist](https://theintercept.com/2018/01/13/we-dont-consider-you-a-legitimate-journalist-how-i-got-blacklisted-by-the-pentagons-africa-command/.) kept by U.S. Africa Command, also within the Pentagon, after he reported on the torture of prisoners at a remote military base in Cameroon used by the U.S. for drone surveillance.

Turse has since filed a public records request seeking a copy of any “lists of journalists that CENTCOM discriminates against or disregards.” The Freedom of the Press Foundation also filed a request for communications and guidance related to the blacklist, as well as any records related to the command’s response to Turse’s article on the matter, [published in August](https://theintercept.com/2026/08/24/pentagon-military-journalist-blacklist-press-media/). The government has yet to provide any such information to The Intercept or Freedom of the Press Foundation.

“The military doesn’t get to decide which reporters it speaks to or ignores, especially when it’s engaged in legally questionable military actions and the human cost is at its highest. It’s not just the journalists who are harmed when the Pentagon behaves this way — the public and Congress are each denied critical information about what the military is doing in our name and with our taxes,” said Lauren Harper, Daniel Ellsberg chair on government secrecy, who filed FOIA requests for the blacklist on behalf of FPF. “If the Defense Department refuses to answer basic questions about how it engages with journalists, we’ll use the Freedom of Information Act to compel them in court.

The Intercept’s Turse called the Pentagon’s journalist blacklist “fundamentally un-American” and a way to avoid accounting for the real human toll of the ongoing war.

“Central Command wants to keep the sordid details of its wars — from civilian casualties in Iran and Yemen to U.S. military casualties across the Middle East — under wraps,” he said. “They need to come clean to the American people. We have to hold them accountable.”

[Related Next Time, Impeach Pete Hegseth for Press Censorship](https://theintercept.com/2026/11/13/pete-hegseth-impeachment-censorship-brendan-carr/)

Hegseth’s Department of Defense has long been hostile toward members of the media. In February 2025, days after Hegseth assumed office, the department forced out outlets such as NBC News, NPR, the New York Times, Politico, CNN, and the Washington Post from their Pentagon press desks. That October, Hegseth issued a new requirement in which journalists could only gain access to the Pentagon if they pledged to only report on information from government employees [pre-approved by the Defense Department](https://theintercept.com/2025/12/12/venezuela-boat-strikes-video-press-coverage/). This prompted most media outlets, except for the right-wing MAGA-friendly One America News Network, to surrender their press passes.

Trump has also targeted specific media outlets and individual journalists by [barring](https://pressfreedomtracker.us/all-incidents/trump-bans-three-outlets-from-white-house-access-citing-fake-news/) them from the White House or Air Force One, though a federal court judge has since paused the bans, cautioning against possible violations of the First Amendment.

The Intercept and FPF’s lawsuits arrive days after Hegseth narrowly [survived an impeachment attempt](https://theintercept.com/2026/11/10/hegseth-no-impeachment-house-vote/) over his [handling of the Iran war](https://theintercept.com/2026/11/05/midterms-hegseth-impeach-pressure-massie-military/). The effort, led by Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., and backed by Democrats, failed to garner enough votes to impeach Hegseth.

[Related “Trump Has Appointed Himself Judge, Jury, and Executioner”](https://theintercept.com/2025/12/12/venezuela-boat-strikes-video-press-coverage/)

In addition to the war on Iran, incoming Democratic members of Congress, along with human rights groups, seek to hold Hegseth accountable for his [bloody airstrike campaign](https://theintercept.com/collections/license-to-kill/) on boats in the Caribbean Sea and Pacific Ocean, in which the U.S. has killed more than 240 civilians, and his overseeing of the U.S. invasion of [Venezuela](https://theintercept.com/2026/01/05/trump-venezuela-war/).

items.articleBody: IntroductionObsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) is clinically heterogeneous, and responses to OCD-relevant images remain incompletely understood. We compared oculomotor activity, stimulus-locked event-related potentials (ERPs), and presaccadic measures.MethodsThirty-eight volunteers with OCD and 38 healthy controls (HC) completed an emotional pro−/antisaccade task with neutral and OCD-relevant images (aggression, contamination, checking, symmetry) during simultaneous electroencephalography (EEG) and eye tracking. Subjective valence and arousal ratings were collected. Clinical subgroup, image-category, and symptom-severity analyses were exploratory.ResultsVolunteers with OCD rated symmetry images as less pleasant and both symmetry and contamination images as more arousing than HC. Antisaccade correction rates were higher in volunteers with OCD. Mean and peak saccade velocities were higher during prosaccade trials when correct and erroneous saccades were analyzed together. These group differences were no longer statistically significant when only correct saccades were analyzed. Volunteers with OCD showed reduced P2 and N2 amplitudes and prolonged N2 latencies. Significant main effects of the image category were observed for P3 amplitude revealed a significant difference between aggression and symmetry stimuli, with symmetry images eliciting lower amplitudes. Stimulus-locked ERPs showed no statistically significant Group × Image Category interactions. Presaccadic measures showed no statistically significant group differences. Exploratory analyses within the OCD group suggested an association between higher Y-BOCS (Yale–Brown Obsessive-Compulsive Scale) scores and shorter P2 peak latency for symmetry images. No statistically significant differences were detected among clinical subgroup.DiscussionResponses to individually symptom-matched and unmatched images were not directly compared. Affective symptoms, treatment exposure, and psychiatric comorbidity limit attribution to OCD alone. Exploratory findings require replication in larger samples with adequate subgroup representation. Non-significant results do not establish equivalence between groups or clinical subgroups.
