items.articleBody:
## THE ARCHITECTURE OF THE MADRID EDITION

[John Pawson](https://www.designboom.com/tag/john-pawson/) takes his cue at The Madrid EDITION [hotel](https://www.designboom.com/tag/designer-boutique-hotel/) from an eighteenth-century baroque portal he inherited. Spanish architect Pedro de Ribera carved it for the chapel of the Monte de Piedad, the charitable pawnshop that Francisco Piquer, chaplain of the Descalzas Reales convent across the square, founded in 1702 to lend to the poor. The savings bank that grew out of that pawnshop demolished the chapel in the 1960s and kept the portal, resetting it on the face of its new office building.

It is this building that [OAB (Office of Architecture in Barcelona)](https://www.designboom.com/tag/oab/) and Ruiz-Larrea convert into [the brand’s](https://www.designboom.com/tag/edition-hotels/) second [Spanish](https://www.designboom.com/tag/architecture-in-spain/) address after the Barcelona EDITION of 2018, with interiors by Pawson and Paris-based François Champsaur, all orchestrated under the eye of Ian Schrager. Pawson names the challenges of the inherited architecture as the project’s defining inspiration, and his response turns on a lobby with two very different entry experiences: a lower entrance clad in dark baroque timber around a sculptural white staircase, and a second entrance through the portal itself on the historic Plaza de las Descalzas.

a copper canopy shelters the Madrid EDITION’s main entrance | all images by Nikolas Koenig Photography

## BAROQUE PORTAL AND A RIBBON OF WHITE LEAD TO THE HOTEL’S LOBBY

From the historic square, [the Madrid EDITION](https://www.editionhotels.com/madrid/) building reads as clean-lined and almost reticent, its single flourish the carved decorative portal that frames the entrance. Around the corner, a copper canopy and a curtain of greenery announce the main entry, with [Pawson’s](https://www.johnpawson.com/) white sculptural spiral staircase, free of visible handrails, coiling up toward the lobby where the two entrances meet.

the entrance’s sculptural spiral staircase ribbons fluidly to the lobby on the upper ground floor above

There, the Lobby Bar sits beneath an undulating plane that softens the room’s proportions, lit almost entirely indirectly, with spotlights reserved for the pieces worth looking at: reissued Jean-Michel Frank sofas and armchairs, recycled bronze stools cast by Maison Intègre at its foundry in Ouagadougou, rope-wrapped chairs by Christian Astuguevieille, and a pool table that Emmanuel Levet Stenne cut from a single slab of white Bianco Neve marble. A hand-scalloped copper bar runs along one side with a backlit caged bottle display behind it, and a U-shaped sofa with backlit shelves anchors the middle of the room.

1/4

long, bright pink arched hallway leading to the lobby from Plaza de las Descalzas
the Lobby Bar sits beneath an undulating plane
the Punch Room's brushed copper bar
basalt stone fireplace in the Punch Room

In a corner off the lobby, the Punch Room goes darker still, with dark oak panels, a basalt stone fireplace, gray pony hair armchairs, a brushed copper bar and a bronze-polished mirror by Paris studio Garnier & Linker.

the eighteenth-century baroque portal by Spanish architect Pedro de Ribera

## A MOTIF REPEATED IN JOHN PAWSON & François Champsaur’S INTERIORS

Ribera’s carving does not stay outside, it reappears in the double-height dining room of the all-day Italian restaurant, which enters directly through the portal from the plaza. There, dark oak wall panels take their pattern from the stonework a few meters away, hung with two alabaster and plaster pendants by Levet Stenne. The room opens into a lounge along a long green marble bar laid over white oak floors, then into a lighter third area of white marble tables.

1/2

the Pórtico's double-height dining room, defined by carved dark oak wall panels inspired by the baroque portal just outside
the restaurant's more casual, light-filled area

The motif travels upstairs too, in each of the hotel’s 200 guest rooms, where custom made plaster headboards are shaped after the elaborate form of the hotel’s baroque portal. The rooms’ interiors carry the contrast of light and darkness down to the threshold. An entrance panelled in dark oak gives onto a light-filled palette of whites and creams, with custom furnishings and the natural textures of linen, limestone and timber forming what the hotel calls an honest and discreet canvas for the detail work.

*‘I am very proud of this project,’* **says Schrager, the visionary pioneer of the boutique and lifestyle hotel brand** **.** ‘Not a single detail has been overlooked and the finished product has created a unique and magical concept.’

custom made plaster headboards shaped after the hotel’s baroque portal

1/4

guestrooms combine a white and cream palette
guest rooms are softly lit at nighttime
many rooms frame views over the Descalzas square, the Royal Palace or Gran Vía
bathrooms are wrapped in marble

23 of the 200 rooms are suites, while two penthouses take the west side of the fourth floor for the sunset, arranged as duplexes with the bedrooms upstairs and the living space and a butler’s kitchen below. The larger of them, the Madrid Penthouse, opens onto a panoramic terrace with its own infinity pool set in greenery, furnished with a leather and wood daybed by BassamFellows and an eight-seat travertine dining table on lacquered metal feet.

the hotel’s penthouses are arranged as duplexes

## INFINITY POOL WITH VIEWS OF THE SPANISH CAPITAL ON THE ROOF

The fourth-floor rooftop holds the property’s showpiece: the largest infinity pool built on the roof of an existing building in Madrid, edged by 25 sunbeds and five cabanas, with the city’s terracotta rooftops unrolling toward the sunset. The rooftop is also home to Oroya, the Peruvian restaurant of chef Diego Muñoz, set in a greenhouse-like dining room of blackened steel, climbing plants and colored glass. Outside, a vine-covered pergola shades the restaurant’s terrace, where a fireplace, a bleached teak bar and a long oak table offer guests a relaxed, convivial atmosphere to enjoy lazy lunches or afternoon cocktails.

items.articleBody:
The entrance to Umm al-Khair in the occupied West Bank. Photograph by Jasper Nathaniel.

This February, the Israeli military installed a gate across a busy road in the South Hebron Hills. It was a simple contraption, maybe twenty feet of yellow steel that swung open like the door of a cattle pen—one of hundreds erected across the West Bank. But this one blocked the only drivable road into the tiny Palestinian village of Umm al-Khair as well as more than twenty other shepherding communities, home to thousands of people.

For the past nine months, soldiers have routinely locked the gate for days at a time, preventing residents from reaching work or school, blocking deliveries of food and supplies, and limiting access to hospitals and emergency medical care. Those who manage to drive through during a brief opening may return to find it locked, leaving them stranded on the wrong side, with no way home. Whenever soldiers close the gate, life in Umm al-Khair grinds to a halt. A closed gate also serves as a warning: a settler attack may be coming.

Umm al-Khair was founded by Palestinian Bedouins expelled from the Negev during the Nakba of 1948. It sits in the shadow of the Israeli settlement of Carmel, which was built on land confiscated from the village in 1980. For decades, settlers backed by the Israeli state have encroached on the land that remains. In the summer of 2025, a group of settlers established an outpost—an unauthorized settlement, illegal even under Israeli law—by installing several mobile homes directly adjacent to Umm al-Khair and moving into them. The construction set off a new wave of violence, one that drew international attention when a settler opened fire on a crowd of Palestinians, killing the community leader Awdah Hathaleen in front of his three-year-old son.

When I got dropped off at the gate on the evening of October 27, 2026, it had been locked for four days—the longest stretch since it went up in February. I was visiting Umm al-Khair as a journalist and activist, alongside my colleagues Andrey Khrzhanovskiy and Adele Shoko, both Russian nationals turned Israeli citizens now living in the West Bank. Andrey, who publishes under the name Andrey X, is one of the region’s most prolific non-Palestinian activists, as well as one of Israeli settlers and soldiers’ most frequent targets. A friend met us on the Umm al-Khair side and drove us into the village.

[https://www.theparisreview.org/blog/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/gate-video.mp4](https://www.theparisreview.org/blog/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/gate-video.mp4)

Residents and activists at the Umm al-Khair gate on October 26, 2026. Filmed by Mothers Against Violence, via [Genocide.live](https://genocide.live/43467).

At ten the next morning, we heard the familiar rumble of military jeeps and rushed to the gate, arriving just in time to see soldiers unlocking it. They gave no explanation of their actions—the IDF rarely does. As word spread, cheers erupted. Cars rushed in and out as residents hurried to work, visited nearby friends and family, and shopped for groceries in Yatta, the nearest city. It didn’t last. At 10:45 A.M., a local settler named Shimon Atiya arrived and locked the gate back up.

Shimon is the founder of an illegal farming outpost near Umm al-Khair. He’s an angry man, perpetually talking into an earpiece, known for overturning dumpsters and kneeing men in the groin. Though he carries a military-grade assault rifle, he is not in the IDF and has no formal authority in the sprawling military occupation that governs Palestinian life. But Israel’s de facto annexation of the West Bank relies on civilian enforcers like him. While the military has long maintain ed the facade of complying with international law, settler leaders like Shimon make no such pretense. They effectively command state-backed militias of men and adolescents who terrorize Palestinian residents to drive them from their land. Once the Palestinians are gone, the Israeli government may retroactively legalize the settlers’ outposts as “neighborhoods” of existing settlements or as new settlements altogether.

In Umm al-Khair, Israeli soldiers arrived at about 3 P.M. They had with them a photo of me and Andrey, likely taken by Shimon hours before. They told the residents to bring us to them. Once we got there, a soldier showed us a map of a newly declared Closed Military Zone (CMZ)—an arbitrary designation used to expel activists and journalists from Palestinian villages—and ordered us to leave.

Ostensibly, CMZs restrict all nonresidents from a designated area. But while we were speaking, a settler drove straight through the restricted zone. When I asked the soldier in charge whether he intended to expel the settler, he shook his head. The order, it seemed, applied only to us. Even so, the map left a small part of the village unrestricted. We pointed this out, and the soldiers reluctantly allowed us to stay. But if we entered the restricted area, they warned us, we would be placed under arrest.

A soldier directing Nathaniel to leave the CMZ on October 28, 2026. Photograph by Adele Shoko.

Two hours later, a resident of Umm al-Khair found me outside the home of Hanady Hathaleen, Awdah’s widow, in the small part of the village not subject to the military order. He asked if I could head to the gate to wait with a Palestinian man from a neighboring village who was afraid to stand there alone. Earlier that day, at around two, the man had tried to drive around the gate—a maneuver that residents whose cars have four-wheel drive capability sometimes attempt, despite the risk of being shot by settlers. Nevo Nadalski, Carmel’s head of security, had raced to the gate, forced him out of his vehicle, and confiscated his keys. Nevo told the man to return in three hours to collect them.

Like Shimon Atiya, Nevo is a local settler with no formal authority in the military occupation. He often plays the proverbial “good cop” to Shimon’s “bad cop,” showing up at the scene of settler attacks and pretending to de-escalate while actually providing cover for the assailants. Many Umm al-Khair residents blame him for Awdah’s murder. They believe he instructed an Israeli construction worker to drive his excavator through the village, provoking the confrontation that led to Awdah’s death.

I joined the Palestinian driver at the gate at 5:20 P.M.— three and a half hours had passed with no sign of Nevo or the man’s keys. Andrey and Adele arrived from elsewhere in the village at around the same time. We watched as a Palestinian car pulled up on the other side and unloaded food supplies, passing them under the gate to a car on the village side. Later, a mother with four small children got out of a taxi, paid the fare, and ran with her family to their home.

A family from Umm al-Khair getting dropped off on the other side of the gate. October 28, 2026. Photograph by Jasper Nathaniel.

None of this seemed out of the ordinary. Then, at 6:15 P.M., a white pickup truck driven by a settler approached from the Umm al-Khair side. (The settlers have alternative roads they can take to Carmel and other settlements, but often prefer to speed through the village when the gate is unlocked, scattering children who play in the street.) The truck stopped and a smirking, curly-haired settler who looked to be in his late teens or early twenties climbed out of the passenger seat. As the Palestinian man fled, the settler produced a key and unlocked the gate. He swung the gate open, waited for the truck to pass through, then closed and locked it behind him.

Andrey, Adele, and I have spent years reporting from the West Bank. Even so, we were shocked. We’d long known that the military could lock Palestinians in place at will. We had learned, months ago, that Shimon also had his own key. But we hadn’t expected to see some random settler, possibly a minor, casually let himself through, then lock the gate behind him. Thousands of Palestinians lived on the other side, and apparently he, too, had the power to decide when they could come and go.

The three of us began filming. Andrey approached the settler to ask how he had gotten a key, but he only smiled and walked back toward the truck. Still filming, Andrey followed, now turning his camera on the driver to ask the question again: “Who gave you this authority?” He stood several feet away from the window. The driver was a large man with brown teeth, a crusty beard, and, we soon discovered, no socks or shoes. We later learned his name, Tomer Liani. He lived in Havat Ma’on, a settlement on Palestinian land two miles away, and had served in the IDF during the genocide in Gaza. Tomer turned his own phone on Andrey and asked, outraged, what authority Andrey had to film him.

Tomer opened the driver’s-side door, revealing an M16 assault rifle slung across his chest. The curly-haired settler began to kick Andrey. Tomer then grabbed Andrey by the collar, snatched his phone away, and struck him in the face with it three times, breaking his glasses and his nose. When I tried to pull Andrey away, Tomer punched me in the eye.

[https://www.theparisreview.org/blog/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/attack-clip-1.mp4](https://www.theparisreview.org/blog/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/attack-clip-1.mp4)

Nathaniel, Andrey X, and Tomer Liani. Filmed by Jasper Nathaniel.

I finally freed Andrey from Tomer’s grip. The settlers climbed back into their truck, still holding his phone. He blocked their way, demanding that they return it. Tomer edged his truck forward, forcing Andrey aside. When Adele reached through his window for the phone, Tomer grabbed her glasses and hit the gas, dragging her several feet and spraining her wrist.

The settlers now had a clear path to drive away. Instead, Tomer flew into a rage. He got out of the truck, cocked his rifle, aimed it at Andrey, and started to shout: “I’ll shoot you! I’ll shoot you!” His nose was bleeding, apparently as a result of the scuffle, and he pointed at it, yelling, “See what you did!” He ordered Andrey onto the ground. When Andrey raised his hands and tried to back away, Tomer grabbed him and forced him onto the pavement.

Adele and I were still filming, but I knew that if we both stayed, there was a good chance we’d get our phones taken too. I whispered to her to run back to the village with hers so we’d have footage of how the attack had started. The settlers, focused as they were on Andrey, didn’t notice Adele slip away.

Photographs by Adele Shoko.

Tomer stood over Andrey now, holding him down by his jacket, kneeing him in the head, and stepping on his face with his bare feet—which, I noticed, were caked with filth. I tried to de-escalate. “We’re leaving,” I said—but Tomer pointed his rifle at me, shouting, “It’s not over!” When I grabbed Andrey’s jacket and tried to pull him away, Tomer trained his rifle on my chest. Leaning down, he whispered in Andrey’s ear, addressing him by name: “You made the worst mistake of your life, Andrey.”

Then the settlers tried to drag Andrey into the truck. I grabbed his jacket, a tug-of-war broke out, and, once again, Tomer pointed his rifle at me as his younger accomplice kicked and punched me. Andrey looked over at me and said, wide-eyed: “Don’t let them put me in the truck.”

Shimon Atiya and Nevo Nadalski arrived soon thereafter, armed with assault rifles too. Tomer seemed to have given up trying to get Andrey into his truck, but the leaders’ presence emboldened him. He dragged Andrey across the ground by his hair, slapped him, kneed him, stepped on him, pulled him up, and body-slammed him back down. At one point, Tomer spit in his hand and rubbed it across Andrey’s face.

When I shouted at Shimon and Nevo to put a stop to it, both men laughed. “He’s resisting,” Nevo said, grinning. “Resisting who?” I snapped, pointing to Tomer. “What authority does he have?” Then, Tomer lifted Andrey’s head and smashed it against the concrete.

Andrey screamed. I tried to reach him, but Nevo and Shimon blocked me. “Jasper, I’m nauseous,” Andrey called out. “I think I have a concussion.”

Photographs by Adele Shoko.

At about 6:40 P.M., the military and police arrived. I was sure the settlers had called them to arrest us. Tomer clicked the safety back on his gun. The soldiers wouldn’t let me approach Andrey either, and my pleas for an ambulance went unanswered. They left Andrey lying on the ground, drifting in and out of consciousness, without medical assistance for more than twenty minutes. One of the soldiers filmed him, laughing, then panned over to me.

Other settlers began trickling down from Carmel, many bearing assault rifles too. They high-fived our attackers and then mingled with soldiers and police, smiling, chatting, and filming us. Some took selfies with Andrey’s motionless body. Other activists arrived to document the scene, but soldiers held them back, threatening them with arrest.

I was still shouting, demanding that the police arrest Tomer and his young accomplice. I told them that Tomer had stolen Andrey’s phone and all they needed to do was search his truck to find it. Instead, three police officers swarmed me and snatched my own phone. I was under arrest, they announced. They dragged me away and shoved me into the back of a police jeep. Settlers lined up to wave at me and photograph me through the window.

Days later, Andrey described what had happened after my arrest. The cops offered him a choice between going to the hospital or the police station. Andrey chose the hospital, and the settler paramedic promised to take him there. (“Don’t worry,” the paramedic said, gesturing at the other settlers, “I’m not with them.”) Once Andrey was in the ambulance, the paramedic drove a few hundred yards, just out of view of the activists’ cameras. He took Andrey’s blood pressure and nothing else: no questions, no neurological exam. Then he helped the police lift Andrey out of the ambulance and shove him into a patrol car.

[https://www.theparisreview.org/blog/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/jasper-1.mp4](https://www.theparisreview.org/blog/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/jasper-1.mp4)

The arrest on October 28, 2026. Filmed by a witness who prefers to remain anonymous.

When I arrived at the police station in the Kiryat Arba settlement—where the national security minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir, lives—officers handcuffed me and shackled my legs. As they led me inside, I saw Andrey being taken from another police car and placed in shackles of his own. My eye was swollen, the side of my face cut and bruised. Andrey was nodding off, his nose bloodied. We were not offered medical treatment.

The officer sitting at the front desk was a bald, gray-bearded, portly man we’d come to refer to as the Burger King. As we entered, he stood up and pointed at me, his face red, shouting, “You son of a bitch!” If he recognized me—as Tomer had recognized Andrey—he didn’t say. The guards sat us in chairs facing each other. I tried to keep Andrey responsive by talking to him and snapping my fingers, but the officers kept ordering me to be quiet. Andrey had suffered a head injury, I explained. I was trying to keep him awake. “Since when is this what you do for a head injury?” an English-speaking officer asked. I told him to Google it. He didn’t. I kept calling out to Andrey until one cop turned my chair around to face the wall, as if putting me in a time-out.

I asked the English-speaking officer whether he’d heard about an attack from earlier that month, when Heidi Levine, a *Washington Post* photographer, was nearly beaten to death by settlers. Surely he’d heard about it, I said. The whole thing had been captured on video: masked settlers kicking her, beating her with clubs as she lay on the ground—leaving her with four fractured vertebrae, a broken rib, puncture wounds to her back and buttocks, and a finger cut down to the bone—before several Palestinians, Andrey, and I got her to safety. The incident had made international news. Even Netanyahu had weighed in, though he’d blamed “Arabs and far-left activists” for the “alleged” attack and claimed that a settler had come to Heidi’s rescue.

I told the officer to Google “Heidi Levine” along with our names. He pretended to ignore me. But out of the corner of my eye, I watched him pull up the video and press play, then scroll through headlines.

He turned to the other officers and spoke to them in a nervous whisper. A few moments later, they turned my chair around to face Andrey. They stopped yelling every time I spoke to him. We were given sandwiches, and the Burger King began speaking to me in his own limited English. It was the day after the election in Israel; he’d voted for Netanyahu—“Israel needs a strong leader,” he told me. “Only Netanyahu is strong *.* ” Didn’t we agree?

Israeli medics order Palestinian medics to stop treatment. Photograph by a witness who prefers to remain anonymous.

The warm treatment was short-lived. At about one in the morning, a plainclothes officer with an M16 and a pistol marched into the police station, looked our way, and grinned: “What are you doing here, Andrey?” The officer, Neriya—he wouldn’t share his last name—had interrogated Andrey a week earlier, after he’d been arrested during a peaceful olive harvest and charged with, among other things, “support for a terror organization.” Neriya’s arrival was our first clear indication that the police’s interest in us extended beyond the events of that evening.

Neriya’s English was halting, so before he read us our charges, he called a translator over speakerphone—by the sound of it, an elderly woman whose English wasn’t much better. The offenses she read out were incomprehensible. We later learned that we were being held on the same seven counts: entering a restricted area; violating a lawful order; assault causing actual bodily harm; insulting a public servant; making threats; obstructing a police officer in the performance of his duty; and using force to prevent arrest.

Neriya took Andrey to another building, where he was allowed to call our shared lawyer, Alon Sapir. He was then interrogated until four in the morning. Andrey would later tell me that the officers used the same translator, who struggled to understand basic statements, sometimes reducing lengthy explanations to a few words, forcing Neriya to resort to Google Translate for terms as simple as “violence.”

In an article about our arrest, police would tell the *Times of Israel* that they were investigating us for “an alleged attempt to steal weapons.” But during our interrogations, no one mentioned weapons or theft. The actual purpose of the “investigation” was clear: they wanted to prove that one of us had given Tomer Liani a bloody nose. Neriya showed Andrey a photograph of the injury and demanded to know why he’d done it. Andrey showed him his knuckles, which bore no swelling or marks. He reminded the officer that he had been beaten that night, and that the assault had been captured on video. All he had to do was recover his phone—or let us access mine.

Then the interrogator turned to the matter of Andrey’s reporting. “Is it normal for journalists to be arrested twice in one week?” And why, he asked, did Andrey keep turning up at the scene of violent incidents? Andrey explained that he went to places known for settler violence, like Abu Falah, where he and I had helped rescue Heidi Levine. Before Neriya could respond, the interpreter interjected. “I heard that the settlers helped her,” she said, parroting Netanyahu’s line. Finally, Neriya accused Andrey, who had fled political persecution in Russia years earlier, of disloyalty: “How could you turn against the country that took you in?”

The interrogation over, an officer handed Andrey a statement and asked him to sign it. Andrey refused—it was written in Hebrew, a language he understood somewhat but could not read. Neriya brought Andrey back to the waiting area, where we waited some more. He was still groggy but more alert than he’d been before.

The officers guarding us mostly slept. One fell backward out of his chair. Burger King had a loud argument with his wife (we heard both sides, since he was on speakerphone) about why he was out all night and would miss taking their child to school. She was worried about the kid’s grades. *His job was dynamic*, he insisted. *He was currently responsible for guarding two criminals! Did she want him to just leave?* After their fight, Burger King played a Hebrew song on repeat. By the third listen, Andrey had picked up enough words to understand what it was about: a woman falling in love with a police officer.

Photograph by Jasper Nathaniel.

At seven in the morning, the interrogator returned for me. I hadn’t slept in twenty-four hours. He refused my request for coffee. In the three hours since questioning Andrey, they’d managed to find a competent translator, who called in on speakerphone. My interrogation began much as Andrey’s had, with questions about who had bloodied Tomer’s nose. As with Andrey, the interrogator showed no interest in establishing what had actually happened—how the assault had started, how I’d gotten my black eye, or how Andrey had been beaten unconscious. Like Andrey, I was asked why I was always present when violence occurred. Like him, I found myself explaining the tenets of conflict reporting.

After two or so hours, a second investigator took over—an irritated, squirrelly man who, despite his petite size, had managed to find a shirt that was several sizes too small. He scoffed when I asked for coffee and then turned to Tomer’s nose, showing no more interest in my injuries than his predecessor. He then turned to the CMZ delineation, which he believed he could prove I had violated. He had obtained footage of my encounter with soldiers hours before the attack—but apparently hadn’t bothered to watch it, unaware that what it captured was the moment when I’d been permitted to stay. When we got to the part where the settler drove into the CMZ, he changed the subject—reeling off various nonexistent laws governing journalism that I had supposedly neglected to follow.

His actual interest became clear when he left the room briefly and returned with a thick folder. This was their file on me, he explained. He dropped the dossier in front of me with a dramatic flourish, then put it away and turned to his computer. Thus began the bulk of my interrogation, which concerned my social-media history. He started with my X bio, which says that I report from the occupied West Bank. He wanted to know what I meant by *occupied*. “This is violent language,” he said. Next, he opened a video I’d posted the week before, showing a police officer shoving me while Andrey was being arrested. Why, he demanded, had I called the officer a *fascist*? My violence, unlike the officer’s—which, he clarified, had been justified—put the state of Israel at risk. For the next several hours, he worked his way through my X feed, grilling me about phrases like *crackdown*, *pogroms*, and even *my Palestinian friends*. “Who exactly are these friends?” he asked.

Finally, he wanted to know who was funding me. Was I being paid by a foreign state? An enemy of Israel? I found myself in the unlikely position of teaching my jailer about the Substack business model. By now, it was after two in the afternoon. I’d been under interrogation for more than six hours and hadn’t slept for more than thirty. In the end, I, too, was handed a statement that I couldn’t read and declined to sign, despite the officer’s assurance that he’d recorded my answers faithfully.

He brought me back to Andrey, and we were loaded into a police car with three plainclothes officers. We were told that we were being taken to court in Jerusalem. As we pulled away, the driver turned to me and addressed me in English: “Are you Jewish?”

“Yes.”

“No, you’re not.”

Then he turned to Andrey and asked again: “Are you Jewish?”

“Yes.”

“No. No, you’re not.”

Demolished greenhouses in the Palestinian village of Umm al-Khair, [CC BY-SA 2.5](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/2.5), via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Demolished_greenhouses_in_the_Palestinian_village_of_Umm_al-Khair,_sorrounded_by_the_illegal_Israeli_Settlement_of_Carmel_06.jpg).

Our lawyer, Alon Sapir, met us outside the courtroom. Adele had made it to safety and had been able to share her footage online. The case was already attracting attention. Alon planned to show the judge the recording and request our unconditional release. He suspected the Israeli authorities were feeling some pressure. They wouldn’t want to do anything too drastic, he said, lest they draw more attention to the attack.

We were unshackled for the first time since our detention the day before, led into the courtroom, and seated on a bench before a small group of spectators, one of whom appeared to sneak a photo. The judge read the charges aloud. The prosecutor refused to look at either of us.

The investigation was ongoing, the prosecutor said, but he was not seeking to keep us in detention while it continued. Instead, he asked the judge to impose eight days of house arrest in Israel (where he seemed to assume we both lived), a no-contact order barring us from communicating with anyone involved in the incident, mandatory further questioning, thousands of dollars in collateral to ensure our compliance, and a six-month ban from the West Bank.

Alon spoke briefly, then showed the judge footage of the attack. The prosecutor presented footage of his own, though of what, I have no idea. The judge reached his ruling in a matter of minutes. It was clear, he said, that the settlers—the “other individuals” he called them—had initiated the violence, not the “respondents,” by which he meant us. Moreover, he went on, he “did not find that there was symmetry between the violence attributed to the respondents and the violence inflicted by the other individuals.” “Accordingly,” he concluded, “the reasonable suspicion of violent offenses is weak.”

As a result, he denied the prosecutor’s request that we be placed on house arrest but granted several of his others. He imposed a two-month no-contact order—meaning Andrey, Adele, and I could not communicate with each other—along with the mandatory further questioning and financial guarantees. The police would be allowed to keep my phone. And we were banned from the West Bank, though for two months rather than six. Just t he previous afternoon, soldiers had tried and failed to expel us from Umm al-Khair. Now, the police and an Israeli judge had achieved something more concrete: the removal of two journalists from the West Bank for the remainder of a particularly brutal olive-harvest season. None of the settlers, whom the judge had just watched attack us, were charged.

Palestinian children looking at destroyed property beside the settler outpost. Photograph by Jasper Nathaniel.

During my detention, the U.S. Embassy made no effort to contact my attorney. Days later, when I bought a new phone, I found a message from a consular officer asking if I was okay—sent to the phone the police had confiscated.

I *was*, in fact, okay, though not thanks to the U.S. government. I was okay because I was not Palestinian. Had three Palestinians approached Tomer’s truck the way we had, they might well have been shot dead. Had they survived to be arrested, they would have entered the military-justice system, where Palestinians can be held indefinitely without charge or trial, on the basis of evidence they aren’t allowed to see. They would have ended up in Ben-Gvir’s prisons, which the Israeli human-rights group B’Tselem has called a “network of torture camps.” Since October 2023, according to Reporters Without Borders, Israel has killed at least two hundred and ten Palestinian journalists in Gaza. As of this fall, per data from the human rights NGO Addameer, Israel is also holding more than nine thousand Palestinian prisoners and detainees on “security” grounds, nearly a third without charge or trial. At least thirty-eight are journalists.

The day before our detention, Ghassan Najjar, a thirty-six-year-old Palestinian activist, was arrested in a predawn military raid on his home in Burin. Andrey and I had both worked with Ghassan before. Like us, he had been documenting the olive harvest and protecting Palestinian farmers from settler violence. But unlike us, he was not released. Instead, he was placed under a four-month administrative detention order, which can be renewed indefinitely.

Andrey and I were extremely lucky. We had lawyers, a civilian court, and enough of an audience that the police knew they were dealing with a story that could draw international attention. Within a day, a judge had watched the footage and ordered our release. But the ban, though short, was strategic: earlier that October, while Andrey and I were in al-Mughayyir, a Palestinian village east of Ramallah where settlers torched our car, Israeli authorities revoked my Electronic Travel Authorization (ETA). Since January 2025, foreigners have needed an ETA in order to board flights to Israel or enter the West Bank from Jordan—but the Population and Immigration Authority has routinely revoked activists’ authorizations to keep them out. I don’t know of anyone who has gotten one back.

The court’s two-month ban covered almost all the time left on my visa, which meant that as long as I stayed, I couldn’t get back to the West Bank, and once I left Israel, I couldn’t board a plane to return. The stakes are higher for Andrey. This very morning, Israel’s Minister of Diaspora Affairs and Combating Antisemitism, citing the October 28 arrest, announced an unprecedented move: he had submitted a request to strip Andrey of his citizenship.

As news of our ban spread, prominent settlers and their allies celebrated online, portraying us as anarchists and provocateurs known for acts of violence against the “Jewish residents of Judea and Samaria.” Others were disappointed the judge hadn’t gone further. Elisha Yered, one of the settler movement’s most violent leaders, who stands accused of murdering a Palestinian teenager, slammed the court for not banning us sooner. “If only they had removed them from here at the start of the harvest season,” he wrote on X, “so much international damage and violent provocations would have been spared.”

Days after we were released, Israeli soldiers and intelligence agents, accompanied by Shimon Atiya, raided Umm al-Khair. They confiscated residents’ phones and warned them to stop inviting journalists and activists into the community. Otherwise, they threatened, they would return with trucks, load the residents into them, and expel them from the village. On their way out, they locked the gate.

*Jasper Nathaniel is a Brooklyn-based writer and reporter. He covers Israel’s occupation of the West Bank and other political and cultural affairs on his Substack,* [Infinite Jaz](http://infinitejaz.substack.com/).

items.articleBody:
Late on a Tuesday night in September 2019, Tina’s phone pinged with a message. The subject line read, in part, “fuck you slut!!!!!” The message contained a link to Pornhub, the world’s most popular porn site.

At the time, Tina — who spoke to the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists on the condition that her last name not be used — had recently ended a relationship with an abusive boyfriend. When she had tried to break up with him months earlier, Tina said he coerced her into making sexually explicit videos. It was his way, she told ICIJ, of controlling her.

Tina’s ex-boyfriend had now published those videos on Pornhub. It was the beginning of a months-long campaign of harassment and death threats: He posted videos and photos of her more than 100 times on Pornhub, according to emails reviewed by ICIJ, using accounts created in her name and including her address, phone number and employer.

He also posted photographs of her underage daughters at the beach in bikinis, along with their names and contact information. He emailed one daughter with a link to the videos of Tina and told her to ask her mother “why she put you all in danger from weirdos all over the country.”

“My ex wanted to kill me,” Tina said. “And he used Pornhub as the gun.”

Pornhub’s owner, the Montreal-based company Aylo, runs some of the world’s most popular websites. Its network of over 100 sites — including Pornhub, YouPorn and RedTube — attracts more than 100 million visits every day and has generated hundreds of millions of dollars in annual revenue, according to the most recent available data.

Aylo’s profits were built in part on some of the most heinous material on the internet. At the time of Tina’s abuse in September 2019, anyone could create a free account on Pornhub and upload videos; Pornhub did not require verification of the uploader’s identity.

Aylo has long employed moderators, whose job includes the identification of instances of sex trafficking, as well as photos and videos of minors. But the company was overwhelmed by the deluge of content: More than 6.8 million videos were uploaded to Pornhub in 2019; the company bragged in its 2019 “year in review” that if a viewer started watching all of them in 1850, they would still be watching.

Tina is just one of the many individuals victimized on the company’s websites. In 2020, Aylo removed more than 347,000 videos for nonconsensual content, according to [a complaint](https://www.ftc.gov/system/files/ftc_gov/pdf/AyloGroupLtd-et-al-Complaint.pdf) filed by the Federal Trade Commission and the state of Utah. Aylo has made numerous changes since then — such as verifying the identity of uploaders — but its own reports show that potentially abusive and exploitative content continues to be published on Pornhub.

ms because, in the words of one employee in an email to a colleague, they were used frequently in BDSM and staged blackmail videos, and thus “relatively compliant” with the company’s terms of service (Pornhub told ICIJ that “blackmail” and “forced” are currently banned on all Aylo platforms).

This exchange was included in court documents reviewed by ICIJ from a class-action lawsuit against Aylo filed in Alabama in February 2021. The documents, which were supposed to be sealed, inadvertently became publicly accessible on the court’s electronic docket for eight months because of a filing error. A judge recently granted preliminary approval to a settlement agreement in that case and a related California class action. As part of the settlement, Aylo committed to the single largest known payout to victims in the company’s history.

Aylo does not want the world to see what these records reveal about its business practices. After ICIJ approached the company for comment for this article, Aylo asked a federal judge in Alabama to bar ICIJ from publishing “any information learned or derived from” the documents. This extraordinary request threatened to muzzle ICIJ’s reporting on Aylo’s behavior, far beyond the contents of the court filings.

The judge rejected Aylo’s motion to prevent ICIJ from publishing an article based on the records.

The documents, which largely concern abusive content posted in 2020 and earlier, show a company that often fell short of those standards. Even notification from law enforcement of CSAM on the company’s sites was no guarantee that the illegal content would be promptly removed. In one instance, according to a deposition of an Aylo employee included in the court filings, Pornhub kept a video featuring the abuse of a 12-year-old boy online for more than a month after being informed of it by an Alabama law enforcement special agent.

In an internal email, an Aylo employee wrote that there was a request in this case “NOT to remove the content.” A separate civil complaint filed by the abused boy’s mother alleged that law enforcement officers informed Aylo that the illegal content was on its site three times, over a period of multiple weeks, and requested that it be removed.

Other CSAM videos remained on the site for years. And when discovered, some Aylo employees viewed their presence more with bemusement than horror.

“You guys want to laugh,” one moderator wrote to colleagues in 2020, as the company tested new CSAM detection software. “It caught a cp [child pornography] video from 2009 … a full on cp video on the site for 11 yrs.”

Another employee described a former moderator as “almost blind,” and wrote that he “put through so much stuff loool.”

Pornhub’s victims described a cycle of trauma as they struggled to scrub their name and images from the internet. Tina said Pornhub was too slow to take down the accounts with her name and contact information. And when they were finally removed, she said, her ex-boyfriend would simply create a new account and post the videos again.

The Pornhub email address used by victims to submit takedown requests included an automated response stating that an employee would respond within two days. Perversely, the response also promoted a program enabling users to “make money from your homemade videos.”

Tina would often realize the videos had been reposted because men would deluge her with lewd calls. Pornhub notified Tina that it “fingerprinted” her videos, a technology that generates a unique digital signature of a video to prevent its reupload, seven months after she first notified the company of them, according to emails reviewed by ICIJ.

Even before Tina’s videos first appeared, Pornhub had publicly touted its “state-of-the-art” fingerprinting technology to prevent revenge porn from being reuploaded. As Tina was struggling frantically to get her videos offline, Pornhub’s executives formulated a policy that called for victims of revenge porn to be offered fingerprinting services. But Tina says Pornhub did not tell her that her videos had been fingerprinted until she sent an all-caps email notifying the company that she was a crime victim. “DO BETTER PORNHUB!!!!,” the email read.

But Tina’s nightmare was still not over. Even after Pornhub removed the videos, it would sometimes leave the page on which they resided that included her personal information, emails reviewed by ICIJ showed. To this day, a Google search of her name brings up Pornhub results, though not the videos themselves; other porn sites also include her address at the time.

Tina eventually moved to a new city because she no longer felt safe in her neighborhood. She became anxious if someone looked at her too long or when she was around large groups of men. She wasn’t in a relationship for years.

“I wish I had been raped physically because then it would only have been once,” she said. The reuploading of the videos, the online comments about her body by strangers, the lewd calls, she said, “felt like a rape every single time.”

The documents in the Alabama case also cast doubt on the company’s assurances about its methods to prevent the spread of CSAM. In a 2020 blog post, for example, the company touted its use of fingerprinting technology, which meant that any CSAM videos it found “cannot be re-uploaded,” it wrote.

But a few months before that blog post was published, Aylo executives drafted a policy covering how to respond when law enforcement officers report the existence of CSAM to the company. Aylo would not “communicate fingerprinting action back to complainant unless asked,” the document stated, “because we do not want to be seen as offering a guarantee” that the content would not reappear. This was necessary because the contractor providing fingerprinting services “has its limitations.”

Aylo’s then-CEO also told a Canadian parliamentary committee that requiring uploaders to provide government-issued identification to verify their age and identity meant that “every piece of content on our websites can be traced back to its uploader.” But the court documents show that the contractor tasked to verify the IDs of uploaders warned Aylo that “sophisticated and determined fraudsters” could defeat its technology.

This requirement would also not have thwarted some of the previous abusers mentioned in the Alabama court documents. The person who abused the Jane Doe at the center of the Alabama class-action lawsuit was verified. The abuser who victimized the 12-year-old boy was not only verified but allegedly sold videos of the abuse for $5 to $20 through Pornhub’s revenue-sharing program, according to the civil complaint filed by the boy’s mother. Some of the videos remained for sale for almost seven months and attracted more than 180,000 views and 1,100 subscribers — meaning that Aylo profited directly from the abuse, the complaint alleges.

**The internet is terrestrial. It’s people going into buildings every day and making decisions.** — Justine Li, cyber exploitation victims’ advocate

Tina and other victims described to ICIJ obsessively searching their names on Google, agonizing over the continued presence of their abuse online. For them, one of the most important interventions is the erasure of their names and intimate images from the internet. But it is often relief that remains out of reach.

Justine Li, a sex trafficking survivor herself, launched the National Center for Victims of Internet and Cyber Exploitation last year to offer victims a single portal through which they can manage takedown requests.

Li’s strategy is to target what she calls the “internet iceberg.” At the top are the operators of the sites that host the illegal content. Below the surface are other companies — hosting providers, payment processors and advertising networks — that keep the sites operational and making money.

She works to identify all of the companies that are supporting a site hosting illegal content, along with their contact information — pressure points on an industry that she says is too callous to act.

Li tells victims she will never stop fighting to get their images off the internet. But she is careful not to offer them any guarantees. “We can’t promise that things will come down,” she said. “That’s not the reality.”

Even failure, Li believes, has a purpose. She can use evidence that the options for victims are not working to push for new laws.

“People think the internet is this celestial realm where laws cannot be enforced,” Li said. “No, the internet is terrestrial. It’s people going into buildings every day and making decisions. … There’s a lot we can do that’s still on the table.”

items.articleBody:
### 🚀 SpaceX catches returning Starship for first time

[↗ Primärquelle: foxbusiness.com](https://www.foxbusiness.com/technology/spacex-makes-history-starship-spacecraft-caught-launch-tower-first-time)

- SpaceX pulled off a first on Saturday, catching its Starship spacecraft with the giant mechanical arms at its Texas launch tower as the vehicle returned from orbit, a key step toward building a fully reusable rocket.
- The catch happened on the 15th test flight, roughly 22 hours after Starship lifted off on Friday, during which the spacecraft released 26 Starlink satellites and circled Earth 14 times before landing back at Starbase.
- SpaceX missed its goal of recovering both stages after the Super Heavy booster's engines shut off early during descent and it exploded over the Gulf, an outcome engineers are now investigating.

### 📣 165,000 sign letter to reinstate Nvidia's Huang

[↗ Primärquelle: cnbc.com](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/16/nvidia-jensen-huang-return-tech.html)

- Elon Musk and more than 165,000 people have signed an open letter urging Nvidia's board to reinstate Jensen Huang as chief, just days after he resigned from the trillion-dollar chip company he co-founded.
- The signatories include Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, Y Combinator's Garry Tan, and Uber co-founder Travis Kalanick, while over 7,500 of them identified as Nvidia employees, about 18% of the company's workforce.
- Huang resigned on Thursday after revelations of extramarital affairs, one with a woman accused of spying for China, and US treasury secretary Scott Bessent said on Sunday that Nvidia needs an outside chief and a "dramatic shake-up".

### 💥 Amazon loses 40 satellites in failed rocket launch

[↗ Primärquelle: geekwire.com](https://www.geekwire.com/2026/amazon-loses-40-leo-satellites-as-ula-vulcan-launch-failure-deals-setback-to-tech-giants-starlink-rival/)

- A United Launch Alliance Vulcan rocket failed about 10 minutes after liftoff yesterday, destroying 40 satellites for Amazon Leo, the Seattle company's planned rival to SpaceX's Starlink internet service.
- The failure, ULA's first total mission loss since 2006, came during the Centaur upper stage burn, after the solid boosters and Blue Origin BE-4 first-stage engines appeared to work normally; ULA says it doesn't yet know the cause.
- Vulcan was the first of 38 launches Amazon bought and is meant to carry over 1,500 satellites; the mishap delays the next Vulcan flight, though an Ariane 6 launch with 36 satellites is targeted for November 23.

### 🇺🇸 US blocks China from renting AI chips abroad

[↗ Primärquelle: techcrunch.com](https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/16/us-tightens-ai-chip-export-controls-to-deter-chinese-companies-from-accessing-compute-remotely/)

- The Trump administration is rolling out new export controls today to stop Chinese firms from sidestepping U.S. restrictions by remotely tapping AI chips and data centers located in other countries.
- Under the interim rule, the Commerce Department will require export licenses for any data center or network able to supply more than 12 million TPP, roughly 750 Nvidia H100 or H200 chips, that may serve companies in China.
- The rule targets the D:5 group of 22 embargoed countries, adds licensing for chip transfers to Malaysia, Singapore, Indonesia, Thailand and Brazil, and scraps the Biden-era AI Diffusion Rule from January 2025.

### 🍎 Apple launches study on trust in health AI

- Apple has started a year-long study, built with the clinical AI tool OpenEvidence, to learn what makes Americans trust health AI chatbots and how well people understand the answers those tools give.
- Up to 200,000 US users can join the Apple Health AI Usage Study, rating responses in monthly surveys, though participants must be at least 21 and own an iPhone 15 Pro or newer running iOS 26.
- Study data won't train AI models, and queries are made anonymous before going to a third-party cloud, where OpenEvidence deletes them after 24 hours; people may also choose to share HealthKit data like sleep and heart rate.

### 🧠 Alibaba's Qwen4-Max cuts task costs 60%

[↗ Primärquelle: csoonline.com](https://www.csoonline.com/article/4249015/alibaba-touts-62-lower-task-costs-with-qwen4-max-adds-cyber-safeguards-2.html)

- Alibaba's new flagship model Qwen4-Max completes professional tasks for 62% less than the version before it, dropping the average cost from $4.43 to $1.67 per task, according to the company's own Work360 benchmark.
- The 2.4-trillion-parameter model activates about 71 billion parameters per token, down from 95 billion, and uses 35% fewer tokens, with new prices of $1.50 per million input tokens and $4.50 per million output tokens.
- Alibaba also filtered training data to keep defensive cybersecurity skills while removing offensive ones, but analysts warned the split needs outside testing and said buyers should measure the real cost of finished tasks, not token prices.

items.articleBody:
Willem de Kooning, “Yellow River” (1958) (image courtesy Christie’s Images Ltd. 2026)

Looking to cash in on marquee week in New York, the Whitney Museum of American Art has consigned a Willem de Kooning painting from its collection to Christie's for its 20th-century evening sale tomorrow, November 17. Once a promised gift to the museum, de Kooning's “Yellow River” (1958) is expected to fetch up to $18 million.

The practice of museum deaccessioning has long been a subject of [controversy](https://hyperallergic.com/the-deaccessioning-debate-in-museums/). In 2022, the Association of Art Museum Directors (AAMD) [loosened its policy](https://hyperallergic.com/museums-can-use-deaccessioning-funds-for-collection-care-aamd-says/) to allow institutions to apply funds from the sale of deaccessioned art toward the “direct care” of their collections.

A lot description for “Yellow River” on Christie's website notes that the proceeds will benefit the Whitney's collection. The Whitney has not yet responded to *Hyperallergic* 's request for comment, but a museum spokesperson told [Artnet News](https://news.artnet.com/market/whitney-deaccession-de-kooning-auction-christies-2835978?ref=hyperallergic.com) that deaccessioning is “a component of the Whitney’s collections strategic plan, allowing the museum to thoughtfully evaluate and refine its holdings in support of its long-term collection priorities.”

The de Kooning painting going under that hammer had a rooted connection to the Whitney before it was bequeathed to the museum in 2023. Postwar art collector, attorney, and museum trustee David Solinger, who would go on to become the museum's first president beyond the Whitney family in 1966, purchased the work from de Kooning's sold-out exhibition at Sidney Janis Gallery in 1959.

“Yellow River” emerged from a series of “highway" paintings representing the artist's shift from cacophonous urban compositions to more airy landscapes, designating the freeway as a conduit connecting New York City to the Hudson River Valley and Long Island's South Fork. In vibrant warm yellow, earthy brown tones, and stretches of deep blue, de Kooning's decisive gestures direct viewers across overlapping paths and visual rest stops throughout the canvas.

“I love to be on those highways,” de Kooning said to British critic and curator David Sylvester about the expansive roads during a *BBC* interview in 1960. “And they are really not very pretty, but the big embankments and the shoulders of the roads and the curves are flawless.”

“Yellow River” hung at the foot of Solinger's bed for some time, serving as a testament to Solinger's fascination with the artist. His wife, Betty Ann Besch Solinger, took ownership of the work after Solinger passed in 1996, and in 2011, she designated the work as a promised gift to the Whitney in honor of her late husband. It officially entered the Whitney's holdings in 2023, the same year that the museum [deaccessioned seven works](https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/whitney-museum-american-art-edward-hopper-deaccession-1234664840/?ref=hyperallergic.com), including an Edward Hopper landscape, and sent them to auction to benefit the collection.

items.articleBody:
**We’re a few weeks into a reboot of our [Beautiful News](https://informationisbeautiful.net/beautifulnews/) project from a few years ago. Refreshed. Revitalised. Re-visualised.**

Once more, every day for a year, we are surfacing and visualising some of the **amazing, progressive and positive things happening around the world**. Trends and events and innovations we can’t always see when fixated on the negativity of the news.

We’ve spruced and updated some of data-visualisations from the original collection, as well as adding 160 more stories to be released over the next weeks, months, year and beyond!

Every graphic is of course underpinned by [open datasets](https://informationisbeautiful.net/beautifulnews/data/) to support full **evidence-based optimism.**

Swing by and join [our weekly newsletter](https://beautifulnews.myflodesk.com/newsletter) or daily on [the website](https://informationisbeautiful.net/beautifulnews/), or social channels of your choosing: [Instagram](https://www.instagram.com/beautifulnews.daily), [Twitter/X](https://x.com/beautiful__news), [Facebook](https://www.facebook.com/beautifulnewsdaily/), [Threads](https://www.threads.com/@beautifulnews.daily).

## Some of my favourite graphics and stories so far

» [34 Countries Now Generate 80% or More of Their Electricity from Renewables](https://informationisbeautiful.net/beautifulnews/3021-countries-electricity-renewables/)

» [Tons of new vaccines are in the pipeline](https://informationisbeautiful.net/beautifulnews/524-new-vaccines/)

» [Polio is very nearly wiped out](https://informationisbeautiful.net/beautifulnews/3037-polio-wiped-out/)

» [The Cost of Renewable Energy is Plunging](https://informationisbeautiful.net/beautifulnews/586-cost-renewables-falling/)

» [The EU Gender Pay Gap is (slowly) Decreasing](https://informationisbeautiful.net/beautifulnews/3030-eu-gender-pay-gap/)

» [Everyone, Everywhere, is Living Longer](https://informationisbeautiful.net/beautifulnews/41-everyone-everywhere-is-living-longer/)

**Towards a more nutritious information diet…**

David

items.articleBody:
### “Creative fantasy, because it is mainly trying to do something else … may open your hoard and let all the locked things fly away like cage-birds.”

*“I do not believe that I have ever written a children’s book,”* the great [Maurice Sendak](https://www.themarginalian.org/tag/maurice-sendak/) once said [in an interview](https://www.themarginalian.org/2011/12/29/tateshorts-maurice-sendak/). *“I don’t write for children,”* he [told Colbert](https://www.themarginalian.org/2012/05/09/grim-colberty-tales-maurice-sendak/). *“I write — and somebody says, ‘That’s for children!’”* This sentiment — the idea that designating certain types of literature as “children’s” is a choice entirely arbitrary and entirely made by adults — has since been [eloquently echoed by Neil Gaiman](http://explore.noodle.org/post/64133968491/i-dont-think-there-is-such-a-thing-as-a-bad-book), but isn’t, in fact, a new idea.

On March 8, 1939, **J.R.R. Tolkien** (January 3, 1892–September 2, 1973), celebrated as one of the greatest fantasy writers in history, gave a lecture titled “Fairy Stories,” eventually adapted into an essay retitled “On Fairy-Stories” and included in the appendix to [Tales from the Perilous Realm](http://www.amazon.com/Tales-Perilous-Realm-J-R-R-Tolkien/dp/0547154119/?tag=braipick-20) ([public library](http://www.worldcat.org/title/tales-from-the-perilous-realm/oclc/243480382&referer=brief_results)). At the crux of his argument, which explores the nature of fantasy and the cultural role of fairy tales, is the same profound conviction that there is no such thing as writing “for children.”

One of Tolkien’s a href=”https://www.themarginalian.org/2011/11/01/art-of-the-hobbit/”>original illustrations for the first edition of *The Hobbit*, 1936

Tolkien begins at the beginning, by defining what a fairy tale is:

> A “fairy-story” is one which touches on or uses Faerie, whatever its own main purpose may be: satire, adventure, morality, fantasy. Faerie itself may perhaps most nearly be translated by Magic — but it is magic of a peculiar mood and power, at the furthest pole from the vulgar devices of the laborious, scientific, magician. There is one proviso: if there is any satire present in the tale, one thing must not be made fun of, the magic itself. That must in that story be taken seriously, neither laughed at nor explained away.

Illustration for Hans Christian Andersen’s ‘The Snow Queen’ by Katharine Beverley and Elizabeth Ellender, 1929. Click image for details.

He then explores the relationship between fairy tales and language, denouncing Max Müller’s view of mythology as a “disease of language”:

> Mythology is not a disease at all, though it may like all human things become diseased. You might as well say that thinking is a disease of the mind. It would be more near the truth to say that languages, especially modern European languages, are a disease of mythology. But Language cannot, all the same, be dismissed. The incarnate mind, the tongue, and the tale are in our world coeval. The human mind, endowed with the powers of generalization and abstraction, sees not only green-grass, discriminating it from other things (and finding it fair to look upon), but sees that it is green as well as being grass. But how powerful, how stimulating to the very faculty that produced it, was the invention of the adjective: no spell or incantation in Faerie is more potent. And that is not surprising: such incantations might indeed be said to be only another view of adjectives, a part of speech in a mythical grammar. The mind that thought of light, heavy, grey, yellow, still, swift, also conceived of magic that would make heavy things light and able to fly, turn grey lead into yellow gold, and the still rock into a swift water. If it could do the one, it could do the other; it inevitably did both. When we can take green from grass, blue from heaven, and red from blood, we have already an enchanter’s power — upon one plane; and the desire to wield that power in the world external to our minds awakes. It does not follow that we shall use that power well upon any plane. We may put a deadly green upon a man’s face and produce a horror; we may make the rare and terrible blue moon to shine; or we may cause woods to spring with silver leaves and rams to wear fleeces of gold, and put hot fire into the belly of the cold worm. But in such “fantasy,” as it is called, new form is made; Faerie begins; Man becomes a sub-creator.

Illustration for Hans Christian Andersen’s ‘The Darning Needle’ by Maurice Sendak, 1959. Click image for details.

Like Sendak and Gaiman, Tolkien insists that fairy tales aren’t inherently “for” children but that we, as adults, simply decide that they are, based on a series of misconceptions about both the nature of this literature and the nature of children:

> It is usually assumed that children are the natural or the specially appropriate audience for fairy-stories. In describing a fairy-story which they think adults might possibly read for their own entertainment, reviewers frequently indulge in such waggeries as: “this book is for children from the ages of six to sixty.” But I have never yet seen the puff of a new motor-model that began thus: “this toy will amuse infants from seventeen to seventy”; though that to my mind would be much more appropriate. Is there any essential connexion between children and fairy-stories? Is there any call for comment, if an adult reads them for himself? Reads them as tales, that is, not studies them as curios. Adults are allowed to collect and study anything, even old theatre programmes or paper bags.
> […]
> Among those who still have enough wisdom not to think fairy-stories pernicious, the common opinion seems to be that there is a natural connexion between the minds of children and fairy-stories, of the same order as the connexion between children’s bodies and milk. I think this is an error; at best an error of false sentiment, and one that is therefore most often made by those who, for whatever private reason (such as childlessness), tend to think of children as a special kind of creature, almost a different race, rather than as normal, if immature, members of a particular family, and of the human family at large.

Illustration for Howard Pyle’s ‘The Swan Maiden’ by Alice and Martin Provensen, 1971. Click image for details.

He argues, instead, that the stereotype of fairy tales being associated with children and native to their world is “an accident of our domestic history”:

> Fairy-stories have in the modern lettered world been relegated to the “nursery,” as shabby or old-fashioned furniture is relegated to the play-room, primarily because the adults do not want it, and do not mind if it is misused. It is not the choice of the children which decides this. Children as a class—except in a common lack of experience they are not one—neither like fairy-stories more, nor understand them better than adults do; and no more than they like many other things. They are young and growing, and normally have keen appetites, so the fairy-stories as a rule go down well enough. But in fact only some children, and some adults, have any special taste for them; and when they have it, it is not exclusive, nor even necessarily dominant. It is a taste, too, that would not appear, I think, very early in childhood without artificial stimulus; it is certainly one that does not decrease but increases with age, if it is innate.
> […]
> The nursery and schoolroom are merely given such tastes and glimpses of the adult thing as seem fit for them in adult opinion (often much mistaken). Any one of these things would, if left altogether in the nursery, become gravely impaired. So would a beautiful table, a good picture, or a useful machine (such as a microscope), be defaced or broken, if it were left long unregarded in a schoolroom. Fairy-stories banished in this way, cut off from a full adult art, would in the end be ruined; indeed in so far as they have been so banished, they have been ruined.

Tolkien then moves on to the subject of fantasy, a frequently misunderstood faculty of the imagination.

> The mental power of image-making is one thing, or aspect; and it should appropriately be called Imagination. The perception of the image, the grasp of its implications, and the control, which are necessary to a successful expression, may vary in vividness and strength: but this is a difference of degree in Imagination, not a difference in kind. The achievement of the expression, which gives (or seems to give) “the inner consistency of reality,” is indeed another thing, or aspect, needing another name: Art, the operative link between Imagination and the final result, Sub-creation. For my present purpose I require a word which shall embrace both the Sub- creative Art in itself and a quality of strangeness and wonder in the Expression, derived from the Image: a quality essential to fairy-story. I propose, therefore, to arrogate to myself the powers of Humpty-Dumpty, and to use Fantasy for this purpose: in a sense, that is, which combines with its older and higher use as an equivalent of Imagination the derived notions of “unreality” (that is, of unlikeness to the Primary World), of freedom from the domination of observed “fact,” in short of the fantastic. I am thus not only aware but glad of the etymological and semantic connexions of fantasy with fantastic: with images of things that are not only “not actually present,” but which are indeed not to be found in our primary world at all, or are generally believed not to be found there. But while admitting that, I do not assent to the depreciative tone. That the images are of things not in the primary world (if that indeed is possible) is a virtue, not a vice. Fantasy (in this sense) is, I think, not a lower but a higher form of Art, indeed the most nearly pure form, and so (when achieved) the most potent.

Illustration for the fairy tales of Hans Christian Andersen by Japanese artist Takeo Takei, 1928. Click image for details.

He goes on to argue that, despite the many misconceptions that envelop it, fantasy is far more challenging an art than nonfiction, for it necessitates the creation of an elaborate, immersive world from scratch, without the crutch of reality:

> Fantasy … is difficult to achieve. Fantasy may be, as I think, not less but more sub-creative; but at any rate it is found in practice that “the inner consistency of reality” is more difficult to produce, the more unlike are the images and the rearrangements of primary material to the actual arrangements of the Primary World. It is easier to produce this kind of “reality” with more “sober” material. Fantasy thus, too often, remains undeveloped; it is and has been used frivolously, or only half-seriously, or merely for decoration: it remains merely “fanciful.” Anyone inheriting the fantastic device of human language can say the green sun. Many can then imagine or picture it. But that is not enough — though it may already be a more potent thing than many a “thumbnail sketch” or “transcript of life” that receives literary praise.
> To make a Secondary World inside which the green sun will be credible, commanding Secondary Belief, will probably require labour and thought, and will certainly demand a special skill, a kind of elvish craft. Few attempt such difficult tasks. But when they are attempted and in any degree accomplished then we have a rare achievement of Art: indeed narrative art, story-making in its primary and most potent mode.

Scandinavian fairy tale illustration by Kay Nielsen, 1914. Click image for details.

Tolkien makes a curious argument about the oil-and-water relationship between fantasy and drama, managing to slip in a subtle dig at none other than The Bard:

> In human art Fantasy is a thing best left to words, to true literature. … It is a misfortune that Drama, an art fundamentally distinct from Literature, should so commonly be considered together with it, or as a branch of it. Among these misfortunes we may reckon the depreciation of Fantasy. For in part at least this depreciation is due to the natural desire of critics to cry up the forms of literature or “imagination” that they themselves, innately or by training, prefer. And criticism in a country that has produced so great a Drama, and possesses the works of William Shakespeare, tends to be far too dramatic. But Drama is naturally hostile to Fantasy. Fantasy, even of the simplest kind, hardly ever succeeds in Drama, when that is presented as it should be, visibly and audibly acted. Fantastic forms are not to be counterfeited. Men dressed up as talking animals may achieve buffoonery or mimicry, but they do not achieve Fantasy....
> In Macbeth, when it is read, I find the witches tolerable: they have a narrative function and some hint of dark significance; though they are vulgarized, poor things of their kind. They are almost intolerable in the play. They would be quite intolerable, if I were not fortified by some memory of them as they are in the story as read. I am told that I should feel differently if I had the mind of the period, with its witch-hunts and witch-trials. But that is to say: if I regarded the witches as possible, indeed likely, in the Primary World; in other words, if they ceased to be “Fantasy.” That argument concedes the point. To be dissolved, or to be degraded, is the likely fate of Fantasy when a dramatist tries to use it, even such a dramatist as Shakespeare. Macbeth is indeed a work by a playwright who ought, at least on this occasion, to have written a story, if he had the skill or patience for that art.

Illustration for The Fairy Tales of E. E. Cummings by John Eaton, 1965. Click image for details.

Another misconception Tolkien debunks — speaking to Susan Sontag’s conviction that [polarities only rob life of dimension](https://www.themarginalian.org/2013/12/03/susan-sontag-stereotypes-polarities/) — is the notion that the fantastical is somehow diametrically opposed to the rational:

> Fantasy is a natural human activity. It certainly does not destroy or even insult Reason; and it does not either blunt the appetite for, nor obscure the perception of, scientific verity. On the contrary. The keener and the clearer is the reason, the better fantasy will it make. If men were ever in a state in which they did not want to know or could not perceive truth (facts or evidence), then Fantasy would languish until they were cured. If they ever get into that state (it would not seem at all impossible), Fantasy will perish, and become Morbid Delusion.
> For creative Fantasy is founded upon the hard recognition that things are so in the world as it appears under the sun; on a recognition of fact, but not a slavery to it. So upon logic was founded the nonsense that displays itself in the tales and rhymes of Lewis Carroll. If men really could not distinguish between frogs and men, fairy-stories about frog-kings would not have arisen.

Returning to his notion of the Secondary World driven by Secondary Belief, Tolkien contributes to [history’s greatest definitions of art](https://www.themarginalian.org/2012/06/22/what-is-art/):

> Art is the human process that produces by the way (it is not its only or ultimate object) Secondary Belief.

Illustration for Seamus MacManus’s ‘Feather O’ My Wing’ by Alice and Martin Provensen, 1971. Click image for details.

He then adds to [the psychological functions of art](https://www.themarginalian.org/2013/10/25/art-as-therapy-alain-de-botton-john-armstrong/) by exploring the psychological functions of fairy tales, chief among which is their capacity for rebooting our [chronically blunted attention](https://www.themarginalian.org/2013/10/25/art-as-therapy-alain-de-botton-john-armstrong/):

> Recovery (which includes return and renewal of health) is a re-gaining—regaining of a clear view. I do not say “seeing things as they are” and involve myself with the philosophers, though I might venture to say “seeing things as we are (or were) meant to see them”—as things apart from ourselves. We need, in any case, to clean our windows; so that the things seen clearly may be freed from the drab blur of triteness or familiarity—from possessiveness. Of all faces those of our familiares are the ones both most difficult to play fantastic tricks with, and most difficult really to see with fresh attention, perceiving their likeness and unlikeness: that they are faces, and yet unique faces. This triteness is really the penalty of “appropriation”: the things that are trite, or (in a bad sense) familiar, are the things that we have appropriated, legally or mentally. We say we know them. They have become like the things which once attracted us by their glitter, or their colour, or their shape, and we laid hands on them, and then locked them in our hoard, acquired them, and acquiring ceased to look at them.
> […]
> Creative fantasy, because it is mainly trying to do something else (make something new), may open your hoard and let all the locked things fly away like cage-birds.

Illustration for The Fairy Tales of E. E. Cummings by John Eaton, 1965. Click image for details.

The full fifteen-page essay, as well as the rest of [Tales from the Perilous Realm](http://www.amazon.com/Tales-Perilous-Realm-J-R-R-Tolkien/dp/0547154119/?tag=braipick-20), is well worth a read. Complement it with [Tolkien’s little-known illustrations](https://www.themarginalian.org/2011/11/01/art-of-the-hobbit/) for the first edition of *The Hobbit*.

### donating = loving

For seventeen years, I have been spending hundreds of hours and thousands of dollars each month composing *The Marginalian* (which [bore the outgrown name Brain Pickings](https://www.themarginalian.org/2021/10/22/brain-pickings-becoming-the-marginalian/) for its first fifteen years). It has remained free and ad-free and alive thanks to patronage from readers. I have no staff, no interns, no assistant — a thoroughly one-woman labor of love that is also my life and my livelihood. If this labor makes your own life more livable in any way, please consider lending a helping hand with a [donation](https://www.themarginalian.org/donate/). Your support makes all the difference.

### newsletter

*The Marginalian* has a free weekly newsletter. It comes out on Sundays and offers the week’s most inspiring reading. Here’s [what to expect](https://mailchi.mp/brainpickings/janna-levin-rebecca-elson-anne-lamott-james-gleick). Like? [Sign up.](https://www.themarginalian.org/newsletter/)
