## Kidnapped Teen Rescued After Using ‘Among Us’ Video Game Chat to Secretly Ask Another Player for Help

[↗ Primärquelle: mymodernmet.com](https://mymodernmet.com/teenager-rescued-using-among-us/)

[Video games](https://mymodernmet.com/worlds-largest-game-tetris/) get a bad rap. Though they’re often looked down upon as a distracting outlet for young adults, despite the creativity and problem-solving that’s often involved, it turns out they can also be essential in saving lives. Teenager Kylie Arellano was rescued after allegedly being held captive for more than 500 days, thanks to an unlikely connection she made with another player through the popular online game [Among Us](https://www.innersloth.com/games/among-us/).

An online multiplayer game that uses social deduction to seek out the “impostors” in a group of players, *Among Us* rose in popularity during the COVID-19 pandemic and served as a great way for friends to keep in touch during quarantine. For Arellano, who went missing from her Utah home in May 2025, the game’s ability to connect players with one another ultimately became a crucial part of her rescue.

Arellano was allegedly held captive in the basement of 39-year-old Adam Hunter Harmel’s home in Huntington, Oregon. Although Harmel had reportedly taken away her original phone, he eventually gave her another device that could connect to Wi-Fi but had no cellular service. This allowed Arellano to play *Among Us* and, more importantly, communicate with other people through the game.

In mid-October 2026, Arellano began talking with another player she met while playing *Among Us*. Their conversations eventually moved to another social media platform, where she revealed her identity and explained that she was being held against her will. The other player (a child) told their mother, who contacted the FBI.

On November 1, the FBI monitored a video call between Arellano and the other player’s family, during which she shared details about her situation. Authorities were able to rescue her from the Oregon home that same day. Harmel was subsequently charged with transporting a minor across state lines with the intent to engage in criminal sexual activity.

While *Among Us* was originally designed as a way for players to work together and identify hidden impostors, for Arellano, it became something much more important. The game provided her with a way to reach the outside world, ultimately helping bring her captivity to an end.

## Teenager Kylie Arellano was rescued from her kidnapper by communicating her need for help in the online game Among Us.

Please consider [giving a donation to FactCheck.org](https://giving.aws.cloud.upenn.edu/fund?fastStart=simpleForm&program=ANS&fund=602014) during our annual end-of-year fundraising drive, which starts today and lasts until the end of the year.

We’re setting a goal of $75,000 in contributions to help fund our work in 2027, as the Democrats take control of Congress and presidential contenders start vying for attention.

Competing claims from President Donald Trump and a Democratic Congress, as well as open presidential primaries for both parties, will surely keep us busy.

Not that we weren’t already.

If you read our midterms coverage of toss-up Senate races and campaign talking points, please consider a donation.

If you appreciate that we keep tabs on the claims the president and leaders in Congress make, sorting fact from fiction, please consider a donation.

If you’re a fan of our SciCheck project, which debunks falsehoods and explains what we know about scientific topics, such as vaccination and climate change, please consider a donation.

We’re a nonprofit project of the University of Pennsylvania’s Annenberg Public Policy Center. We don’t keep our content behind any paywalls, and we don’t accept advertising. We avoid even the appearance of a conflict of interest by not accepting contributions from unions, partisan organizations or political advocacy groups.

Our funding overwhelmingly comes from an APPC endowment, which includes funding from the Annenberg Foundation and the Annenberg School for Communication Trust at the University of Pennsylvania. But individual donations have helped to keep us operating, 23 years after we first started holding politicians accountable for the claims they make. Thank you for your support.

If you’d like to make a gift, credit card donations may be made through [our “Donate” page](https://giving.aws.cloud.upenn.edu/fund?fastStart=simpleForm&program=ANS&fund=602014).

If you prefer to give by check, send to: FactCheck.org, Annenberg Public Policy Center, P.O. Box 58100, Philadelphia, PA 19102. Checks can be made payable to “The Trustees of the University of Pennsylvania” with a note in the memo field indicating the donation is for FactCheck.org.

The University of Pennsylvania is a 501(c)(3) organization, and your contribution is deductible from U.S. federal income taxes to the full extent allowed by law.

Our policy is to disclose the identity of anyone who contributes $5,000 or more in a given year. Most of the contributions we receive are much smaller — $25 or less. You can read our annual and quarterly [financial reports](https://factcheck.us5.list-manage.com/track/click?u=17a60fa3d47b33b686b744ff5&id=e457de04e7&e=6f09f3a9d3) on our website.

We greatly appreciate your support.

items.articleBody: Single neurons can perform complex exclusive-or (XOR) computation which is conventionally thought to need multilayer networks, yet the biophysical mechanisms and the robustness of such computations under stochastic synaptic drive remain unclear. Using biologically realistic modeling, we demonstrate that dendritic depolarization block provides a universal and robust mechanism for XOR-like computation. Voltage-gated calcium channels enable a non-monotonic input-output relationship: moderate asynchronous drive evokes spiking, whereas excessive drive induces a sustained plateau that suppresses output, naturally implementing XOR logic computation. This computation is strictly gated by temporal distribution of synaptic inputs rather than spatial distribution; the XOR-like response is robust across diverse dendritic configurations but collapses under synchronous activation. Dendritic depolarization block propagates to the soma via dendrite-soma coupling, establishing a neuronal output-limiting mechanism. The computation is highly efficient, leveraging a frequency–synapse-count trade-off to ensure stable logic operations across varying levels of background activity. Cross-morphological validation confirms that XOR-like computation is morphology-independent, representing a generalizable biophysical principle of neural information processing.

items.articleBody:
The [Department of Philosophy](https://www.trincoll.edu/philosophy/) at Trinity College in Hartford, Connecticut has adopted a new policy banning students from using AI in classrooms or for coursework.

The policy states:

> Deliberate use of AI in philosophy courses, in any capacity and for any purpose, is forbidden. This includes, but is not limited to: using AI to summarize reading assignments; using it to “brainstorm” and come up with ideas; as a research tool for presentations or oral examinations, or as a tool to aid in the writing or editing process (e.g., research, drafting, editing, compiling a bibliography, etc.). Philosophy is focused on cultivating our abilities to think, to read, to write, to speak, to reason, and to live ethically. AI undermines all of these goals.

According to the *[Trinity Tripod](https://trinitytripod.com/news/philosophy-department-becomes-first-at-trinity-to-ban-ai/)*, the faculty vote in favor of the policy was unanimous.

[Shane Ewegen](https://internet3.trincoll.edu/facProfiles/Default.aspx?fid=1479899), a professor in the Philosophy Department, told the student newspaper:

> Ultimately, we wanted to avoid having six different AI policies that contradict each other. So after having some discussion about our attitudes and understandings of AI—and the dangers that it’s posing to thinking and the ability of students to think—we were able, after some back and forth, to agree upon a single blanket policy, which simply forbids the use of AI in any capacity in any philosophy course.

Professor Ewegen has also led a faculty movement to encourage Trinity College to [divest from AI software companies](https://trinitytripod.com/news/professors-call-on-trinity-to-divest-from-artificial-intelligence/), which resulted in a [letter](https://trinitytripod.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/AI-Divestment-Letter.pdf) from faculty to the college administration about AI policy, the *Tripod* reports:

> “We, the below signatories, request that Trinity College immediately and thoroughly divest from AI companies and the software companies that support them. The technology is too fresh, too unregulated, too dangerous and too unpredictable to safely integrate into the college’s operations. Currently, the support of such technology is incommensurate with Trinity’s stated commitments to fostering intellectual and ethical growth, to protecting the environment, and to building and protecting a safe future for the next generation,” the letter reads. It also requests that the administration take “a firm, immediate, and public stance against such technologies” until they have been deemed safe for academic use, “if [such a] time ever comes,” and that future AI policy be subject to faculty vote.

Regarding the Philosophy Department ban on AI use, Ewegen says, “So part of what our hope was, at least my hope, in adopting a policy like this, is to get more faculty and more students, and hopefully more administrators, to think a bit more critically about the role that this technology is playing in academia right now and the distinct threats that it poses.”

Have other philosophy departments enacted similar policies?

**UPDATE:** I asked if the policy also applied to faculty. Professor Ewegen wrote, “Currently, at least, it applies to all of the philosophy faculty. (None of us use AI or want to.) Were we to hire new faculty members, we would not impose it upon them; instead, we would talk with them about their position *vis a vis* AI and invite them to revise the policy with us.”

items.articleBody: SHP2, a protein tyrosine phosphatase (PTP) crucial in Ras-MAPK signaling, is associated with various human congenital diseases and cancers. Here, we show that the catalytically inactive Shp2C459S mutation results in communicating hydrocephalus, similar to the catalytically activating Shp2E76K and Mek1DD mutants. Unlike previous mutants, however, Shp2C459S/+ mutation uniquely affects ciliary development rather than neurogenesis, leading to structural abnormalities in cilia and impaired ciliary motility. Differential scanning fluorimetry suggested that SHP2C459S, SHP2E76K, and SHP2C459S/E76K mutations all induce an open SHP2 conformation, but only SHP2C459S leads to aberrant GAB1 phosphorylation in cells expressing wild-type SHP2. Consistent with this distinct signaling profile, brain ventricular tissues from Shp2C459S/+ mice exhibit elevated GAB1 and AKT phosphorylation despite normal ERK and STAT3 activities, implicating dysregulated PI3K–AKT signaling in the pathogenesis of hydrocephalus. Importantly, pharmacological inhibition of PI3K markedly rescues ciliogenesis defects and alleviates hydrocephalus in mutant mice. Furthermore, the allosteric SHP2 inhibitor SHP099 increases the thermal stability of SHP2C459S protein, consistent with a shift toward a closed state, and ameliorates hydrocephalus in Shp2C459S/+ mice. These findings suggest that, in this engineered mouse model, Shp2-associated hydrocephalus is driven by conformational changes rather than altered catalytic activity. Our results underscore the therapeutic potential of conformation-specific allosteric inhibitors in targeting both catalytically active and inactive SHP2 mutants.

items.subtitle: The Detroit ghettotech pioneer on overthinking, Record Time and why he’s still waiting for his dues, thirty years in.
items.feedText: Detroit’s Filthiest is one of the original ghettotech pioneers. Born in Iraq and raised in Detroit, Julian Shamou started DJing as a teenager in the mid-1990s and has since produced more than 100 tracks under a string of aliases, including Digitek, DJ Nasty and 313 Bass Mechanics. In 2015 Disclosure sampled his 2002 track ‘Pass Out’ on ‘Bang That’, and he has gone on to release on Defected, Moveltraxx and his own Motor City Electro Company label. Thirty years in, he’s still making music and still waiting for his…
items.articleBody:
*The Detroit ghettotech pioneer on overthinking, Record Time and why he’s still waiting for his dues, thirty years in.*

Detroit’s Filthiest is one of the original ghettotech pioneers. Born in Iraq and raised in Detroit, Julian Shamou started DJing as a teenager in the mid-1990s and has since produced more than 100 tracks under a string of aliases, including Digitek, DJ Nasty and 313 Bass Mechanics.

In 2015 Disclosure sampled his 2002 track [‘Pass Out’](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=R5nszd0O0hE) on ‘Bang That’, and he has gone on to release on Defected, Moveltraxx and his own Motor City Electro Company label. Thirty years in, he’s still making music and still waiting for his dues. We asked him to tackle our Q&A.

## What’s your greatest fear?

That I lose my passion for making music.

## What trait do you most deplore in yourself?

I always overthink things. My mind never stops racing.

## If you weren’t making or playing music, what would you be doing?

Something creative, probably marketing or advertising.

Detroit's Filthiest

## What was your most embarrassing moment?

Telling someone who I am and them telling me they’d never heard of me.

## What would your superpower be?

Invincibility.

## If you could bring something extinct back to life, what would you choose?

My father, who passed away in 2021.

## What was the last lie that you told?

I lie to myself all the time.

## Must-visit record store or studio?

Record Time, when they were still around.

## How do you like to finish your sets?

It’s been so long I can’t remember what I used to do.

## If not yourself, who would you most like to be?

Jesus Christ.

## When’s the last time you changed your mind about something significant?

Asking for help when I’m down.

## What sparks your creativity?

The challenge of doing something I haven’t done before.

## Who’s the next name everyone should know?

Detroit’s Filthiest.

## Favourite sportsperson ever?

Zlatan Ibrahimović.

## What’s been your best moment in a club or studio?

In 1996, going to a club in Detroit and seeing 2,000 people dancing to my song live on the radio.

## Who taught or helped you the most?

I was fortunate to meet a few people who taught me a lot.

## Worst job you’ve ever had?

Working at Chrysler as a supervisor.

## Which track do you wish you’d made?

None.

## What’s the worst track or set you’ve ever done?

Too many to name.

## How do you organise your music collection for your sets?

[quote align=right text="The music industry has become a spectacle. It’s not about the music but about how many followers you have"]

## Recommend a film.

*The Godfather*.

## Recommend a book.

*The Bible*.

## Favourite internet clip of all time, music or otherwise?

[Back up, Terry.](https://youtube.com/shorts/I6F-yGpqbx4)

## Who or what deserves more credit?

Me! I’ve been doing this for 30 years, and I don’t get the credit I deserve.

## What gets too much hype?

Whatever the latest fad is.

## What can’t you stop doing?

Making music.

## What’s your guilty pleasure?

Cigarettes.

## What’s your biggest frustration in the music world?

The music industry has become a spectacle. It’s not about the music but about how many followers you have.

## Favourite label and why?

Twilight 76. They put out my first record.

**Find Detroit’s Filthiest on [Instagram](https://www.instagram.com/djnasty313/?hl=en) or [Bandcamp](https://mcec.bandcamp.com/).**

items.articleBody:
Early in the coronavirus pandemic, as I sat at home channeling my anxiety into publishing daily essays on this newsletter (a streak I kept up for six weeks), I had a revelation: none of my advice, ideas, or systems really mattered if you didn’t build them on the foundation of a meaningful life.

Who cares about losing yourself to social media or letting work devolve into email whack-a-mole if the world outside of your phone and inbox isn’t that compelling?

On March 17th of that infamous spring, I captured these notions in an essay titled [“The Deep Life: Some Notes.”](https://calnewport.com/the-deep-life-some-notes/) As I explained:

> “To me, the deep life is about focusing with energetic intention on things that really matter — in work, at home, and in your soul — and not wasting too much attention on things that don’t.”

In the weeks that followed, I wrote [several](https://calnewport.com/on-productivity-and-the-deep-life/) [more](https://calnewport.com/work-and-the-deep-life/) [essays](https://calnewport.com/more-on-cultivating-a-deep-life-mindset/) on pursuing the deep life. Later that summer, when I [launched my podcast](https://podcasts.apple.com/at/podcast/ep-1-my-new-task-system-deep-work-with-kids-and/id1515786216?i=1000476077409), I dedicated a third of my inaugural episode to this concept. (My original tagline: “a show about work, technology, and the deep life.”)

Two years later, as we returned to normalcy, I convinced my publisher to let me try writing a book on these ideas. I then set out on the long, patient process of elaborating and developing my thoughts into a coherent system.

All of this brings me to the current moment. I’m proud to finally announce that my next book, [ The Deep Life: A Structured Approach ](https://www.thedeeplife.com/), is now [available for pre-order](https://www.thedeeplife.com/).

*The Deep Life* brings together and significantly expands on my past thinking on this topic. It presents a step-by-step approach to achieving the intentional-living goal laid out in that original March 2020 post. It’s less an idea book than a classic-style advice guide, offering practical details on how to identify what resonates, refine it into an actionable vision, and then move toward that vision systematically.

My friend [Oliver Burkeman](https://www.amazon.com/Four-Thousand-Weeks-Management-Mortals/dp/1250849357/), to whom I sent a proof copy of the manuscript, had the following reaction:

> “It’s hard to imagine a more timely or inspiring manual for a life of sanity and accomplishment, or a better guide than Cal Newport. This is a profound book, but just as importantly, a profoundly practical one: it shows that depth is something we can do.”

I believe that this book is *the* *key* that unlocks the value in almost everything else I write about. If you’ve followed me this far, then you need to read this one.

With this in mind, here are some of the places where you can pre-order the book right now in advance of its March publication date:

- [Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/Deep-Life-Structured-Approach/dp/0593544870/)
- [Barnes & Noble](https://www.barnesandnoble.com/w/the-deep-life-cal-newport/1150475131)
- [Bookshop.org](https://bookshop.org/p/books/the-deep-life-tk-cal-newport/e0548b9282c19397)
- [Amazon UK](https://www.amazon.co.uk/Deep-Life-Structured-Approach-Meaning/dp/024184777X?maas=maas_adg_5415FAC779DFD0467C9715278D881B94_afap_abs&ref_=aa_maas&tag=maas&th=1)
- [Waterstones ](https://www.waterstones.com/book/9780241847770?sv1=affiliate&sv_campaign_id=117976&awc=3787_1794332947_70780920f00186c80dbe28e794089d47&utm_source=117976&utm_medium=affiliate&utm_campaign=Penguin+Books)

You can also pre-order [ a signed copy ](https://peoplesbooktakoma.com/product/the-deep-life/) from my local bookstore here in Takoma Park.

If you think you’ll eventually read this one, **I humbly ask that you consider pre-ordering it**, as these early purchases signal to booksellers that the book is worth stocking on their shelves. (And if you do pre-order, hold on to your digital receipt, as I’m working on a pretty cool bonus that I’ll announce soon.)

Most of all, however, I want to extend my thanks for your support over all these years as I’ve explored these fundamental ideas. We only get one life. *Why not make it deep?*

items.articleBody:
Introduction
Lassa fever is a priority disease in Nigeria. Periodic evaluation of its surveillance systems is essential to strengthen performance and ensure efficient use of limited public health resources. This study evaluated the Lassa fever surveillance system in Edo State, Nigeria.
Methods
The evaluation followed the 2001 CDC guidelines and used a cross-sectional mixed-methods design. We reviewed statewide surveillance data from 2024–2025 and selected respondents from 26 health facilities across 15 of the 18 (83.3%) local government areas (LGAs), as well as from the state surveillance unit and WHO. We assessed the surveillance system’s evolution, structure, and resource availability. We analyzed surveillance data by person, place, and time and audited the data for completeness, errors, outliers, and timeliness. Case investigation forms, laboratory forms, and line lists were reviewed to assess variable usefulness and identify data gaps. Structured questionnaires were administered to 30 stakeholders, including 11 key informant interviews, to assess the system’s usefulness, simplicity, acceptability, timeliness, and representativeness. Quantitative data were analyzed descriptively, while qualitative data were analyzed thematically.
Results
Since 1969, the Lassa fever surveillance system has evolved from sporadic paper-based reporting to a coordinated, case-based digital platform. Structurally, the system operates from the community to the national level and relies on human resources, surveillance tools, and physical and digital infrastructure. Between 2024 and 2025, 6,296 suspected Lassa fever cases were reported, of which 461 (7.3%) were confirmed, among which 69 (15.0%) died. Three LGAs, Etsako West (204; 44.3%), Esan West (95; 20.6%), and Esan North-East (79; 17.1%), accounted for 378 (82%) confirmed cases. Cases occurred year-round, with increased frequency between November and April. Data completeness exceeded 95%, while errors and outliers were both below 5%. Timeliness assessment indicated that 88.5% of laboratory results were returned within 48 hours and 91.2% of cases were notified within three days. However, 18.7% of cases presented to facilities later than one week after symptom onset. Overall, the system demonstrated strong performance across the assessed attributes. Key operational challenges included delayed or incomplete laboratory feedback, high clinician workload, reliance on Disease Surveillance and Notification Officers to complete forms, and defective electronic devices. Identified data gaps included an unclear definition of the variable “department,” incomplete documentation of “date of death” and “department,” and the absence of a “cause of death” variable.
Conclusion
The Lassa fever surveillance system in Edo State is simple, acceptable, and effective for case detection and outbreak monitoring. Addressing identified operational and data quality gaps could further strengthen system efficiency, sustainability, and public health impact.

*“Hey, I’ll get a job…when I hear the true call.” — Slacker (1990)*

About 10 years ago, I met a woman who worked as a mid-level software engineer at Facebook. She didn’t work on machine learning, but just for fun, she read a bunch of papers and got into the subject as a hobby. Later, in the pandemic, she quit her boring corporate job and spent a few years unemployed, contemplating the meaning of life. She made her own clothes, learned ballet, made cute Instagram videos, dyed her hair, and went to a bunch of hackathons (almost all of which she won).

Also in the late 2010s, I knew a man who had been a promising software engineer and data scientist, and before that a top performer on the International Math Olympiad. But when I met him, he was spending a few years unemployed — crashing at his girlfriend’s place, playing Hearthstone (and becoming one of the top-ranked players in the world), learning to skateboard, going on hippie retreats, and contemplating the meaning of life.

Both of those people are billionaires now. They are Sasha Sheng and Diogo Almeida, two of the three founders of [TypeSafe AI](https://techcrunch.com/2026/10/09/the-maker-of-non-text-ai-model-jev-valued-at-7-5b-just-weeks-after-launch/), a startup that was recently valued at $7.5 billion (and in which I invested a small amount of money). TypeSafe invented Jev, an all-new kind of AI model that bypasses human language, and so is able to make decisions much faster and more cheaply than Claude or GPT. It was an incredibly creative idea — one that the big labs are [racing to copy](https://techcrunch.com/2026/09/30/openais-jev-clone-could-help-the-frontier-lab-stop-its-swarming-agents/) — and it took an incredible amount of hard work to realize.1

Sasha’s and Diogo’s roundabout, seemingly improbable route to stunning success is actually more common in the tech world than you might think. Steve Jobs is the most famous example — he famously dropped out of college, not to start Apple, but to do psychedelic drugs, crash on friends’ floors, immerse himself in hippie spirituality, live on a commune, and travel around India looking for enlightenment before eventually inventing the personal computer and becoming the most beloved tech icon in American history. Jack Dorsey, Larry Ellison, and Mitch Kapor all had their own periods of aimlessness.

Nor is this sort of life path confined to the tech world. History is full of examples of people who looked lackadaisical until they suddenly rose to greatness:

- [Ulysses S. Grant](https://www.ericfoner.com/reviews/110212washpost.html) drank copiously, worked as a clerk in a leather store, engaged in various failed business ventures and was said to lack ambition — until one day he rejoined the military and became the most successful and important military commander in the entire Civil War, as well as President of the United States.
- [Charles Darwin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Darwin#Early_life_and_education) neglected his medical studies and turned in a mediocre performance on his exams at Cambridge, routinely going hunting and riding instead of studying, before becoming a naturalist, signing up for an ocean voyage, and inventing the theory of evolution.
- [James Cameron](https://achievement.org/achiever/james-cameron/) was a college dropout and a truck driver, before seeing Star Wars prompted him to quit his job and teach himself how to make movies, ultimately becoming one of the most commercially successful movie directors of all time. ([Kevin Smith](https://blogs.iu.edu/establishingshot/2017/08/10/no-one-is-supposed-to-be-anywhere-at-anytime-the-irreverence-and-freedoms-of-clerks/) had a similar path to success, except his inspiration was the movie Slacker.)
- [Haruki Murakami](https://stephenphelan.co.uk/articles/murakami/) ran a jazz bar and had little ambition, before suddenly deciding to become a novelist, and eventually becoming one of the most celebrated writers in the world.

I like to tell these stories because they demonstrate an approach to success in life that I believe is overlooked and deserves more recognition. I call it “bumbition”.

“Bumbition” is an obvious portmanteau of “bum” and “ambition”. In general, we think of ambitious people and slackers as polar opposites — ambitious people work hard, set goals for themselves, and are constantly motivated, while slackers drift aimlessly, laze around, or fail to apply their talents. A lot of our culture is oriented around pushing young people to be ambitious instead of turning into bums.

Bumbition, however, defies placement on the ambitious/bum spectrum. It exhibits elements of both. For a significant portion of their life, a bumbitious person doesn’t strive hard, or apply themselves to definite goals…until a clear and compelling opportunity presents itself. When that opportunity to do something really interesting or impactful *does* come up, the bumbitious person is quick to recognize it, and works very hard to exploit it.

The key here is that bumbition is not simply *intermittent ambition*. It’s a fundamentally different approach to life — it has different goals and motivations, and when it succeeds, it succeeds for different reasons.

An ambitious person is always working toward a set of goals — either those they define for themselves, or those defined by the people around them. Those goals could include:

- “Make partner by age 30”
- “Start a unicorn startup”
- “Get a tenured job at a top 10 research university”
- “Make a hundred million dollars”
- “Conquer Central Asia”

…And so on. The purpose of achieving those goals — the motivation that drives ambitious people — is to feel a sense of personal success.

A bumbitious person does *not* automatically have a goal at all times,2 because they tend to be motivated less by the need to feel successful than by the desire to do something intrinsically *interesting or worthwhile*. Such projects are inherently in short supply, in part because what constitutes an inherently “interesting” or “worthwhile” project is highly subjective. An ambitious person can always identify some brass ring that would make them feel like a success; a bumbitious person will often wait years or even decades before finding that one magical opportunity or life calling.

In fact, this is bumbition’s inherent limitation. Sitting around waiting for the right opportunity to present itself is a highly uncertain, risky endeavor. There’s always the possibility that it won’t come until you’re old, or that it’ll come but you’ll fail to see it in time.

The other problem with bumbition is that waiting around for the right opportunity comes with a bunch of costs and risks. Your technical skills and work ethic can decay over time. You can get caught up in life’s various stumbling blocks — bad relationships, drug addictions, depression, etc.

But bumbition also has some big advantages over the ambitious life. One is that *ambition can keep people overly busy*. If you’re the kind of person that always has to be working toward a goal, and you can’t find a truly great project to work on, you’ll end up working on a modest or mediocre one. If Steve Jobs had become distracted by getting a perfect GPA at Reed College, he might never have had time to start Apple. If Ulysses S. Grant had focused on owning his own leather goods store, he might not have leapt at the chance to join the U.S. Army. If Sasha Sheng had focused on climbing the corporate ladder at Meta, she wouldn’t have founded TypeSafe.

Paul Graham talks about this in his essay “[How to Do Great Work](https://www.paulgraham.com/greatwork.html)”:

> Ambition comes in two forms, one that precedes interest in the subject and one that grows out of it. Most people who do great work have a mix, and the more you have of the former, the harder it will be to decide what to do…The trouble with planning is that it only works for achievements you can describe in advance. You can win a gold medal or get rich by deciding to as a child and then tenaciously pursuing that goal, but you can't discover natural selection that way.

In his book *Zero to One*, Peter Thiel — who I’d classify as an ambitious rather than a bumbitious person — recounts a vivid example of how his ambition almost prevented him from becoming a tech titan:

> [A]fter a conventionally successful undergraduate career, I enrolled at Stanford Law School, where I competed even harder for the standard badges of success. The highest prize in a law student’s world is…a Supreme Court clerkship…I was invited to interview for clerkships with Justices Kennedy and Scalia. My meetings with the Justices went well. I was so close to winning this last competition. If only I got the clerkship, I thought, I would be set for life. But I didn’t.
> At the time, I was devastated…With the benefit of hindsight…winning that ultimate competition would have changed my life for the worse…Had I actually clerked on the Supreme Court, I probably would have spent my entire career taking depositions or drafting other people’s business deals instead of creating anything new.

Nor is this bumbition’s only advantage. The “bum” phase — the time spent traveling in India, or working at a convenience store, or playing Hearthstone on a couch — isn’t just a holding pattern. The seeming aimlessness of this period of life can serve several important functions that facilitate rapid success once a good opportunity gets spotted.

First, and most importantly, time away from the grind of constant striving allows people to *broaden their perspective*. A lot of unique and original ideas come from *recombinant innovation* — from combining insights and perspectives from vastly different fields.3 Even something as simple as changing the context of your surroundings can [improve creativity](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19210055/). For an intelligent person with a restless mind, the “bum” phase of life leads to a lot of play and exploration that can end up sparking novel ideas. Here’s [a fun example](https://www.asc.ohio-state.edu/kilcup.1/262/feynman.html) from Richard Feynman:

> I used to enjoy doing physics. Why did I enjoy it? I used to play with it. I used to do whatever I felt like doing - it didn't have to do with whether it was important for the development of nuclear physics, but whether it was interesting and amusing for me to play with…Now that I am burned out…I'm going to play with physics, whenever I want to…
> Within a week I was in the cafeteria and some guy, fooling around, throws a plate in the air. As the plate went up in the air I saw it wobble…I had nothing to do, so I start to figure out the motion of the rotating plate…I went on to work out equations of wobbles. Then I thought about how electron orbits start to move in relativity. Then there's the Dirac Equation in electrodynamics. And then quantum electrodynamics.

Steve Jobs’ study of calligraphy, during his hippie period, [famously helped him](https://news.stanford.edu/stories/2005/06/youve-got-find-love-jobs-says) to think about what would make the letters on a personal computer look beautiful to the eye.

A related advantage is that the “bum” phase also allows people to develop their *interests*. [Paul Graham talks about](https://www.paulgraham.com/greatwork.html) how “excited curiosity” will often lead people to their most important life’s work. Bumbitious people aren’t just waiting around; they’re *playing* around, actively searching for something that sparks their interest. In contrast, if you’re constantly grinding away, it can be hard to develop that curiosity.

A “bum” phase also gives people a chance to broaden their *human networks*. When you’re working hard towards a goal, you usually don’t have much time to meet a lot of people outside work — i.e., outside your narrow current field of endeavor. Ambitious people are *always* working toward a goal, and thus get relatively little time to go meet interesting people from other walks of life. But the “bum” phase gives bumbitious people time to meet all kinds of folks. This can lead to hearing about radical new opportunities, getting insights from other fields, or even meeting useful partners for a new venture.

Broadly speaking, the “bum” phase of bumbition serves two purposes. It represents *waiting and exploration time*, as people patiently wait for the big opportunity that will define their career. But it also represents *personal development time*, either deliberate or unconscious, that helps bumbitious people to better see the big opportunities when they come along.

Now, I don’t mean to claim that bumbition is better than ambition, or vice versa — either in terms of personal success, or in terms of changing the world. Among the greats of any field — politics, business, academia, literature — you can find plenty of examples of both ambitious and bumbitious people.

But I think our society *underemphasizes bumming*. We have a tendency to frown on people who spend years unemployed, neglecting work in order to play video games or make Instagram videos. We assume that these people are being lazy or squandering their potential, and we tell them to get back to the grind and make something of themselves. Other societies, of course, tend to be even worse on this score — China treats its slacker generation as [a national security threat](https://thediplomat.com/2026/05/why-china-treats-lying-flat-as-a-national-security-threat/).

In the AI age, this could be even more consequential. AI algorithms are consummate hill-climbers — set them to a task, give them some data, and they’ll be more ambitious than the hardest-working Stanford law student. In a world of abundant AI, *setting AI on the right goals* will be an increasingly central human task. Figuring out the right goals requires exploration, unique perspectives, and curiosity — all things that bumbition facilitates. We should be teaching our young people to be more bumbitious.

At the same time, we should remember that being bumbitious isn’t just a matter of sitting around on the couch. Just because you tell yourself you’re waiting to hear the true call doesn’t mean you’ll actually hear it when it comes. You have to actually want to do something great — whatever that means to you — and you have to be ready to work incredibly hard for years when that something presents itself. Bumbition isn’t the same as ambition, but it also isn’t the same as being a lifelong bum.

Diogo’s rise as an AI researcher didn’t start with TypeSafe. He was also a key researcher for OpenAI, creating key features of the original ChatGPT and GPT-4 that kicked off the AI boom.

There are actually a few bumbitious people who somehow manage to always find huge passion projects — David Holz of Midjourney comes to mind.

items.articleBody: Stroke is a leading cause of death and disability worldwide, and ischemic stroke is its most common subtype. Cerebral ischemia-reperfusion injury (CIRI) involves oxidative stress, inflammation and blood-brain barrier disruption, making mitochondrial quality control and regulated cell death important targets for mechanistic research. This review examines mitophagy, ferroptosis and emerging evidence for cuproptosis within a mitochondrial framework, while distinguishing established mechanisms from model-dependent findings and untested hypotheses. Ferroptosis is supported by substantial experimental evidence in stroke. Thrombin–ACSL4 signaling and NCOA4-mediated ferritinophagy can promote lipid peroxidation and iron dysregulation, respectively, whereas the system Xc–/GSH/GPX4 axis counteracts ferroptosis by supporting lipid-hydroperoxide detoxification. FSP1–CoQ10, DHODH–CoQ10 and GCH1–BH4 provide additional antioxidant mechanisms, although their stroke-specific contributions remain incompletely defined. Mitophagy operates through PINK1/Parkin, BNIP3/NIX and FUNDC1 pathways and can have protective or detrimental effects depending on pathway activity, lysosomal function and mitochondrial reserve. Experimental studies support selected connections between mitochondrial quality control and ferroptosis, but proposed competition between mitophagy and ferritinophagy remains unverified. Itaconate-mediated GPX4 alkylation and IRG1-associated mitophagy represent distinct mechanisms reported in different hemorrhagic stroke models. In contrast, copper-homeostasis changes and FDX1 perturbation in ischemic models do not establish the complete cuproptosis mechanism. We therefore distinguish copper/FDX1 intervention evidence, bioinformatic associations and contextual mechanistic clues. A possible mitophagy–cuproptosis tolerance relationship is presented as a testable hypothesis whose selective recognition signals, receptors and quantitative requirements remain unresolved. Therapeutic timing is discussed conceptually without fixed intervention windows. Future progress requires mechanism-specific assays, time-resolved mitophagic flux measurements, genetic rescue and validation across relevant brain cell types and clinically representative models.
